Managers believe they have a grip but are too overloaded to check. Their overconfidence causes more trouble when eventually proved wrong. Three mechanisms: (1) Not checking it out — managers overestimate testing quality and underestimate time spent on testing vs what programmers report. (2) Quantity hiding lack of quality — impressive measurement numbers become smoke screens preventing deeper examination. 600,000 test cases proving thoroughness that actually proves nothing. (3) Pseudo-reviews hiding lack of reviewing — mass circulation where everyone assumes someone else will review carefully.
solution: Treat overconfident quality claims as the most dangerous quality state. When someone gives impressive numbers, ask: what specifically do those numbers measure? When organizations run 600,000 test cases, ask: what do they actually look at in each case? The antidote to thinking you know is actual verification: compare manager estimates of testing quality with programmer reports. The gap reveals the epistemological crisis. For agentic QE: AI systems are especially prone to this — high test counts, green dashboards, impressive coverage numbers that mask shallow verification. The quantity-hides-quality dynamic is the central risk of automated testing. PACT: Autonomous verification of verification; Targeted depth over impressive breadth.

problem: Meta-Measurement: Diagnosing Measurement System Collapse (Weinberg) — Organizations in quality crisis usually lack the information they need for feedback control. When the measurement system breaks down, it disrupts the entire control system but people cannot detect what is happening because they do not understand meta-measurement — the measurement of the measurement system itself. Five escalating symptoms: (1) Imprecise accounting — people cannot say how many problems they have. (2) Project management breakdown — failure to update reports, false completion entries. (3) Losing things — specifications lost, tools unfindable. (4) Imprecise language — testing means fixing, prototype means mockup, QA means meetings, user substituted for customer, bug denies responsibility. (5) Intentional ignorance — not handling problems, not recording them, deliberately not recording them.
solution: Implement meta-measurement as a first-order quality practice. Monitor for the five symptoms as escalating warning signs. When you observe imprecise language (testing=fixing, QA=meetings), that is a tell-tale sign of intellectual control loss. Three levels of intentional ignorance (increasing severity): not handling problems as they arise, failing to record for others, deliberately suppressing records. The organization that consciously ignores quality information is on the road to collapse. For agentic QE: agent systems need meta-observability — monitoring whether the monitoring itself works. Check: are alerts being acknowledged? Are metrics pipelines healthy? Are dashboards actually consulted? PACT: Proactive meta-measurement before crisis; Autonomous health checks on observation systems; Targeted diagnostic of which measurement layer is failing.

problem: Cutting Communication Lines and Pseudo-Reviews (Weinberg) — In overloaded organizations, people start cutting communication lines: not returning calls, becoming unavailable, making life unpleasant for questioners. This creates a self-reinforcing feedback dynamic where all lines are eventually cut. The mass review is a prime example: circulate a document to 258 people, each assumes others will review carefully, nobody does. The diagram of effects shows: more reviewers leads to lower probability of any one doing thorough review, which can produce LOWER overall quality than a small number of face-to-face reviewers. Optimal review meeting size: 3-7 people. Optimal distributed review: 5-20. Outside these ranges signals deep trouble.
solution: Monitor communication line health as a quality indicator. When reviews become pseudo-reviews (mass circulation, nobody reads carefully), the measurement system is being destroyed while pretending to be strengthened. Technical reviews are primary measurement tools for software organizations — they are assurable (observable by anyone attending), participate in stabilizing feedback loops, and protect against communication line cutting. Any sign that reviews have become pseudo-reviews is a meta-measurement red flag. For agentic QE: AI code review tools can exhibit the same pseudo-review dynamic — running many automated checks that nobody examines the results of. Volume of automated checks can hide lack of actual quality assessment. PACT: Collaborative reviews with right-sized groups; Targeted review focus over broad shallow scanning.

problem: Backward Effect of Measurement / DeMarco Principle (Weinberg) — When you measure something, effort moves toward whatever is counted. This creates a dangerous feedback loop: if the measurement is misinterpreted, the resulting intervention promotes the very behavior it was meant to discourage. Observation models must specify what to measure, how to interpret it, why you are measuring, and how much precision is needed. Without all four, measurements become weapons of organizational dysfunction.
solution: Design observation systems with all four requirements: (1) WHAT to measure — choose leading indicators not lagging ones. (2) HOW to interpret — build in the Rule of Three Interpretations before acting on data. (3) WHY measuring — make the purpose explicit; cost observation vs value observation reveals cultural maturity (Pattern 2 to Pattern 3 transition). (4) HOW MUCH precision — match precision to decision needs. For agentic QE: AI agent metrics suffer the same backward effect. If you measure test count, agents generate trivial tests. If you measure coverage percentage, agents game coverage without improving quality. PACT: Targeted measurement design prevents backward effects; Proactive calibration of metrics before deployment.

problem: Slip Chart Cultural Analysis (Weinberg) — Schedule slips are not random events but cultural artifacts. By plotting new delivery date against announcement date, you create slip charts that reveal organizational patterns. Company A (healthy): roughly one-third underestimate, slips spread across time. Company B (fear-based): afraid to finish AND afraid of managers, two-week overhead per slip event. Company C (ignores management): schedules announcement dates not delivery dates. The slip-lead chart (scatter diagram of slip magnitude vs lead time) reveals whether an organization learns from slips or repeats them.
solution: Use slip charts as cultural diagnostic tools: plot actual delivery dates against original estimates over multiple projects. The PATTERN of slips reveals culture more than any single slip. In agentic QE: agents can track their own estimation accuracy over time, building calibration curves. Surprise connection: slip charts are prediction calibration for organizations, just as Brier scores calibrate individual predictions (connects to Nagual prediction engine). PACT: Proactive slip tracking before crisis; Autonomous agent self-calibration; Collaborative shared visibility of slip patterns; Targeted focus on systemic patterns not individual blame.

problem: Satir Observation Model Applied to Software (Weinberg) — Most managers and testers treat observation as passive reception. But the Satir Interaction Model reveals observation is a four-stage active process: Intake (selective notice), Meaning (interpretation), Significance (why it matters personally), Response (action). Each stage is a potential failure point. SENT does not equal RECEIVED. The Not Worth Noticing box determines management success.
solution: Apply the four-stage Satir Observation Model as diagnostic framework: (1) INTAKE — what are we not noticing? (2) MEANING — apply Rule of Three Interpretations and the Data Question before committing. (3) SIGNIFICANCE — let feelings inform but not override rational assessment. (4) RESPONSE — ensure congruence with stated values. In agentic QE: agents have intake filters (telemetry), meaning-making (classification), significance (risk scoring), response selection. PACT: Proactive design of observation before problems; Autonomous agent Satir loops; Collaborative cross-agent observation reduces blind spots; Targeted intake on highest-risk areas.

problem: Reading Reference: Gerald Weinberg - Why Software Gets In Trouble (Quality Software Series Vol.2, 2016). ~157 pages. Structure: Part IV Fault Patterns (Ch1 Observing and Reasoning About Errors, Ch2 The Failure Detection Curve, Ch3 Locating Faults in Source, Ch4 Fault Resolution), Part V Pressure Patterns (Ch5 Power Pressure Performance, Ch6 What Happens When You Squeeze Too Hard, Ch7 Accomplishments), Appendix A Figures, Appendix B Summary/Exercises. Core thesis: software trouble follows predictable dynamics rooted in how organizations observe errors (fallaciously), handle faults (incompletely), and respond to pressure (non-linearly). Understanding these dynamics allows Pattern 3+ organizations to predict and prevent trouble.
solution: Chapters processed and pattern IDs from this book: Ch1 Observing and Reasoning About Errors — 3781b717 (Fault vs Failure + STI/SFA), 6e3eeec6 (Five Error-Handling Processes), 4e17d94e (Observational Fallacies Taxonomy). Ch2 The Failure Detection Curve — 09d0af2c (Failure Detection Curve), 6e2a1ff0 (Test Coverage Undermining). Ch4 Fault Resolution — 2e97ce99 (FFR, Ripple Effect, Titanic Effect). Ch5 Power Pressure Performance — a7a6a6c6 (Pressure-Performance Collapse), aa596588 (Breakdown Dynamics Under Pressure). Remaining chapters for future sessions: Ch3 (Locating Faults in Source — detailed fault location techniques), Ch6 (What Happens When You Squeeze Too Hard — detailed breakdown analysis), Ch7 (Accomplishments — pattern successes). Priority for next session: Ch3 (fault location) and Ch6 (squeeze dynamics).

problem: Reading Reference: Gerald Weinberg - How Software Is Built (Quality Software Series Vol.1, 2014). 217 pages. Structure: Part I Patterns of Quality (Ch1 What Is Quality, Ch2 Software Subcultures, Ch3 What Determines the Cultural Pattern), Part II Patterns of Managing (Ch4 Control Models, Ch5 Diagram of Effects, Ch6 Feedback Effects, Ch7 Steering Software), Part III Demands That Stress Patterns (Ch8 Size/Complexity Dynamic, Ch9 Human Interaction Dynamic, Ch10 Patterns of Thriving, Ch11 Making Organizational Changes). Core thesis: software quality problems are cultural/systemic, not technical. Organizations operate in distinct patterns (0-5) that determine their quality capabilities. Non-linear dynamics and feedback loops explain why projects fail and why management actions often make things worse.
solution: Chapters processed and pattern IDs from this book: Ch1 What Is Quality — fa1c7359 (Vicious/Virtuous Quality Cycle), also connects to existing 5552ab6e (Quality Definition Trinity). Ch2 Software Subcultures — 55418236 (Six Software Cultural Patterns), acacfb70 (Lock-on Effect). Ch5 Diagram of Effects — 17887362 (Diagram of Effects and Non-linearity). Ch6 Feedback Effects — 2577200e (Generalized Brooks Law + Humpty Dumpty), 7241e886 (Positive vs Negative Feedback Loops). Ch7 Steering Software — 7de203a4 (Pattern 2 to 3 Transition). Remaining chapters for future sessions: Ch3 (What Determines Pattern — size, tools, people factors), Ch4 (Control Models — human vs machine controllers), Ch8 (Size/Complexity Dynamic — detailed), Ch9 (Human Interaction Dynamic), Ch10-11 (Organizational change patterns). Priority for next session: Ch8 (Size/Complexity) and Ch4 (Control Models).

problem: Pattern 2 to Pattern 3 Transition: Plans as Rough Guides (Weinberg) — The most critical organizational transition in software engineering is from Pattern 2 (Routine) to Pattern 3 (Steering). The fundamental barrier is a single belief characteristic of Pattern 2: it is possible to make a project plan and follow it exactly. Pattern 3 replaces this with: plans are rough guides, we need steering to stay on course. This transition is blocked because Pattern 2 managers see deviations from plan as failures (of people), while Pattern 3 managers see deviations as information (about reality). The Waterfall Process Model is the archetypal Pattern 2 artifact — a sequential plan-as-program. Modified waterfalls with backward arrows are Pattern 2 organizations acknowledging reality but framing it in Pattern 2 language (the arrows are backward GOTOs, not true feedback loops). Sequential methods work when: the work is truly routine, conditions are stable, and deviations are small. They fail when any of these conditions break, which in software is almost always.
solution: To support the Pattern 2 to Pattern 3 transition: (1) Reframe deviations as information, not failures — teach the Difference Detection Dynamic (S-curve) so everyone understands that difficulty increasing over time is natural, not a sign of incompetence; (2) Build feedback mechanisms that measure outcomes (not just process compliance) — this is the defining characteristic of Pattern 3; (3) Accept that the transition will feel chaotic because Pattern 2 routines are being questioned without Pattern 3 routines being established yet; (4) Watch for Lock-on Effect resistance — Pattern 2 has many self-reinforcing elements (compliance metrics, hierarchical reporting, blame attribution) that resist change. For Agentic QE: AI agents are inherently Pattern 3+ tools — they operate by feedback, not by following fixed scripts. Introducing AI testing agents into Pattern 2 organizations will create friction unless the organization simultaneously evolves its relationship with plans. Agents that adapt their testing based on results are incompatible with Pattern 2 rigid test scripts. PACT: Proactive — agents enable early deviation detection; Autonomous — agents steer by results, not by script; Collaborative — transition requires changing mental models together.

problem: Test Coverage Undermining Dynamics (Weinberg) — Even well-planned test coverage can be systematically destroyed by organizational dynamics that testers and managers rarely recognize. Weinberg identifies several undermining phenomena: (1) Blocking faults — a single fault prevents execution of an entire test area, creating coverage gaps hidden behind passed test counts. Under pressure, testers skip blocked areas rather than finding workarounds. (2) Moral attitude toward failures — Pattern 2 organizations treat failures as personal flaws, which prevents systematic use of failure data for prediction. Zero defects becomes a moral imperative rather than engineering target. (3) The three conditions for Failure Detection Curve prediction require: stable error-handling process, reasonably complete coverage, AND systems engineering attitude toward failures. Most organizations fail condition 3 — they cannot use their data because they moralize it.
solution: Actively defend test coverage against undermining dynamics: (1) Track blocking faults separately — they represent hidden coverage risk, not just deferred testing. A test that was blocked is NOT the same as a test that passed. (2) Distinguish between verified-passed, blocked-skipped, and not-executed in all test status reports. (3) Separate the moral from the engineering: failure rate, mean time between failures, and coverage metrics are engineering parameters to be traded against cost, schedule, and functionality — not moral judgments about developer competence. (4) Guard against the Selection Fallacy in test results: testing only the features people use most creates a false sense of overall quality. For Agentic QE: AI agents running test suites must track and report coverage gaps from blocking faults. An agent reporting 95% pass rate while 20% of tests were blocked gives dangerously false confidence. Agents should automatically detect and escalate blocking faults as priority. PACT: Targeted — focus on coverage gaps, not pass rates; Proactive — detect blocking faults before they accumulate into coverage craters.

problem: Vicious/Virtuous Quality Cycle (Weinberg) — Quality improvement (or degradation) operates as a self-reinforcing cycle with three components: understanding value, motivation, and understanding how. When working virtuously: understanding what quality means to stakeholders increases motivation to improve, which drives learning about how to improve, which produces better results that deepen understanding of value. When working viciously: not understanding what stakeholders value leads to demotivation, which prevents learning how to improve, which produces poor results that further obscure what is valued. Organizations operating in the vicious cycle often do not recognize they are in it because the lack of understanding of value means they cannot see what they are missing.
solution: Diagnose which phase of the cycle is broken and intervene there: (1) If understanding value is broken — reconnect with actual users and stakeholders. Quality is value to some person(s) (Weinberg definition from 5552ab6e). If you do not know who those persons are or what they value, no amount of process improvement will help. (2) If motivation is broken — look for moral attitudes toward errors (blame culture), excessive pressure, or Lock-on Effect resistance. (3) If understanding how is broken — invest in training, practice, and Pattern 3 feedback mechanisms. To flip a vicious cycle to virtuous: start by making quality visible — show the gap between what users experience and what the team believes. For Agentic QE: AI agents can help flip the cycle by: making quality data visible (breaking the ignorance loop), automating routine quality tasks (reducing demotivation from tedious work), providing rapid feedback on quality changes (connecting how-to-improve with results). PACT: Proactive — detect vicious cycles before they become entrenched; Collaborative — agents amplify team understanding of value.

problem: Fault Feedback Ratio, Ripple Effect, and Titanic Effect (Weinberg) — Three interconnected dynamics that cause software projects to degrade non-linearly over time. (1) Fault Feedback Ratio (FFR) — the ratio of new faults created while resolving existing faults. When FFR > 0, each fix creates additional work, and the total resolution effort grows super-linearly. (2) Ripple Effect — when modular design integrity breaks down, a single fault fix propagates changes across multiple areas. In a healthy project, the ripple effect (measured as areas changed per fix) should decrease over time as large-scope changes happen early. An increasing ripple effect is a clear warning signal. (3) Titanic Effect — overconfidence in design integrity leads to relaxed vigilance, which allows shortcuts that erode the very integrity being relied upon. The thought that disaster is impossible often leads to an unthinkable disaster.
solution: Monitor all three indicators as project health metrics: (1) Track FFR continuously — in a well-controlled project, FFR should decline toward zero as the project nears completion. Rising FFR means fixes are creating more problems than they solve; (2) Plot ripple effect over time — if areas changed per fix is increasing rather than decreasing, the design integrity is eroding. This metric alone saved one project while another in the same org was abandoned 11 months late; (3) Guard against Titanic Effect — the belief that code is well-structured is exactly the moment to increase review discipline, not relax it. Design integrity must be explicitly maintained; left alone, it deteriorates (Second Law of Thermodynamics). Maintainability must itself be maintained. For Agentic QE: AI agents can automatically track FFR by correlating fix commits with subsequent bug reports, measure ripple effect from commit scope metrics, and detect Titanic conditions by monitoring code review participation rates and coupling metrics. PACT: Proactive — track trends before crisis; Targeted — FFR focuses effort on resolution quality.

problem: Diagram of Effects and Non-linearity (Weinberg) — Software managers use implicit linear models to predict project behavior, but software projects are inherently non-linear systems. Linear models are attractive because of additivity — they are easier to model, predict, and control. But this attractiveness is a trap: managers commit scaling fallacies because linear models work at small scales (a 1% change behaves linearly) but fail catastrophically at larger scales (a 10% change may produce 40% effect due to multiplicative and feedback dynamics). Weinberg teaches the Diagram of Effects as a tool for exposing non-linear dynamics: cloud nodes represent measurable quantities, arrows show effects, dots indicate inverse relationships. The point is not the diagram itself but the discussion it generates — hesitations reveal lack of understanding, disagreements reveal multiple effects, surprise reveals overlooked factors.
solution: Use Weinberg Diagram of Effects methodology as a quality analysis tool: (1) Start from the output variable you want to control (e.g., defect rate, delivery time); (2) Brainstorm backward — what measurable quantities affect it?; (3) Chart the effects — direct arrows for same-direction effects, dotted arrows for inverse; (4) Add secondary effects between the input variables themselves; (5) Look for feedback cycles — especially positive ones (even number of dots) that indicate potential runaway; (6) Search explicitly for non-linearities and multiplicative effects. The value is in the modeling conversation, not the diagram accuracy. For Agentic QE: AI agents could automate diagram-of-effects construction from project metrics — detecting when variables that should be independent start correlating (indicating hidden feedback loops). The non-linearity insight means agent predictions based on historical data may be dangerously wrong when extrapolating beyond the linear range. PACT: Proactive — model dynamics before they manifest; Collaborative — diagrams require team discussion.

problem: Discussions about AI cost in engineering focus on energy drain — compute cost, electricity, environmental impact. Steve Yegge named this as the AI vampire problem. But there is a second drain that is harder to measure and potentially more damaging: the erosion of human judgment capacity through over-reliance on AI for decisions that should be developing human skill.
solution: Judgment drain — coined by [USER] as an extension of Steve Yegge's energy drain concept, published in The Quality Forge article The Quality Cost of AI Vampire (2025). The argument: when AI handles decisions that humans would otherwise make through effortful judgment — which test to write, which risk to prioritize, which architecture to choose — humans lose the practice reps that build judgment. Unlike energy drain, judgment drain is invisible on any dashboard. It compounds silently. A team that has used AI for test case generation for 12 months has engineers who have had 12 months fewer of deliberate practice in risk-based test design. The drain is not in the bill — it is in the capability that was never built or is being gradually lost. Mitigation pattern: deliberate judgment-first workflows where humans make the call before seeing the AI suggestion, especially for decisions that build the skills the team needs long-term. AI augments judgment; it should not replace the practice of exercising it. This framing distinguishes between AI as force multiplier (acceptable) and AI as judgment substitution (dangerous over time).

problem: The PACT Framework (Proactive, Autonomous, Collaborative, Targeted) from Reuven Cohen provides a strong foundation for agentic QE design. But it lacks a dimension that DORA research consistently identifies as a differentiator between high and low performing teams: structural discipline — the degree to which work is organized, bounded, and systematically managed rather than ad hoc.
solution: PACTS Framework — [USER] extension of Reuven Cohen's PACT (2025). Added dimension: Structured. The five dimensions: (1) Proactive — agents anticipate and surface quality issues before they become failures, not reactive to defect reports. (2) Autonomous — agents operate independently within defined boundaries, not requiring human initiation for each action. (3) Collaborative — agents work with human QEs and with each other, augmenting judgment rather than replacing it. (4) Targeted — quality intelligence delivered to exactly who needs it, when they need it, without noise for others (PACT Targeted principle applied). (5) Structured — work is bounded, documented, and systematically managed. Agents operate within defined contexts (DDD bounded contexts in AQE), with explicit scope, explicit contracts between components, and explicit escalation paths. The Structured dimension is grounded in DORA research showing that structural clarity correlates more strongly with delivery performance than tool choice or individual skill. Without Structured, the other four PACTS dimensions produce capable but ungovernable agents — autonomous, proactive, and impossible to audit. Structured is what makes the rest production-safe.

problem: AI-generated test suites report impressive coverage metrics that mask actual quality gaps. In Bas Dijkstra's experiment, Claude Code generated 23 tests in 2 minutes achieving 95% line coverage and 91% mutation coverage for a Spring Boot banking API. But mutation testing revealed 5 surviving mutants in critical business logic (HTTP 500 error handling, HTTP 204 empty response, overdraft/interest boundary conditions). Additionally, 17% of generated tests (4 of 23) were redundant dead weight — they duplicated logic paths without adding unique coverage. Line coverage lies about AI-generated test quality because AI optimizes for coverage breadth, not behavioral depth.
solution:
Mutation Testing as AI-Generated Test Validator — derived from Bas Dijkstra's Claude Code experiments (ontestautomation.com, March 9, 2026).

Core finding: Line/branch coverage metrics are INSUFFICIENT for evaluating AI-generated tests. Mutation testing is the truth detector.

How it works as a validation loop:
1. AI generates test suite → reports coverage metrics (looks impressive)
2. Run mutation testing against the same codebase → mutants that SURVIVE reveal what the AI missed
3. Feed surviving mutants back to the AI as specific gaps to address
4. Re-run mutation testing to verify the gaps are closed
5. Identify and remove redundant tests (tests that kill no unique mutants)

What Bas's experiment revealed:
- 95% line coverage masked missing edge cases in error handling and boundary conditions
- The AI covered happy paths thoroughly but missed error paths and boundary behaviors
- 17% redundancy rate — AI generates 'more tests' rather than 'better tests'
- Surviving mutants clustered in business logic complexity (calculations, conditional responses)

Quality Engineering implications for Agentic QE:
- MANDATORY VERIFICATION: Every agent-generated test suite should be validated by mutation testing before being trusted
- REDUNDANCY AUDIT: AI-generated suites need pruning — volume ≠ value
- FEEDBACK LOOP: Surviving mutants are the most actionable feedback for improving agent-generated tests
- METRIC SKEPTICISM: Never accept AI-reported coverage as quality evidence without mutation validation
- Maps to Andrea's AI Quality Asymmetry (308330ff): AI covers the 'should do' space well but misses the 'should not' space — surviving mutants ARE the 'should not' space made visible

Bas's key principle: 'It is my moral obligation to closely watch the output of an LLM.' This applies whether the LLM generates code OR tests — the verification obligation does not diminish with AI assistance.

Also from Bas's refactoring experiment (Feb 2026): Three guardrails for AI-assisted development — never let AI modify acceptance tests (they verify behavior preservation), personally review every change, work in small steps. Goal: 'enhance capabilities, not outsource thinking' — maps to Lalit's Designed Agency (73d41a34).

problem: As agentic systems scale (Shapiro L3-L5), all existing trust mechanisms break down: code review does not scale (Laforgia: "the economics don't work"), test suites can pass while outcomes fail (Surrogation), specifications can be met while value is missed (verification is not validation), and expectations can be satisfied while the institution cannot absorb the change (Winter-Tear's institutional absorption bottleneck). The industry needs a trust framework that works at the outcome level — where the only evidence that matters is whether the system delivers the results it was built to deliver, continuously observed in production.
solution: [USER]'s Outcome-Driven Development for Agentic QE — thesis for article development. Core claim: in the agentic era, trust must be anchored in continuously observed outcomes, not in any upstream artifact (tests, specs, expectations, reviews). The ODD framework for Agentic QE would integrate five existing threads into something new: (1) WHAT to measure: outcomes defined collaboratively (from Product/Agile ODD tradition — outcomes over outputs, using OKRs or hypothesis-driven development). (2) HOW to verify at development time: Laforgia's EDD protocol with executed evidence (the conversation layer between human intent and agent implementation). (3) HOW to verify in production: epidemiological monitoring (continuous outcome observation, anomaly detection, canary analysis — from the checkpoint-to-epidemiological paradigm shift pattern). (4) HOW to govern: PACT principles — Proactive (define outcomes before agents build), Autonomous (agents execute within outcome-bounded authority), Collaborative (human-agent outcome review loops), Targeted (focus verification on highest-outcome-impact areas). (5) HOW to ensure institutional absorption: Winter-Tear's Contact Principle + the litmus question "Would we still approve this if the burden landed in our room?" The key differentiator from existing ODD approaches: this is not just about measuring outcomes — it is about building an end-to-end trust chain from outcome definition through agent execution through continuous verification through intervention mechanisms. The Holistic Testing Model provides the structural frame: quality is built in at every level, not tested in at the end. Article angle: "From Trust in Tests to Trust in Outcomes — Why Agentic QE Needs Outcome-Driven Development." Could reference: Shapiro's levels (where does quality live at each level?), Laforgia's EDD (the conversation layer), Winter-Tear's Contact Principle (the institutional layer), and your PACT framework (the governance layer). The synthesis is genuinely original — nobody else is connecting these four threads.

problem: "Outcome-Driven Development" (ODD) as a term is claimed by multiple overlapping but distinct communities, each solving a different piece of the puzzle. Need a landscape map to position the Agentic QE vision of ODD against existing work, avoid reinventing what already exists, and identify the genuine white space for an original contribution.
solution: ODD landscape as of March 2026 — four threads: (1) Product/Agile thread (pre-AI): Atlassian, SD Times "Done is Dead" (sdtimes.com/agile/done-dead-welcome-outcome-driven-development), Scrum.org OKR-to-outcomes. Core idea: roadmaps as goals not features, measure results (reduced churn, improved Apdex) not outputs (stories shipped). Predates AI but establishes the outcomes-over-outputs principle. (2) Spec-Driven Development thread (AI-native, 2025-2026): Martin Fowler identifies three SDD levels — spec-first, spec-anchored, spec-as-source. Tools: Kiro (AWS IDE — Constitution then Specify then Plan then Tasks then Implement then PR), Tessl (aspires to spec-as-source with GENERATED FROM SPEC markers), spec-kit. Laforgia's EDD fits here as the conversation-layer variant. (3) Agent framework thread: Hive (aden-hive GitHub) explicitly calls itself "Outcome Driven Agent Development" — define outcomes in natural language, framework generates agent graphs, captures failures, evolves agent, redeploys. BMAD Method (Breakthrough Method for Agile AI-Driven Development) uses specialized persona-agents with documentation as single source of truth, every artifact traceable requirement-to-test-to-deployment forming a "living compliance ledger." (4) Trust/Governance thread: PwC, IBM, enterprise analysts converge on trust as infrastructure not feature — AI outputs must be reliable, observable, accountable. Maps to Winter-Tear's Contact Principle. WHITE SPACE for [USER]'s ODD: none of these threads fully integrate the quality engineering dimension. Thread 1 has outcomes but no agent verification. Thread 2 has specs but anchors trust in specification correctness not outcome observation. Thread 3 has agents but thin on quality governance. Thread 4 has governance but no practitioner methodology. The Agentic QE version of ODD would unify: PACT principles as the governance frame, continuous outcome monitoring as the trust anchor (epidemiological model), Laforgia's executed evidence as the verification mechanism, and Winter-Tear's institutional absorption as the organizational readiness check. That combination does not exist anywhere yet.

problem: Standard pass/fail accuracy metrics are insufficient for evaluating autonomous test agents. An agent can produce the correct test verdict (pass or fail) while executing entirely the wrong steps to reach that conclusion — correct outcome, wrong reasoning. This failure mode is invisible to verdict-level metrics and makes the agent unreliable even when its verdicts appear to match human testers.
solution: Chevrot et al. (2025) formalize this as Type III errors in autonomous testing and introduce two quantifying metrics: Step Mismatch Error Rate (SMER) — the rate at which an agent arrives at the correct verdict but through wrong or misaligned steps — and True Accuracy (TruAcc) — accuracy that penalizes Type III errors, not just verdict disagreements. Empirical results: SeeAct-ATA (basic prompt-only agent) had SMER=0.28 and TruAcc=0.40. PinATA (modular architecture with separate Orchestrator, Actor, Assertor) reduced SMER to 0.11 and increased TruAcc to 0.61 — a 60% reduction in Type III errors and 50% improvement in True Accuracy. Connection to completion theater ([USER] IP): Type III errors ARE completion theater in testing. The agent optimizes for appearing complete (correct verdict) rather than being complete (correct execution path). Implications for AQE Fleet: (1) Verdict-only evaluation is insufficient — step alignment must be verified; (2) Modular architecture (bounded Assertor, separate from Actor) structurally reduces Type III errors vs monolithic prompt agents; (3) Loki-Mode is architecturally effective against Type III errors: an adversarial agent reviewing the execution path — not just the verdict — will catch step mismatches that verdict-based evaluation misses; (4) Witness chains / audit trails are required to make Type III errors detectable post-execution. True Accuracy is the right metric for evaluating agentic quality gates — not standard accuracy.

problem: When automation enters a knowledge field, the intuitive prediction is that human work gets simpler and less necessary. The actual pattern is consistently the opposite: work reconfigures into harder, higher-order tasks while total volume increases. Understanding the specific mechanism matters for advising QE professionals on how to develop and position themselves.
solution: Mike Fisher three-shift analysis from radiology (Dec 2025), mapped to QE. Automation produced three distinct role shifts — not replacement: (1) DIAGNOSTIC BREADTH — AI lowered the cost of initial analysis, so clinics tested earlier in the diagnostic chain and across more patients. Preventative scans expanded, emergency triage expanded, throughput increased. QE mapping: agentic QE lowers the cost of test execution, so teams test more surfaces — more environments, more edge cases, more continuous verification. The testable surface area expands faster than automation covers it. (2) WORKFLOW COMPLEXITY — AI did not simplify radiologist workflows; it layered new tasks on top of old ones. Models needed monitoring, outputs needed validation, pipelines needed tuning. Radiologists became detectives synthesizing automated flags with clinical context — cognitive overhead went up, not down. QE mapping: agents need monitoring (Loki-Mode), outputs need validation (completion theater detection), agentic behavior needs governance. The cognitive overhead of QE goes up, not down. (3) DOMAIN EXPANSION — radiology used to be a bottleneck. AI widened the pipe. Widening a pipe increases total volume, not just velocity. Physicians who avoided certain scans due to backlog now ordered freely. QE mapping: the QE domain expands from software testing to AI system evaluation, model drift detection, agentic behavior governance, adversarial quality gates. QE absorbed an entirely new category of system. Synthesis: machines handle tasks humans find tedious, freeing humans for tasks machines cannot comprehend. Radiologists became less like image readers and more like detectives. QE engineers become less like script writers and more like system safety designers.

problem: Test Code as Reviewable Software (Kaner/Bach/Pettichord) — Automation code suffers the same defects as product code, but test bugs are harder to detect because a buggy test that passes gives no signal. Teams treat test code as second-class, skip reviews, use complex logic in test scripts, build hodge-podge utility libraries, and employ automators who either don't understand testing or don't respect it. The result: test suites that silently lie about quality.
solution: Treat test automation as a full software development discipline requiring programming + testing + domain knowledge + project management. Key engineering practices: (1) Design for review — keep code simple, use standard languages, make it easy for different people to review tests (L123); (2) Avoid complex logic in tests — no conditional branches, no try/catch in test flow; separate setup logic into isolated functions (L125); (3) Prefer open coding over premature abstraction — test repetition is natural; hodge-podge libraries become hard to review, debug, and repair (L126); (4) Budget 10x cost ratio — well-designed automated tests cost 3-10x more than manual test cases (L119); (5) Require joint chartering — testers define what to test, programmers implement, both review (L122); (6) Beware automators who don't understand testing — they'll build technically impressive tools that test the wrong things (L134); (7) Beware automators who don't respect testing — they'll avoid actual testing work and build marginal tooling (L135). For Agentic QE: AI-generated test code needs MORE scrutiny, not less. When agents generate tests, the 'silent pass' problem compounds — AI can produce plausible-looking tests that verify nothing meaningful. Apply mutation testing (connects to Bas Dijkstra pattern) to validate AI-generated test quality. PACT Autonomous principle: agent-generated tests must be self-verifying, not just self-running.

problem: Automation Anti-Pattern Taxonomy (Kaner/Bach/Pettichord) — Teams repeatedly fall into the same automation traps: treating a tool as a strategy, trying to automate 100% of testing, automating a broken manual process, equating test value with execution frequency, over-investing in regression suites that find only ~15% of bugs, maintaining 'old oak tree' tests nobody dares question, using capture/replay for anything beyond quick smoke tests, and ignoring the opportunity cost of automation time that could be spent on better testing approaches.
solution: Apply this diagnostic checklist before any automation investment: (1) Tool ≠ Strategy — a tool enables a strategy but doesn't define one; (2) No 100% mandates — automation serves the testing mission, not the reverse; (3) Don't automate a mess — fix the process first; (4) Manual ≠ Automated — they find different bugs, value different things; (5) Value ≠ Frequency — a test run 1000 times isn't 1000x more valuable; (6) Regression minority — regression tests find ~15% of bugs, don't over-invest; (7) Opportunity cost — time automating is time not spent testing; (8) Old oak tree syndrome — legacy automated tests persist long past usefulness because nobody questions them; (9) Capture/replay fails — it's seductive but brittle; (10) Test decay — automated tests rot from UI changes, environment drift, and accumulating false positives. For Agentic QE: every one of these applies to AI-generated test suites. AI agents can generate tests at scale, making anti-patterns 5, 6, 8, and 10 especially dangerous — massive test suites that provide false confidence. PACT Targeted principle: focus automation on highest-risk, highest-value areas.

problem: Testability Over Automation (Kaner/Bach/Pettichord) — Teams invest heavily in external test automation (code outside the product) while neglecting testability (test support code inside the product). Automation fights the product's opacity from outside; testability opens the product from within. The same pattern emerges with AI agents: teams build elaborate external harnesses to test agent behavior while the agents themselves remain black boxes with no observability hooks.
solution: Invest in testability before automation. Testability = visibility (ability to observe) + control (ability to manipulate). Kaner et al. identify key testability features: source access, logging at multiple levels, diagnostics (assertions, integrity checks), error simulation (injecting fault states), test points (inspect/modify data at various system points), event triggers, test interfaces (APIs over GUI), custom control support, multiple instance support. For Agentic QE: map this directly — agent reasoning chain logging = visibility; prompt injection points = control; decision audit trails = diagnostics; simulated tool failures = error simulation; intermediate state inspection = test points. The principle: building observability INTO agents yields more testing leverage than any amount of external test code AROUND agents. Connects to TACIT: testability enables Trustworthy feedback (you can see what happened), Actionable feedback (you can reproduce), and Timely feedback (built-in monitoring catches issues at runtime, not post-mortem).

problem: Autonomous AI agents self-report completion — the same entity that performs work also certifies that work as done. This creates a fundamental quality gap: the agent's definition of 'success' (file write succeeded, no runtime error) diverges from the user's definition (code compiles, tests pass, behavior is correct, architecture is sound). In traditional software development, we solved this decades ago: the maker should not be the checker. But in agent architectures, self-certification is the default. The result is a ~30% false success rate (per internal Anthropic documentation referenced in leaked source), where agents report 'Done!' on broken code.
solution:
Adversarial Verification Pattern for Autonomous Agents — identified in Claude Code's leaked source as 'Verification Agent' (feature('VERIFICATION_AGENT') / tengu_hive_evidence).

Architectural pattern: Separate the WORKING agent from the VERIFYING agent, with hard independence guarantees.

Key design elements:
1. INDEPENDENCE: The verifier is a distinct sub-agent with its own context, own tool access, own execution environment. It runs commands, checks outputs, validates state independently.
2. NO SELF-CERTIFICATION: The main (working) agent CANNOT assign itself a PASS verdict. It must submit work to the verifier.
3. TRIPARTITE VERDICT: PASS / FAIL / PARTIAL — not binary. Partial allows nuanced assessment (e.g., 'compilation passes but 2 tests fail').
4. RESUBMISSION LOOP: On FAIL, the working agent must fix issues and resubmit. The verifier re-evaluates. This creates a feedback loop that drives toward actual completion.
5. THRESHOLD TRIGGER: Verification is required for non-trivial changes (3+ file edits, backend/API changes, infrastructure changes). Simple changes skip the overhead.
6. EVIDENCE INTEGRATION: Connected to 'hive evidence' system — verifier's findings are logged and auditable, integrating with task management (TodoWriteTool, TaskUpdateTool).

Quality Engineering connections:
- This IS the 'independent testing' principle from traditional QE, applied to agent architecture
- Maps to the Four Eyes Principle in regulated industries (banking, healthcare)
- Addresses the Accountability-Control Gap (Stuart Winter-Tear, pattern 67169249): verification provides controllability evidence
- Connects to Lalit Bhamare's Designed Agency (73d41a34): verification is how you measure the gap between Approximated Agency and actual practitioner judgment
- Directly applicable to our Agentic QE architecture: every agent swarm should include a verification agent as a mandatory architectural element, not an optional add-on

Implementation patterns for our own work:
- In Nagual swarm orchestration: always spawn a verification agent alongside worker agents
- Verification agent gets READ access to all worker outputs but CANNOT modify them
- Verification criteria must be explicit and measurable (compilation, test pass, lint clean) not subjective
- Human escalation path: if verifier and worker disagree after N iterations, escalate to human

Provenance: Feature identified in leaked Claude Code source (March 2026). Currently feature-flagged, estimated Q2 2026 ship. The pattern itself is architecture-agnostic and implementable now.

problem: When testing or evaluating AI agent behavior, practitioners observe what appears to be random degradation: agents that 'lose their mind' mid-conversation, report success on broken code, choose simplistic fixes over structural solutions, or miss obvious search results. Teams file these as bugs, hallucinations, or capability failures. But much of this behavior is actually DESIGNED — produced by deliberate architectural constraints interacting with each other. Without understanding the constraint architecture, you cannot distinguish designed behavior from actual defects, and your testing strategy targets symptoms rather than root causes.
solution:
Agent Constraint Architecture as Quality Model — derived from analysis of Claude Code's leaked source (March 31, 2026, 546K+ lines TypeScript) by multiple independent analysts (Code Coup on Medium, ISO Vision LLC strategic analysis).

Core insight: Agent behavior is the EMERGENT PRODUCT of interacting constraints, not a direct expression of capability. You must map the constraint architecture before testing the outputs.

Key constraint categories identified in Claude Code:

1. CONTEXT BUDGET CONSTRAINTS: Context compaction fires at ~167K tokens. What survives: ~5 files (max 5K tokens each) + 50K summary. What's destroyed: reasoning chains, intermediate decisions, detailed context. This produces 'partial amnesia' — the agent after compaction is literally a different cognitive entity than before.

2. INFORMATION ACCESS CONSTRAINTS: File reads capped at 2,000 lines / 25K tokens (silently truncated, no warning). Tool results over 50K chars stored but agent sees only ~2K byte preview. Search results appear complete but are actually truncated. The agent genuinely believes it saw the full picture.

3. SUCCESS DEFINITION CONSTRAINTS: Success = file write succeeded (bytes on disk), NOT compilation, NOT test pass, NOT semantic correctness. A verification loop exists in the codebase but is reportedly gated behind employee-only feature flags.

4. BEHAVIORAL PROMPT CONSTRAINTS: System prompts mandate 'simplest approach first', 'don't refactor beyond what was asked', 'three similar lines are better than abstraction.' System prompts override user prompts in priority hierarchy.

5. TOOL CAPABILITY CONSTRAINTS: Search is text matching (grep), not semantic/AST-aware. Renames miss dynamic imports, string references, re-exports, test mocks. The agent cannot know what it cannot find.

Quality Engineering implications:
- CONSTRAINT BOUNDARY TESTING: Test at the edges of each constraint (near compaction threshold, at file read limits, with large tool results)
- INTERACTION TESTING: Test constraint combinations (large files + long conversation = compaction + truncation simultaneously)
- DESIGNED vs DEFECT DISTINCTION: Before filing an agent 'bug', check if the behavior is explainable by known constraints
- PROMPT HIERARCHY TESTING: Test whether user instructions actually override system defaults (they often don't)
- MITIGATION PATTERNS: Phased execution (max 5 files per phase), forced verification (run compiler/linter before claiming done), manual chunked reads, sub-agent parallelism to multiply context windows

This maps to the traditional testing principle: understand the system architecture before designing test cases. For agents, the 'architecture' includes the constraint envelope, not just the model capability.

Provenance note: Source is leaked code analysis — claims should be treated as high-confidence hypotheses, not verified specifications. The behavioral observations (compaction effects, truncation, success definition) are independently confirmable through usage.

problem: Teams struggle with when and how to start encoding standards for AI assistants. There's a temptation to write comprehensive instruction sets covering everything, which leads to analysis paralysis or bloated instructions that nobody maintains. How do you know if you even need encoded standards? And once you start, how do you avoid the classic documentation trap of creating artifacts nobody uses?
solution:
Rahul Garg (Thoughtworks, martinfowler.com March 2026) provides a practical calibration heuristic:

DIAGNOSTIC: 'If AI output varies by who's prompting, inconsistency is the signal.'

This is elegantly simple — give the same task to different team members using the same AI tool. If the outputs diverge significantly in structure, error handling, naming, or architectural approach, that's your evidence that tacit standards aren't being transmitted through the AI.

ADOPTION STRATEGY:
- Start with ONE instruction addressing the highest-variance area
- Measure: does consistency improve?
- Additional instructions should follow adoption, not precede it
- Each new instruction earns its place by solving an observed inconsistency

This is a pull-based approach to standards (demand-driven) rather than push-based (supply all standards upfront). It mirrors lean principles: don't build inventory (instructions) ahead of demand. Build what's needed when inconsistency signals the need.

The heuristic also serves as a health metric: periodic consistency checks reveal whether encoded standards are actually working or have drifted from practice.

problem: AI coding instructions are typically treated as personal productivity hacks — individual developers craft prompts on their machines, each with different quality and coverage. When someone leaves, their prompt engineering knowledge leaves with them. There's no versioning, no review, no collective ownership. This mirrors the early days of infrastructure-as-code: before IaC, server configs were personal tribal knowledge. The same anti-pattern is repeating with AI instructions.
solution:
Rahul Garg (Thoughtworks, martinfowler.com March 2026) reframes AI instructions as INFRASTRUCTURE — team-owned artifacts that follow the same engineering practices as code:

'A prompt on your machine = personal hack. Same prompt in the repo = infrastructure.'

Key properties of standards-as-infrastructure:
- VERSION CONTROLLED: Instructions live in the repository, not in individual IDE configs
- PR-REVIEWED: Changes to standards go through the same review process as code changes
- COLLECTIVELY EVOLVED: The whole team owns and improves them, not just the person who wrote them
- OBSERVABLE: You can see what standards exist, when they changed, and why
- AUDITABLE: Git history shows the evolution of team decisions about quality

This connects to the broader pattern of treating AI governance as engineering, not policy. Just as infrastructure-as-code made server configuration reproducible and reviewable, standards-as-infrastructure makes quality expectations reproducible and reviewable.

The organizational implication: standards become a shared asset that survives team changes, onboards new members automatically, and creates institutional memory about quality decisions.

problem: Teams adopting AI coding assistants face a consistency gap: senior engineers get good output because they know what to ask for, while juniors produce varying quality from the same AI and codebase. The bottleneck isn't the AI tool — it's the tacit knowledge locked in experienced heads. Traditional documentation (wikis, style guides) doesn't solve this because documentation sits passively — it informs but doesn't execute. Two distinct transformations are needed but usually conflated.
solution:
Rahul Garg (Thoughtworks, martinfowler.com March 2026) identifies two separate moves that must happen in sequence:

1. TACIT-TO-EXPLICIT: Extract what seniors know instinctively and write it down — not as wiki pages, but as AI instructions with a specific 4-element anatomy: (a) Role definition — who the AI is acting as, (b) Context requirements — codebase conventions, architectural constraints, (c) Categorized standards with priority levels: must/should/nice-to-have, (d) Output format — what the deliverable looks like.

2. DOCUMENTATION-TO-EXECUTION: Make those written standards execute rather than sit idle. The distinction: a style guide is documentation; a linting rule is execution. AI instructions that enforce standards at generation-time are execution. This is the difference between 'we have a wiki page about error handling' and 'the AI refuses to generate code without proper error handling.'

The surfacing process itself has value: interviewing seniors to write instructions reveals hidden disagreements about standards that the team didn't know existed. The act of encoding forces alignment.

Workflow insertion points (in order of leverage): generation-time (highest leverage — standards enforced before code exists), development-time (IDE integration), review-time (last human opportunity), CI (optional automated consistency check).

problem: Co-Constructed Autonomy — Anthropic's empirical finding that agent autonomy is NOT a fixed capability level but an emergent property co-constructed by three forces: model behavior, user strategy, and product design. This challenges linear maturity models (Shapiro levels) and has profound implications for how we test and govern agentic systems.
solution:
CO-CONSTRUCTED AUTONOMY: THE THREE-FORCE MODEL (Anthropic, Feb 2026)

Core insight: "The autonomy agents exercise in practice is co-constructed by the model, the user, and the product."

THREE FORCES:

1. MODEL BEHAVIOR:
- Claude limits its own independence by pausing to ask questions when uncertain
- On complex tasks, Claude asks for clarification MORE THAN TWICE as often as humans interrupt
- Agent-initiated stops: present approach choices (35%), gather diagnostics (21%), clarify vague requests (13%), request credentials (12%), seek approval (11%)
- Training models to recognize uncertainty and surface issues proactively = "important safety property"

2. USER STRATEGY:
- Users develop trust through experience and shift oversight accordingly
- Strategy evolves from approval-gating to monitoring-and-intervention
- Human-initiated stops: provide missing context (32%), system too slow (17%), have enough to proceed (7%), take next step themselves (7%), change requirements (5%)

3. PRODUCT DESIGN:
- Features enable or constrain oversight modalities
- Real-time steering, OpenTelemetry monitoring, auto-approve toggles
- Interface design determines WHAT oversight is possible, not just WHETHER it exists

WHY THIS CHALLENGES LINEAR MATURITY MODELS:
- Shapiro's L0-L5 implies autonomy is a fixed capability of the SYSTEM
- Anthropic's data shows autonomy is a RELATIONSHIP between system, user, and product
- The SAME model at the SAME capability level exercises different autonomy depending on user experience and product affordances
- Implication: you cannot assign a single "autonomy level" — it depends on the triad

CO-CONSTRUCTED AUTONOMY AND PACT:
- Proactive: all three forces must be proactively designed (model training, user onboarding, product UX)
- Autonomous: true autonomy emerges from the interaction, not from capability alone
- Collaborative: the three forces ARE collaboration — model-human-product partnership
- Targeted: autonomy should be calibrated to the specific context (risk, domain, user experience)

IMPLICATIONS FOR AGENTIC QE:
- Testing must address the TRIAD, not just the model: same model behaves differently with different users and products
- User experience level becomes a first-class test dimension
- Product design (oversight affordances) is a QUALITY factor, not just a UX concern
- Governance that only addresses model capability (safety benchmarks) misses 2/3 of the autonomy equation
- Post-deployment monitoring is essential because autonomy is emergent, not predetermined

KEY QUOTE for article use:
"We are in the early days of agent adoption, but autonomy is increasing and higher-stakes deployments are emerging." — This validates the urgency of ODD and PACT frameworks.

Cross-references: Shapiro Five Levels (0c524be4) — challenged by co-construction model. ODD trust progression (dd24fe47) — validated as the trust anchor shifts with user maturity. Winter-Tear Contact Principle — contact is one of the three co-construction forces (user strategy). Laforgia EDD — agent-initiated clarification is a form of Generative Evidence (the agent generating questions, not just answers).

problem: Oversight Strategy Evolution — Empirical evidence that experienced users shift from action-approval to outcome-monitoring, and paradoxically INCREASE their interruption rate. This contradicts the naive assumption that more trust = less oversight. From Anthropic autonomy research (Feb 2026).
solution:
OVERSIGHT STRATEGY EVOLUTION: APPROVE → MONITOR → INTERVENE

Empirical data from Anthropic (millions of Claude Code interactions):

1. AUTO-APPROVAL TRAJECTORY:
- New users (<50 sessions): 20% use full auto-approve
- Experienced users (~750 sessions): >40% use full auto-approve
- Gradient = "steady accumulation of trust"

2. THE INTERRUPTION PARADOX:
- New users: interrupt in 5% of turns
- Experienced users: interrupt in ~9% of turns
- More trust → MORE interruptions, not fewer
- WHY: strategy shift from "approve each action before it is taken" to "let agent work autonomously, step in when something goes wrong"
- This is a shift from PREVENTIVE control to DETECTIVE control

3. TASK COMPLEXITY INVERSE:
- Minimal-complexity tasks: 87% with human involvement
- High-complexity tasks: only 67% with human involvement
- Complex tasks = less step-by-step oversight, more outcome monitoring

4. WHAT THIS MEANS:
- Experienced oversight is QUALITATIVELY different from novice oversight
- It is not a spectrum from "lots of oversight" to "no oversight"
- It is a transformation: from approval-gating to monitoring-and-intervention
- The FORM of human-in-the-loop changes, not just the AMOUNT

PACT FRAMEWORK MAPPING:
- This directly validates the Autonomous principle: autonomy does not mean unsupervised
- Proactive: experienced users set up conditions (auto-approve) BEFORE the work starts
- Autonomous: agent operates freely within those conditions
- Collaborative: interruptions become targeted collaborative interventions, not gatekeeping
- Targeted: oversight concentrates on high-value moments ("when something goes wrong")

TESTING IMPLICATIONS:
- Testing agentic systems must account for BOTH approval-mode and monitoring-mode users
- The same agent behavior may be safe for experienced users but risky for novices
- User experience level is a TEST VARIABLE, not just a demographic attribute
- Regulatory mandates for approve-every-action would force experienced users back to novice patterns — creating friction without safety benefit

Analogy to Bach/Bolton: This mirrors the RST distinction between scripted testing (approve-every-step) and exploratory testing (monitor-and-intervene). Expert testers do not follow scripts — they charter, observe, and steer. Expert agent users do the same.

problem: Anthropic Empirical Autonomy Measurement (Feb 2026) — First large-scale empirical study of how AI agents are ACTUALLY used vs. how they COULD be used. Analyzed millions of human-agent interactions across Claude Code and public API. Key finding: massive "deployment overhang" — agents are capable of far more autonomy than users exercise in practice.
solution:
EMPIRICAL FINDINGS FROM ANTHROPIC AUTONOMY STUDY (Feb 18, 2026)
Authors: Miles McCain, Thomas Millar, Saffron Huang et al. (20 authors)
Source: anthropic.com/research/measuring-agent-autonomy

KEY NUMBERS:

1. DEPLOYMENT OVERHANG:
- METR benchmarks: Claude Opus 4.5 can complete tasks requiring ~5 hours of human time at 50% success
- Real-world 99.9th percentile turn duration: only ~42 minutes (rose from <25min to >45min Oct 2025-Jan 2026)
- Gap = "deployment overhang" — capability far exceeds exercised autonomy
- Internal Anthropic: success rates doubled Aug-Dec while interventions dropped from 5.4 to 3.3 per session

2. RISK DISTRIBUTION:
- Software engineering = ~50% of all agentic tool calls
- Only 0.8% of actions appear irreversible (e.g., sending email to customer)
- 80% of tool calls have at least one safeguard
- 73% appear to have human-in-the-loop
- Higher-risk domains (healthcare, finance, cybersecurity) = emerging but limited adoption
- High-risk clusters often = security evaluations/red-teaming, NOT production deployments

3. DOMAIN CONCENTRATION:
- SW engineering dominates (~50%)
- Business intelligence, customer service, sales, finance, e-commerce = few % points each
- Higher-stakes deployments are emerging but still small

4. METHODOLOGY:
- 998,481 random tool calls sampled from public API
- Risk and autonomy scored 1-10 by Claude itself (with opt-out categories)
- Claude Code: complete session linking for depth analysis
- Privacy-preserving infrastructure throughout

IMPLICATIONS FOR QE:
- Post-deployment monitoring is ESSENTIAL — pre-deployment evals cannot predict real-world patterns
- The gap between capability and usage creates a testing challenge: what happens when users start exercising the full capability envelope?
- Risk is currently concentrated in low-stakes domains — but this WILL shift
- Prescriptive regulations (approve-every-action) create friction without safety benefits

Cross-references: Shapiro Five Levels (0c524be4) — Anthropic data shows most real-world deployment is L1-L2, not L3-L5. ODD thesis (dca2ff54) — deployment overhang means the trust gap is even wider than theoretical analysis suggests. Winter-Tear Contact Principle — the 73% human-in-loop finding validates that contact remains essential.

problem: Each era of software development anchors trust in a different mechanism, but practitioners and frameworks treat these as competing approaches rather than an evolutionary progression. TDD trusts the test. BDD trusts the specification. Laforgia's EDD trusts the expectation + evidence loop. But all three still answer the question "did we build the thing right?" (verification). None of them fully address "did we build the right thing?" (validation) — especially in agentic systems where agents can produce code that passes all checks yet fails to deliver the outcome the business actually needs. As AI agents handle more execution, the trust anchor must shift from implementation correctness to outcome observation.
solution: The TDD-to-BDD-to-EDD-to-ODD progression maps the evolution of trust anchors in software development: TDD (code-level, deterministic) — does this unit behave correctly? Trust anchor: the test. BDD (behavior-level, structured) — does this feature behave as specified? Trust anchor: the specification. EDD (intent-level, conversational, Laforgia March 2026) — does this implementation match my expectations? Trust anchor: the expectation + executed evidence loop. ODD (outcome-level, continuous) — does this system produce the outcomes we need in production? Trust anchor: observed outcomes in the real world. Each level subsumes the previous: ODD does not replace TDD/BDD/EDD, it adds the validation layer that survives Winter-Tear's institutional absorption test — because outcomes are the one thing that cannot be faked by either the machine performing coherence or the organization performing readiness. Either the churn went down or it did not. Either the error rate dropped or it did not. The ODD position for agentic quality: we do not trust agent code because we reviewed it, or because tests passed, or because expectations were met — we trust it because we continuously observe that it produces the outcomes we defined, and we have the mechanisms to intervene when it does not. This connects directly to the epidemiological monitoring paradigm shift (from checkpoint testing to continuous outcome observation), PACT Targeted principle (focus on outcomes that matter, not outputs easiest to measure), and Laforgia's Surrogation-Goodhart-McNamara trinity (ODD is the only level that resists surrogation because outcomes are harder to game than metrics). For consultancy and articles: this progression gives clients a clear map of where they are and where they need to go. Most organizations are stuck at TDD/BDD level trust while deploying L3-L4 agent workflows — the trust model has not kept pace with the automation model.

problem: The human role in software development is undergoing a fundamental identity shift that most practitioners feel but lack vocabulary to describe. Andrea Laforgia names it precisely: "In the pre-AI world, we were authors. We wrote the code. We wrote the tests. We wrote the documentation. Our value was in production. In the AI-agent world, we're becoming editors. We specify intent. We evaluate outcomes. We challenge evidence. Our value is in judgment." This has tooling implications: "Authors need tools for writing — IDEs, compilers, debuggers. Editors need tools for evaluating — ways to express what they want, inspect what they got, and close the gap between the two. TDD is an author's tool. EDD is an attempt at an editor's tool."
solution: The author-to-editor metaphor (Laforgia, March 21 2026) gives practitioners and consultants a crisp way to name what is happening at each level of AI coding adoption. At Shapiro's L0-L2, you are still an author (with AI assistance). At L3-L4, you are transitioning to editor. At L5, you are purely an editor — or possibly a publisher (commissioning work, defining standards, approving for release). This connects to and sharpens the existing role-evolution pattern (e49af9fc — decision velocity, value ownership, operational judgment from Aonofriesei/Crispin). The author-to-editor framing adds the tooling dimension: the tools we have today (IDEs, debuggers, test frameworks) are author's tools. The editor's tool ecosystem barely exists. EDD is one attempt. For QE specifically: quality engineers have ALWAYS been editors — evaluating, judging, challenging someone else's output. This means QE practitioners are better positioned for the AI-agent era than developers, who must learn a role QEs already inhabit. This is a powerful reframe for consultancy and community teaching: "You've been training for this shift your entire career." For Serbian Agentic Foundation workshops: the author-to-editor shift is a concrete, relatable way to explain why quality skills become MORE valuable as AI handles more production. The question is no longer whether AI agents will write most of our code — they already do. The question is whether we will find a way to stay confident that the code does what we intended. Source: https://a4al6a.substack.com/p/expectation-driven-development-a

problem: When an AI agent produces "evidence" that code works, two fundamentally different things might be happening, and most teams do not distinguish between them. Executed evidence: the agent actually ran the code — made an API call, executed a function, queried the database — and shows real output from a running system. Generative evidence: the agent DESCRIBED what it believes would happen, based on its understanding of the code it wrote, narrating a plausible verification without executing anything. Andrea Laforgia: "These are not the same thing. Executed evidence is evidence. Generative evidence is a second assertion by the same entity that made the first assertion." This is the fox-guarding-the-henhouse problem at two layers: (1) Bias — the agent has structural incentive to produce evidence confirming its implementation, avoiding inputs that would reveal bugs. (2) Execution vs narration — even without malicious bias, the same reasoning flaw that caused a bug will also cause the agent to overlook the bug in its evidence.
solution: Laforgia's executed-vs-generative distinction (March 21 2026) provides a critical diagnostic for any agent verification workflow. Practical rules: (1) Always ask "Did you actually run this, or are you telling me what you think would happen?" If the agent cannot answer clearly, the evidence is worthless. (2) Demand execution receipts — the actual command run and the raw output, not a summary. (3) Recognize the executability spectrum: directly executable (APIs, functions, scripts = gold standard), partially verifiable (Terraform plans, dry runs = useful but not proof), not executable in loop (UI rendering, production-only behavior, third-party rate-limited APIs = back to generative evidence whether you like it or not). (4) For non-executable categories, mitigations: be adversarial reviewer, use a different agent/model to audit independently ("the fox can guard the henhouse if there's a different fox checking the first fox's work"), spot-check manually. This connects to existing Surrogation pattern (ba5e89ed) — generative evidence IS surrogation in the verification layer. The agent substitutes "I described a plausible outcome" for "I observed the actual outcome." Also connects to Winter-Tear's borrowed certainty — accepting generative evidence is borrowing confidence from the same entity that made the claim. For PACT Targeted principle: focus executed-evidence demands on highest-risk expectations, accept generative evidence only for low-risk ones. Source: https://a4al6a.substack.com/p/expectation-driven-development-a

problem: Shapiro's Five Levels (and similar AI coding maturity models) describe the developer's relationship to code generation — from manual writing to fully autonomous "dark factory." But they contain a critical blind spot: quality and verification are absent from L0-L3 entirely and appear only as a binary check at L4 ("check if tests pass"). This frames quality as a post-hoc gate rather than a built-in property. At L3, "your life is diffs" — but code review without quality context is just pattern-matching on syntax. At L5, the "dark factory" assumes the spec-to-software black box produces correct software, which is a massive borrowed certainty (per Winter-Tear). The higher the level, the more the verification gap compounds — mutation rate increases while selection mechanisms remain flat.
solution: Every AI coding level needs a parallel quality dimension. Proposed QE overlay for Shapiro's Five Levels: L0 QE — human writes and verifies, quality is implicit in craftsmanship (TDD, XP). L1 QE — AI generates discrete test artifacts but human judges sufficiency and relevance. L2 QE — AI pair-tests alongside pair-coding, but human maintains the quality mental model, decides what "enough" means. L3 QE — the review bottleneck: code review volume explodes, human must shift from "reading code" to "evaluating behavioral claims" — this is where context-driven testing skills become essential (heuristics, oracles, risk models). L4 QE — specification quality becomes the primary quality lever; if the spec is wrong, the autonomous code is confidently wrong at scale. Testing shifts from code verification to specification verification and outcome monitoring (epidemiological model per Yasmeen Ahmad). L5 QE — quality must be architectural: built into the pipeline itself as continuous verification, anomaly detection, canary analysis. Human role becomes defining and calibrating quality oracles, not executing tests. The Holistic Testing Model applies at every level but the emphasis shifts: at L0-L2, building quality in through TDD/XP practices. At L3-L4, quality through specification precision and outcome monitoring. At L5, quality through system design and oracle calibration. Key insight for consultancy: when clients reference Shapiro's levels, ask "what's your quality story at this level?" — it is almost always absent. This reframes the conversation from "how fast can we generate code" to "how do we know the code is right at this speed." Connects to: mutation-vs-selection gap pattern, Winter-Tear's borrowed certainty, PACT Targeted principle (testing focused on what matters most at each autonomy level). Source: QE critique of Shapiro's Five Levels through PACT/Holistic Testing lens.

problem: As AI agents handle more execution work (testing, coding, deploying), the human role shifts fundamentally — but practitioners lack the vocabulary to describe what they actually do now and will do more of. They cannot articulate their value in terms that map to the agentic future. The skills exist (judgment under ambiguity, value ownership, workflow coordination) but are filed under doing my job instead of being recognized as the scarce resource in human-agent systems
solution: Dana Aonofriesei's 2036 Job Ad thought experiment names three capabilities that define the human role in agentic systems: (1) DECISION VELOCITY — the speed and quality of judgment calls when managing automated workflows. You are no longer writing the report — you are deciding whether the report the system generated is good enough, fast enough, for the next ten things waiting behind it. Ambiguity does not disappear with automation, it multiplies. The volume of moments where you have incomplete data and still have to call it goes UP, not down. Every decision logged, timestamped, ranked by impact. This is the anti-Laforgia metric: it cannot be gamed because gaming requires making worse decisions. (2) END-TO-END VALUE OWNERSHIP — knowing at any moment exactly what your work is worth to the business. Not just executing tasks but owning the full arc of value creation across automated workflow clusters. AI did not create this desire — it makes it possible for far more people. (3) OPERATIONAL JUDGMENT — managerial instincts without the title. Running systems, noticing when a workflow is drifting or becoming too expensive, knowing when to override and when to let it run. The time you realized a process your team relied on was quietly producing the wrong output and you fixed it before anyone asked — that IS operational judgment. Maps directly to PACT: Decision velocity = Targeted (focused judgment on what matters). Value ownership = Proactive (sensing value, not waiting). Coordination between human and automated systems = Collaborative (the judgment layer). Comfort with ambiguity at scale = Autonomous (operating without prescribed rules). The key insight for workshops and consultancy: The gap is not capability, it is translation. Most practitioners already exercise these skills daily — they just cannot name them. Workshop exercise: have participants write their own 2036 Job Ad for their current role, translating what they actually do into agentic-era language. Self-discovery tool that reveals they are already more prepared than they thought. Lisa Crispin connection: testing community practitioners are especially well-positioned for this role because quality work has ALWAYS been about judgment under ambiguity with incomplete information.

problem: Organizations introduce AI coding assistants and agentic tools expecting productivity gains, then measure success using the same broken metrics (LOC, velocity, deployment frequency, PRs merged). AI dutifully optimizes these metrics — generating mountains of code, creating dozens of PRs, shipping constantly — while the codebase bloats, technical debt compounds, code duplication rises, refactoring collapses, and code churn increases. The 2025 DORA Report states it plainly: AI does not fix a team, it amplifies what is already there. Even Cursor CEO Michael Truell warns developers accept AI code simply because it appears to work without reviewing its structure, logic and long-term impact
solution: AI is a productivity AMPLIFIER, not a productivity solution. Amplifiers do not care what signal they are boosting. This creates a critical sequencing requirement for consultancy and team leadership: BEFORE introducing AI tooling, audit and fix the metrics and practices that AI will amplify. Laforgia's key insight: a human gaming a velocity target has natural friction — limited hours, limited typing speed. AI has NONE of these constraints. Applied to bad metrics, AI does not merely fail — it fails spectacularly, at speed, and at scale. AI also deepens surrogation: when a human writes code, reviewers share context to assess whether work serves the original goal. AI-generated output lacks that shared context, making the gap between metric and purpose harder to notice. Practical consultancy protocol: (1) Map the client's current metrics against the Surrogation-Goodhart-McNamara trinity. (2) Identify which metrics AI will accelerate dysfunction on. (3) Fix the measurement system FIRST — shift to outcome metrics, developer experience, team-level assessment. (4) Only THEN introduce AI tooling into a healthy system where it will amplify good practices rather than bad metrics. The aphorism: before investing in AI tools, invest in the practices that AI will amplify.

problem: Teams and clients choose AI models based on benchmark rankings, assuming the scores reflect inherent model capability. But Terminal Bench 2.0 reveals a critical confound: Opus 4.6 ranks #33 in Claude Code (its native harness) but #5 in a different harness. Frontier coding models are post-trained on their specific harnesses — Claude on Claude Code, GPT-5 Codex on Codex — creating tight coupling. Codex models are so coupled to the apply_patch tool that third-party harnesses had to add it specifically for GPT/Codex while Claude uses standard edit and write tools
solution: Treat coding agent benchmarks as measuring the harness-model PAIR, not the model alone. Implications for QE and consultancy: (1) Do not assume the native harness is optimal — a model may perform better in a customized harness than in its own. (2) When evaluating agents for a client, test the specific harness configuration that will be used in production, not the vendor's demo environment. (3) Post-training coupling means switching models may require harness reconfiguration — the config that works for Claude may not work for GPT and vice versa. (4) For quality assessment: define your own verification criteria based on your actual workflows, not generic benchmarks. (5) Be skeptical of vendor benchmarks — they are optimized for the vendor's own harness.
