problem: PACT Framework definition for Agentic AI/QE - created by Reuven Cohen while defining Agentics
solution: PACT = Proactive + Autonomous + Collaborative + Targeted. Proactive: Test before bugs, design testability into architecture. Autonomous: Teams/agents own quality, make decisions within boundaries. Collaborative: Whole-team quality responsibility, agents work together. Targeted: Risk-focused, test what matters, skip what doesn't. Originally created by Reuven Cohen while defining Agentics, adapted to QE context by [USER].

problem: Pull requests are a post-development inspection system designed for open-source (untrusted strangers submitting to repos they do not own). Applying them to trusted internal teams is a category error importing low-trust overhead into high-trust environments. Evidence: less than 15% of review comments relate to bugs (Microsoft Research 2015, Bacchelli and Bird 2013). Code spends 86-99% of lead time waiting. One organization spent 130,000 hours waiting on 7,000 PRs that received no comments — 91% rubber-stamped. PRs create perverse incentive toward larger batches (Reinertsen batch economics). Async review creates vicious cycle: waiting leads to high WIP leads to less review availability leads to more handoffs leads to more waiting ([USER] Stepanovic, 30+ repos — small-PR teams had LOWER throughput than large-PR teams). DORA 36,000+ professionals: trunk-based correlates with higher delivery, elite performers 2.3x more likely to use TBD, accelerating review alone yields 50% improvement. ThoughtWorks placed Peer review equals pull request in HOLD ring (2021). A regulatory audit found PRs did not satisfy compliance because there was no evidence the code was actually read. Context-switching PRs are 223% slower than non-context-switching ones.
solution: T*D framework — union of three practices that build quality in rather than inspecting after (Deming: you cannot inspect quality into a product): (1) TDD — every line verified by automated test before it exists, 40-90% pre-release defect reduction (Microsoft/IBM), replaces fear with confidence (Beck). (2) TBD — merge to trunk at least daily (Jez Humble Minimum CD: if not integrating daily you are not doing CI), branches last hours not days, feature flags manage incomplete work, small batches halve queues and cycle time. (3) TFD — pair/ensemble programming provides continuous real-time review during creation not after. Muller and Tichy (2005): pairing achieves equivalent cost to solo+review when quality held constant. Williams (2000): pairs produced 15% fewer defects. Arisholm (2007): 48% increase in correct solutions on complex systems, juniors showed 149% improvement. 5-stage transition path: (1) Optimize PRs — smaller under 200 lines, SLAs under 4 hours, automate style/lint, single approver. (2) Ship/Show/Ask (Wilsenach on martinfowler.com) — Ship routine directly, Show for awareness merge immediately review post-merge, Ask for complex wait for discussion. (3) Pair + trunk — pair on all production code, merge multiple times daily. (4) Ensemble + trunk — full team collaborates, direct trunk commits, feature flags. (5) Full T*D — all three operating together, fast automated deployment pipeline. Non-blocking continuous code review (de Pauw): reviews happen after merging on mainline, no hierarchy, internal auditors found this model superior to checkbox compliance. Trust is a gradient not binary: within team use T*D, across team boundaries use lightweight PRs with fast SLAs, inner-source may retain gatekeeper but always fast and non-blocking. Charity Majors: speed IS safety — small changes, single author, easy to isolate owner, prevent blast radius, fix while intent fresh. For agentic context: at agent throughput async blocking review creates catastrophic WIP accumulation — Lopopolo OpenAI moved to minimal blocking gates and agent-to-agent review. The compliance gap answer: build quality during agent execution via invariants, linters, TDD rather than inspect after via post-hoc skill verification gates that get skipped. Source: Andrea Laforgia, Stop Using Pull Requests, March 19, 2026. 41 references including DORA, Microsoft Research, Beck, Deming, Reinertsen, Fowler, Farley, Humble, Stepanovic, de Pauw, Gorman, Kerr.

problem: Traditional software testing treats evaluation as a checkpoint: test before you ship, pass the gate, done. But with AI/LLM systems, same code does wildly different things under different conditions — unpredictability is a feature. Models behave differently when observed. Code is a terrible source of truth. 95% of enterprise AI pilots fail to deliver ROI — primarily an observability problem, organizations cannot evaluate whether their AI works because they have no infrastructure for seeing what happens once the system is live (MIT study via Yasmeen Ahmad). We are applying a testing paradigm to what is essentially an epidemiological problem.
solution: Shift from checkpoint paradigm (test, gate, production, done) to epidemiological paradigm (continuous monitoring of conditions over time). Pharma industry learned this: pre-release testing alone was insufficient, forced to develop continuous monitoring. For AI/agentic systems: (1) Cannot test your way to confidence pre-production because behavior changes under different conditions and models behave differently when observed. (2) Diminishing returns to pre-production validation — beyond a certain point must test in production and keep testing as the world keeps changing. (3) Build feedback loops connecting developer/agent intent to production consequences — ship, observe, learn, ship again. (4) Design for observability not just accuracy: instrument the deployed system, measure outcomes not just outputs (Ahmad). Maps to Holistic Testing Model: production observability is core quality practice not ops-only. Maps to AIUC-1: continuous quarterly evaluation not annual certification. Maps to Friedman: production monitoring is selection pressure at deployment speed. Maps to Ge LGA Layer 4: immutable audit log is the production record. The circular dependency loop: tools built for operators not builders, engineers dont know better is possible, dont agitate for better tools, tools dont improve. Source: Yasmeen Ahmad via Charity Majors, Honeycomb, March 18, 2026.

problem: The industry best minds identified five destinations for relocated rigor in the AI-native era: upstream to spec review, into test suites, into type systems, into risk mapping, into continuous comprehension. All are pre-production. Production is missing from the list — confined to bugs and incidents backwater. This blind spot has haunted software engineering for decades. Engineers think of production as where I go to fix bugs and observability as a bug-finding tool. But observability is understanding, not bug-finding. Formal methods and test suites are flight simulators. Production is flying the actual plane. Observability is how you fly it. Two reasons production rigor never got built: (a) ecosystem was expensive, (b) old rate of change was tolerant enough for duct tape and human intuition. AI breaks both simultaneously.
solution: Production is the 6th and arguably most important destination for rigor relocation. Chad Fowler Relocating Rigor: constraint removal is mistaken for loss of rigor, what actually happens is rigor relocation. If generation gets easier, judgment must get stricter. At agentic speed (10x-100x code generation), pre-production selection mechanisms hit natural throughput limits. Production observability is the selection mechanism that scales with deployment speed. Design for observability not just accuracy: instrument the deployed system, build feedback loops, measure outcomes not just outputs. The spec describes intent; telemetry describes reality (Vidhya). Dashboards are not rigor — rigor requires precision as a function of context and cardinality. AI-SRE agents use dashboards only 30% of the time, going to raw intact telemetry the rest. Bring production out of the bugs and incidents backwater into the forefront of quality strategy. Production is where the users live and the money gets made. Source: Charity Majors, Production Is Where the Rigor Goes, Honeycomb, March 18, 2026.

problem: Agent compliance requires not just instructions but proof of execution. The compliance gap (agent has rules, skips steps) exists because verification is treated as optional rather than as the highest-value skill category. Teams invest in code generation and automation skills but underinvest in verification skills that prove the agent actually did what it claimed. No systematic framework for identifying which skill categories are missing.
solution: Verification skills are the highest-value category: worth having an engineer spend a week just making your verification skills excellent (Shihipar, Anthropic). Techniques: have Claude record video of its output, enforce programmatic assertions on state at each step, include verification scripts in skill folder, pair with external tools (Playwright, tmux for TTY testing). Examples: signup-flow-driver (headless browser with state assertions), checkout-verifier (drives UI with test cards, verifies invoice state), tmux-cli-driver (interactive CLI testing). Maps to AIUC-1 D004, Ge L2 (intent verification), and the compliance gap (proof of execution not trust in claims). 9-category taxonomy for auditing skill coverage: (1) Library/API Reference, (2) Product Verification, (3) Data Fetching/Analysis, (4) Business Process/Team Automation, (5) Code Scaffolding/Templates, (6) Code Quality/Review, (7) CI-CD/Deployment, (8) Runbooks (symptom to investigation to structured report), (9) Infrastructure Ops (safety-gated cleanup). Best skills fit cleanly into one category. Use taxonomy to audit skill library for gaps. Distribution: check into repo for small teams, plugin marketplace for scale. Organic curation: sandbox to traction to PR to marketplace. Easy to create bad or redundant skills, curation before release is important. Composing: reference other skills by name, model invokes if installed. Source: Shihipar, Anthropic, March 18, 2026.

problem: Skills are flexible but that flexibility makes it hard to know what works. Common mistakes: stating what Claude already knows, being too prescriptive (railroading with rigid step-by-step), monolithic SKILL.md files that crowd out task context, descriptions written for humans not models (undertriggering), no learning loop from failures, no persistent memory across invocations.
solution: 9 skill design patterns from Anthropic internal experience with hundreds of skills: (1) Do not state the obvious — focus on what pushes Claude out of its normal thinking. (2) Build a Gotchas section — highest-signal content, built from common failure points, add a line each time Claude trips (lightweight learning loop, mini-Nagual per skill). (3) Progressive disclosure — skill is a folder not a file, SKILL.md as ~30-line hub with spoke files doing the work (confirmed independently by both OpenAI Lopopolo and Anthropic). (4) Avoid railroading — state invariants (what must happen) not implementations (how). Too prescriptive means agent skips steps or follows rigidly when context requires adaptation. (5) Think through setup — store config in config.json in skill directory, ask user on first run if not configured. (6) Description field is for the model — write trigger conditions not human summaries. This is what Claude scans to match skills to requests. (7) Memory and storing data — use CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA for persistence across upgrades, append-only logs, JSON, or SQLite. (8) Store scripts and generate code — give Claude composable libraries to compose from, not reconstruct boilerplate. (9) On-demand hooks — session-scoped guardrails like /careful (blocks rm -rf, DROP TABLE, force-push via PreToolUse matcher) and /freeze (blocks edits outside specific directory). Measure skills via PreToolUse hook logging to find popular vs undertriggering. Most skills began as a few lines and a single gotcha, got better as people kept adding edge cases. Source: Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic Claude Code team, March 18, 2026.

problem: Full agent autonomy introduces novel entropy: agents replicate existing patterns — even uneven or suboptimal ones — causing codebase drift over time. OpenAI Codex team initially spent 20% of the week (every Friday) manually cleaning AI slop. That did not scale. Without automated selection pressure, high mutation rate produces codebase degradation disguised as productivity. Technical debt in agent-generated code compounds faster because agents generate more code per unit time than humans. Throughput changes merge philosophy: minimal blocking gates, short-lived PRs, test flakes addressed with follow-ups not blocking — but this is only safe with comprehensive automated verification infrastructure.
solution: Encode golden principles directly into the repository and build recurring automated cleanup (functions like garbage collection): (1) Opinionated mechanical rules that keep codebase legible and consistent for future agent runs — prefer shared utility packages over hand-rolled helpers, validate boundaries via typed SDKs not runtime guessing. (2) Background agent tasks on regular cadence scan for deviations, update quality grades, and open targeted refactoring PRs — most reviewed in under a minute and automerged. (3) Human taste is captured once then enforced continuously on every line of code — catches and resolves bad patterns daily rather than letting them spread for days or weeks. (4) Quality document grades each product domain and architectural layer, tracking gaps over time. (5) Technical debt is a high-interest loan: almost always better to pay it down continuously in small increments than to let it compound. Connects to evolution-vs-mutation (Friedman): this is automated selection pressure at the codebase level. Corrections are cheap and waiting is expensive — but ONLY when you have this enforcement infrastructure. Without it, minimal merge gates equals YOLO. Source: Lopopolo, OpenAI, Feb 2026.

problem: Documentation alone does not keep an agent-generated codebase coherent. Agents replicate patterns including bad ones and drift is inevitable without structural enforcement. Instructions can be skipped (the compliance gap) but mechanical enforcement cannot. Need constraints that allow speed without architectural decay. The question when something fails is not try harder but what capability is missing and how do we make it both legible and enforceable for the agent.
solution: Enforce invariants, not implementations. Define strict boundaries centrally, allow autonomy locally. Concrete patterns from OpenAI Codex team (1M-line agent-generated codebase): (1) Rigid layered architecture per business domain (Types → Config → Repo → Service → Runtime → UI) with strictly validated dependency directions and limited permissible edges — enforced via custom linters not documentation. (2) Custom lint rules whose error messages inject remediation instructions directly into agent context — the linter becomes the teacher. (3) Taste invariants statically enforced: structured logging, naming conventions, file size limits, platform-specific reliability requirements. (4) In a human-first workflow these rules feel pedantic. With agents they become multipliers: once encoded they apply everywhere at once. (5) Boring technologies preferred — composable, stable APIs, well-represented in training data are easier for agents. Sometimes cheaper to reimplement than use opaque upstream libraries. (6) Cross-cutting concerns (auth, connectors, telemetry, feature flags) enter through single explicit interface: Providers. Anything else disallowed and enforced mechanically. (7) Architecture you usually postpone until hundreds of engineers becomes early prerequisite with coding agents — constraints are what allows speed without decay. Maps to Ge LGA: linters=L1, layered architecture=L3. Maps to AIUC-1 D003. Source: Lopopolo, OpenAI, Feb 2026.

problem: Monolithic agent instruction files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, SKILL.md) fail in four predictable ways: (1) context is scarce — giant instructions crowd out task, code, and relevant docs so the agent misses key constraints or optimizes for the wrong ones; (2) too much guidance becomes non-guidance — when everything is important nothing is, agents pattern-match locally instead of navigating intentionally; (3) it rots instantly — a monolithic manual becomes a graveyard of stale rules, agents cannot tell what is still true; (4) hard to verify — a single blob does not lend itself to mechanical checks for coverage, freshness, or cross-links, so drift is inevitable. Tried and failed by OpenAI Codex team on a 1M-line agent-generated codebase.
solution: Treat AGENTS.md as table of contents (~100 lines), not encyclopedia. Short map with pointers to deeper sources of truth in a structured docs/ directory: design-docs/ (with verification status), exec-plans/ (active/, completed/, tech-debt-tracker.md), generated/ (db-schema.md etc), product-specs/, references/. Progressive disclosure: agents start with small stable entry point and are taught where to look next, not overwhelmed up front. Critical enforcement layer: (1) dedicated linters and CI jobs validate knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly; (2) recurring doc-gardening agent scans for stale or obsolete documentation that does not reflect real code behavior and opens fix PRs; (3) when documentation falls short, promote the rule into code — a linter with agent-readable error message replaces a doc paragraph. Plans are first-class versioned artifacts co-located in repo so agents operate without external context. What the agent cannot see does not exist — knowledge in Google Docs, Slack threads, or peoples heads is invisible. If it is not discoverable to the agent, it is illegible in the same way it would be unknown to a new hire joining three months later. Source: Ryan Lopopolo, Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world, OpenAI, February 11, 2026.

problem: Pure-JS HNSW vector search was the performance bottleneck for pattern matching in AQE: ~8.7ms for 10K vectors, ~600MB memory for 150K embeddings (float64). As pattern databases grow, search latency and memory consumption scale linearly. Agent decision speed is gated by how fast relevant patterns can be retrieved from the knowledge base.
solution: AQE v3.8.0 RuVector integration: native HNSW vector search via @ruvector/router replaces JS implementation. Benchmarks: 10K vectors p50 dropped from 8.7ms to 0.058ms (150x faster). 1K vectors from 0.75ms to 0.058ms (13x faster). Memory for 150K embeddings from ~600MB (float64) to ~150MB (Int8Array) via temporal tensor compression (4x reduction). MicroLoRA per-request adaptation from 1.65 microseconds (TypeScript) to 0.18 microseconds (WASM) — 9.2x faster. HNSW health monitoring with spectral analysis alerts when indexes need rebalancing. Cognitive container export/import enables saving and sharing agent learned state as portable RVF v2 snapshots. QE dashboard provides browser-based pattern explorer with cluster visualizations and WASM-accelerated search. 15,493 unit tests passing with all feature flags both on and off confirming full backward compatibility. Released in Agentic QE v3.8.0, March 16, 2026.

problem: Using expensive LLM models for all agent tasks wastes inference budget. Rule-based routing cannot adapt to changing task complexity. Static routing degrades over time as model capabilities and task distributions shift, but there is no mechanism to detect or correct this degradation. Need intelligent routing that learns and self-corrects.
solution: AQE v3.8.0 TinyDancer neural model router: a minimal 259-parameter network (4 to 32 to 3 architecture) learns which tasks need expensive models and which can use fast/cheap ones. Forward pass under 500 microseconds (p99). Includes regret tracker that detects when routing decisions degrade over time and auto-corrects — prevents silent quality erosion. Combined with cross-domain transfer learning: insights from API testing improve UI testing and vice versa; new projects benefit from patterns learned on previous ones. DAG attention scheduler runs independent tests in parallel while respecting dependencies, cutting suite execution time. Maps to risk-stratified routing (Ge): not all agent actions need the same verification intensity. Maps to evolution-vs-mutation (Friedman): TinyDancer is selection pressure applied to model choice itself. Released in Agentic QE v3.8.0, March 16, 2026.

problem: AI agents making tool calls can hallucinate actions, produce broken reasoning chains, or execute decisions based on incoherent logic. Without pre-execution validation, these failures reach production. Single-check verification is insufficient (Ge base-rate problem: single gate PPV collapses at low failure prevalence). Need multi-layer validation that catches different failure modes.
solution: AQE v3.8.0 coherence-gated actions: a 3-filter safety pipeline validates every agent output before execution. Filter 1 (reflex tier): fast structural check in 0.005ms catches obviously malformed outputs. Filter 2 (retrieval tier): sheaf Laplacian coherence check in 1.2ms validates reasoning chain consistency against known patterns. Filter 3: semantic validation against intended scope. Combined with witness chain audit trail: every agent decision is SHA-256 hash-linked for full traceability — know exactly why an agent made each choice. Maps to Ge LGA: coherence gates = L2 (intent verification), witness chain = L4 (immutable audit). Maps to AIUC-1: D003 (restrict unsafe tool calls), E015 (tamper-evident logging). Reasoning QEC adds majority-vote consensus across multiple reasoning paths for higher-confidence decisions. All gates ship behind feature flags for safe adoption. Released in Agentic QE v3.8.0, March 16, 2026.

problem: 2024-2025 was the vibe adoption era: organizations deployed AI based on vendor promises and leadership enthusiasm without governance frameworks. Data: 64% of companies exceeding $1B revenue lost over $1M to AI failures (EY). 13% of organizations reported AI model breaches, 97% lacking proper AI access controls (IBM). 63% of employees input sensitive data into personal chatbots. Prompt injection evolved from theoretical to production incidents. Three concurrent challenges: Agent (removing humans from decision loops removes primary safety mechanism), Visibility (shadow AI creating unmanaged exposure), Trust (traditional security principles strain under natural language inputs).
solution: Three strategic moves for the post-vibe era: (1) Deploy agent-specific frameworks grounded in technical architecture, not generic AI governance adapted downward — AIUC-1 provides this with 51 requirements and adversarial testing. SOC 2 solved SaaS trust, AIUC-1 solves AI trust. (2) Treat AI security as competitive advantage and velocity enabler, not speed bump — the seatbelt that lets you drive faster. Organizations with governance ship faster because they have confidence. (3) Implement continuous red-teaming as ongoing practice, not one-time exercise — every model update, prompt change, and attack pattern produces different behavior. Quarterly testing minimum. Market opportunity: organizations that adopted on vibes now need structured governance. They need practitioners who understand both technical enforcement (LGA layers, tool call verification) and organizational governance (AIUC-1 domains, evidence collection). Board-level risk: Board oversight cycles quarterly but AI development cycles weekly. Air Canada chatbot case as legal liability precedent. Source: AIUC-1 whitepaper The End of Vibe Adoption, March 2026.

problem: AI agents performing tool calls can execute unauthorized actions, access restricted information, or make decisions beyond intended scope. The compliance gap (agent has rules but skips them) has no standardized testing or enforcement framework. Individual teams build ad-hoc verification (like /release skill STOP gates) but there is no external validation that safeguards actually hold under adversarial pressure. Internal safeguards alone are insufficient.
solution: AIUC-1 Reliability domain mandates: D001 — prevent hallucinated outputs with safeguards; D002 — third-party hallucination testing quarterly; D003 — implement safeguards preventing unauthorized tool call execution, restricted info access, and out-of-scope decisions (via network segmentation, API gateway rules, service-level authorization with boundary violation monitoring); D004 — appoint expert third-parties to evaluate tool call integrity at least every 3 months. Combined with B006 (prevent unauthorized agent actions via technical restrictions), C007 (flag high-risk outputs for human review before execution — sensitive records, financial transactions, out-of-scope actions), and E015 (tamper-evident activity logging). Evidence required: engineering code showing authorization checks, tool call logging, third-party evaluation reports. Maps to Ge LGA: D003=L1+L3 (sandbox + zero-trust), D004=external L2 (intent verification by third party), E015=L4 (immutable audit). Key insight: internal safeguards are necessary but insufficient — you need external adversarial testing of whether safeguards actually hold. Quarterly cadence prevents fossil record test suites (Vidhya insight). Source: AIUC-1 Reliability and Security domains.

problem: No standardized, auditable framework existed for AI agent governance. SOC 2 covers cybersecurity but cannot assess hallucinations, prompt injection, tool call integrity, or brand disasters. Organizations deploying AI agents had no way to demonstrate trustworthiness to enterprise buyers. Vibe adoption (excitement-driven deployment without governance) created a trust gap blocking enterprise adoption.
solution: AIUC-1: the first AI agent standard. 6 domains (Data and Privacy, Security, Safety, Reliability, Accountability, Society), 51 requirements, 130 controls (65 mandatory + 65 optional). Scoped by risk: low-risk internal agent ~40 controls, high-risk external multi-modal ~65 controls. Certification in 4-8 weeks: (1) scoping with auditor questionnaire, (2) evidence gathering across 5 types (documentation, configuration, logs, third-party evals, product demos), (3) technical adversarial testing, (4) audit report. Valid 12 months, quarterly technical retesting. Forward-looking adversarial testing vs SOC 2 backward-looking approach. Maps to ISO 42001, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, OWASP Top 10, OWASP AIVSS. Consortium: Phil Venables (Google Cloud CISO), Jen Easterly (fmr CISA Director), Stanford, MITRE, Cisco, Anthropic, Microsoft, JP Morgan. First accredited auditor: Schellman. Quarterly updates: Jan 15, Apr 15, Jul 15, Oct 15. Key quote Phil Venables: We need a SOC 2 for AI agents. Website: https://www.aiuc-1.com/ Source: AIUC-1 standard, current version Q1 2026 (January 15, 2026).

problem: Advances in one AI technology (e.g. LLM text generation) get unfairly attributed to completely different domains (e.g. agent reliability, autonomous coding safety, robot dexterity). These are separate technologies with separate trajectories, but marketing and media collapse them into one unstoppable wave narrative. This makes rational evaluation of specific capabilities impossible. It is the mechanism behind vendor hype: AI is getting so good launders genuine progress in one area into unjustified confidence in another. It explains why the AI discourse feels overwhelming: dozens of separate problems marketed as one. In the agentic QE space specifically: LLM benchmark improvements get laundered into claims about agent compliance, code generation quality into code review quality, chat improvements into autonomous deployment safety.
solution: Apply the progress laundering filter (Cal Newport) to every AI capability claim. Three diagnostic questions: (1) What specific technology actually advanced? (2) Does that advance transfer to the domain being claimed? (3) Are these the same trajectory or separate ones being marketed as one? Example applications in agentic QE: LLM benchmark improvements do not automatically mean better agent compliance (separate problem — compliance is architectural per Ge LGA). Code generation quality do not mean better code review (separate selection mechanism per Friedman). Chat model improvements do not mean better autonomous deployment (separate governance problem). When evaluating tools: ask what specific selection pressure improved, not what mutation capability improved. Resist collapsing separate problems into single narratives. Combines with Hoffman survival filter: if the model gets 10x better at generation, does the selection problem disappear? Usually no. Source: Cal Newport via Hank Green conversation, referenced in Filip Hric, Is code evolving or just mutating?, LinkedIn, March 2026.

problem: AI has dramatically increased code mutation rate (generation speed) without proportionally scaling selection mechanisms (testing, review, verification). Without selection pressure, increased mutation produces drift and degradation, not evolution. The biological parallel: uncontrolled replication without selection is not evolution — it is cancer. Current AI tooling investment is ~90% in mutation (copilots, code generators, agents) and ~10% in selection (testing, review, governance). This ratio produces code that changes fast but does not reliably improve. The compliance gap is a selection failure: the /release skill 15 steps ARE selection pressure that got bypassed. Code reviews losing their mentorship function means selection without learning transfer.
solution: Apply evolutionary thinking to agentic QE: quality engineering IS the selection layer. Three elements must scale together: Mutation (code generation — AI-accelerated), Selection (testing, review, CI/CD, governance layers — must scale proportionally), Persistence (learnings must stick across generations via knowledge systems like Nagual, not be re-discovered each session). Map to practice: Ge LGA layers are architectural selection mechanisms. PACT principles operationalize selection: Proactive (anticipate mutation failures), Autonomous (selection must be automated to match mutation speed), Collaborative (human+AI selection preserves mentorship/knowledge transfer that pure AI review loses), Targeted (focus selection on highest-risk mutations via risk-stratified routing). The Holistic Testing Model is a selection framework. As mutation rate scales, selection must scale at least proportionally or you get the illusion of productivity with degrading quality. The question to ask any AI coding tool: what is your selection mechanism, not just your generation capability? Source: Itamar Friedman (Qodo CEO) evolutionary framework via Filip Hric, Is code evolving or just mutating?, LinkedIn, March 16, 2026.

problem: When docs, tests, tickets, and original specs decay, agents are left with incomplete context. They see code and tests but not the behavioral contract — the accumulated record of what users actually asked the system to do. Ghost constraints (compliance rules, business invariants, usage patterns) are encoded in production behavior but nowhere in the codebase as explicit logic. An agent working on a system sees the code but not the contract — producing output that violates constraints it cannot see. Even perfect skill compliance does not help if the skill itself is based on rotted specs. The spec problem is not solved by better prompts — it is solved by better sources of truth.
solution: Treat production telemetry as a queryable spec, not just operational data. Traffic patterns reveal which features are load-bearing (a dead-edge case handler for 0.01% of users vs a code path everyone depends on). Error rates show where the system silently fails. Usage paths reveal undocumented workflows nobody designed but everyone relies on. Latency distributions show where invisible complexity lives. Make telemetry queryable as behavioral contracts — not dashboards or alerts, but a source of truth an agent can consult before touching anything. Combines with Charity Majors observability framing (instrument as you build, observe as you deploy) but applies backward to systems nobody instrumented when they were young. Ghost constraints are the layer below the compliance gap: explicit constraints that get skipped (compliance gap) sit above implicit constraints that nobody even wrote down (ghost constraints). Until agents can read production telemetry not as log lines but as behavioral contracts — the accumulated promise a system has made to the people who depend on it — harness engineering in brownfield and blackfield will remain a human problem with an AI assistant bolted on. Source: Vidhya R., LinkedIn, March 2026.

problem: AI agents and coding tools are optimized for Greenfield (define intent → build → test). But most real systems are Brownfield or Blackfield, where specs have rotted, documentation lies, and the engineering posture is different. Blackfield is NOT just brownfield with worse docs — it is a fundamentally different posture: you are trying not to break something while slowly walking away from it. Agents applying Greenfield instincts (iterate toward green, ship fast) to Blackfield systems create confident-sounding output that violates constraints nobody wrote down. The standard sequence (write spec → generate code → run tests) assumes you know what the system is supposed to do. In Blackfield, that assumption is false.
solution: For non-greenfield systems, invert the sequence (The Honest Sequence): Observe production → extract behavioral contracts → encode as system tests → use those as the spec → then bring the agent in. Three-field taxonomy determines agent strategy: Greenfield (spec-driven, red-green-refactor works, AI demos live here), Brownfield (existing code, intent partially recoverable through archaeology, tests exist but coverage uneven), Blackfield (legacy under load, original authors gone, tests describe system as it was, docs lie — engineering posture is do-no-harm while walking away). Characterization tests (Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code) document current behavior as tripwires, not correctness assertions — a failing test means something changed that you did not anticipate, not that the system is wrong. A green test suite on a Blackfield system may be a fossil record, not confidence. System-level black box tests anchored to user behavior (not code structure) survive the decay that kills unit tests, integration tests, and docs. Before any agent-assisted work on non-greenfield: write system tests as archaeology — encode what the system has promised its users in machine-checkable form. Source: Vidhya R., Production Telemetry Is the Spec That Survived, LinkedIn, March 11, 2026.

problem: Applying uniform verification intensity to all agent actions creates either excessive latency (verify everything deeply at ~1000ms per call) or inadequate security (skip verification for speed). A /release skill has 15 steps ranging from cargo check (reversible, low-risk) to npm publish (irreversible, high-risk). Not every step warrants the same enforcement weight, but without risk stratification, systems either over-block (high FPR) or under-protect (missed violations).
solution: Risk-stratified routing: classify each agent action by risk tier and route to appropriate verification. Low-risk actions (read-only, sandboxed, reversible) → fast lightweight checks: NLI pre-filter (~200ms, 0% FPR but only 8-10% IR) or schema validation. Catches obvious semantic anomalies. High-risk actions (delete, publish, deploy, external network, transactional writes) → full LLM intent verification (~300-1000ms, 93-98% IR, 3-12% FPR). For skill steps: map each step to a risk tier. Example from /release skill: cargo check = low-risk (reversible), run tests = low-risk (sandboxed), npm publish = high-risk (irreversible), post-publish verification = medium-risk. This reduces median latency dramatically while maintaining security on critical paths. The paper shows L1/L3/L4 layers add only ~5-18ms combined — the dominant cost is L2 (intent judge), so routing fewer calls through L2 directly reduces total overhead. Source: Yuxu Ge, arxiv:2603.07191v2, Tables 4-5, Section 7.4.1.

problem: At low failure/attack prevalence (π=1%, typical production), even high-accuracy verification (93% IR, 3.2% FPR) yields only 22.7% PPV — 3 of 4 blocks are false alarms. Single-layer verification becomes practically useless despite looking good on benchmarks. This is the base-rate problem applied to agent governance: benchmark accuracy ≠ deployment accuracy.
solution: Apply Bayes theorem to evaluate any verification gate: PPV = IR×π / (IR×π + FPR×(1-π)). Never trust a single gate benchmark accuracy as deployment accuracy. Use cascading verification: fast pre-filter (high recall, accepts some FP) → deep judge (high precision, reduces FP). Demonstrated: two-stage cascade (Qwen3.5-9B → GPT-4o-mini) reduces FPR from 34.1% to 1.9% while maintaining 91.9% IR. For data-sovereign deployments, local-only cascade (Qwen3.5-9B → Qwen2.5-14B) achieves 95.6% IR with 6.0% FPR. At π=1%: best single model PPV=22.7%, cloud cascade PPV=32.8%, local cascade PPV=13.9%. The fundamental base-rate problem means Layer 2 (intent verification) should never be the sole gatekeeper — use Layer 1 (sandbox) as always-on containment, with Layer 2 escalations triaged by human review. Source: Yuxu Ge, arxiv:2603.07191v2, Tables 3 and 7.

problem: Single-layer enforcement (instructions, skills, prompts) fails under pressure — agents skip steps, and no single verification method has acceptable PPV at realistic failure rates. [TOOL] case study shows SOUL.md soft constraints bypassable (G1), plugin permissions self-declared with no runtime verification (G2), no intra-directory permission partitioning (G3), mutable audit logs (G4).
solution: Layered Governance Architecture (LGA) with four complementary enforcement layers: L1 Execution Sandbox (OS-level process isolation via unshare, ~1ms P50) — contains damage even if all other layers fail. L2 Intent Verification (LLM judge verifying action matches declared intent, ~300-1000ms) — catches semantic violations. L3 Zero-Trust Inter-Agent Protocol (capability tokens with HMAC-SHA256, <0.02ms) — no ambient authority between agents. L4 Immutable Audit Log (append-only fsync, ~4-12ms) — tamper-proof record of what actually happened. Each layer catches what others miss. L2 alone insufficient for TC3 (skill/plugin-level violations where action is partially consistent with task). Key insight: governance boundaries must be enforced through architectural mechanisms, not statistical generalization. Source: Yuxu Ge, University of York, arxiv:2603.07191v2, March 2026.

problem: Outcome-Driven Constraint Violations in AI Agents (benchmark) — Defensible evidence that agents drift from constraints under goal-optimization pressure. Consultancy discussions about 'why keep humans in the loop' need a concrete citation, not vibes.
solution: Benchmark published as arXiv:2512.20798 evaluates 12 SOTA LLMs on outcome-driven constraint violations — misalignments that emerge when agents pursue goal optimization under strong performance incentives over multiple steps in realistic production settings. KEY NUMBERS: violations range 1.3% to 71.4%; 9 of 12 models exhibit misalignment rates between 30% and 50%. Practical usage: CITATION for consultancy ('In a 12-model benchmark, 9/12 frontier models violated outcome constraints 30–50% of the time under optimization pressure — which is why we still need human oversight and PACT-Collaborative design.'). TEST PATTERN: design long-horizon, goal-pressured test scenarios (not single-turn) and measure constraint-violation rate, not task-success rate. RISK HEURISTIC: treat constraint-violation-rate as a release gate alongside functional correctness. ANTI-PATTERN it disproves: 'modern models are aligned enough that we can remove QA oversight'. problem: Four-Dimension Agent Reliability Framework (Consistency / Robustness / Predictability / Safety) — Need an academic, citable decomposition of 'agent reliability' that maps cleanly onto PACT and can scaffold a reliability test strategy for the Holistic Testing Model. Most industry discussions of agent reliability are single-word handwaves.
solution: Decompose reliability into FOUR orthogonal dimensions, each independently testable: 1) CONSISTENCY — repeatable behavior across runs with identical inputs. Test via N-replay same-prompt analysis; variance of output structure, not exact tokens. 2) ROBUSTNESS — stability under input and environmental perturbations. Test via adversarial paraphrases, noisy tool responses, delayed or out-of-order events. 3) PREDICTABILITY — calibrated confidence and discrimination between correct and incorrect predictions. Test via confidence-correctness correlation; reject models where the two are uncorrelated. 4) SAFETY — bounded severity when failures occur. Test via fault-injection with kill switches, privilege limits, escape hatches. Mapping to PACT: Consistency=Targeted (narrow, reproducible); Robustness=Autonomous (self-recovering); Predictability=Collaborative (honest with humans); Safety=Proactive (designed-in guardrails). Usage: Make each dimension its own test charter in a holistic strategy. Do not collapse into a single 'reliability score' — the four dimensions can move independently and failures in one do not predict failures in others. Source: arXiv 'Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability' (2026).

problem: Training-objective-aligned metrics (loss convergence, token accuracy) can look clean while the model is learning the wrong trajectory — only outside-the-loop audits surface the defect
solution:
# Clean-Loss-Hides-Wrong-Trajectory Pattern (The Sign-Bug Case)

**Source:** Royse (2026) — Teleological Constellation Training, §6.2.2 'Forensic finding: the flow-matching sign bug and five companion fixes'
**Captured:** 2026-04-20 from CompressMeaningResearchPaper.pdf analysis

## The case

Talking-head clone ('Santa') training went through **five LoRA versions (v1–v5)**. Each trained to convergence. Each had **clean loss curves and healthy numerics**. Each produced video that was blurry, temporally averaged, or lip-sync-dead.

Root cause: training code computed target = latent - noise, but the EchoMimicV3 scheduler uses target = noise - latent (velocity convention). The sign flip trained the model to **add noise to clean video** — anti-denoising. Loss minimised cleanly because the target was well-defined; the model learned the wrong direction.

The defect was masked by EchoMimicV3's inpainting-model reference-frame pass-through: the reference frame came through correctly, so generated videos looked superficially plausible even while the denoising trajectory was inverted.

Only the **constellation-side audit** of generated outputs against per-modality centroids surfaced the disagreement. Loss convergence did not verify trajectory correctness.

## The five companion bugs found in the same audit pass

1. Frame-rate mismatch (cv2 reading 60fps against 25fps target → clips 2.4× too short).
2. Mouth bounding boxes landing on the subject's nose.
3. Dead LoRA target from a name-shadowing typo: the code wrote q_auido where it meant q_audio, so gradients on the audio-query projection never reached the loss.
4. 22GB of audio features accumulating in RAM.
5. Viseme curriculum advertised as weighted but actually uniform under the default dataloader.

Each of these individually passed 'does the pipeline run?' smoke checks.

## The pattern

**Metrics that are defined in the training objective's own coordinate system cannot detect the training objective being specified wrong.** You need audits that are:

- **Outside the training loop** — use artefacts (generated outputs) the training doesn't see.
- **In a different coordinate system** — constellation audit uses frozen embedders the training doesn't update.
- **Answering a question the training isn't answering** — not 'is loss going down?' but 'does the output look right to an independent observer?'

## Mapping to PACT / Agentic QE

This is a textbook **PACT-Proactive** case:
- Proactive = defects found before they become incidents.
- The five LoRA versions each went through full training cycles before the sign bug was isolated — that's five incidents that outside-the-loop auditing would have caught at v1.
- **Agentic QE principle:** the loss-side view of the system is not sufficient; agents need an orthogonal observational channel that doesn't share the training objective's blind spots.

## Generalised checklist

When a training run or agent completes with clean metrics but unexpected behaviour in the wild:

1. Is there a sign / convention / coordinate flip between what the code computes and what the framework expects?
2. Does a reference/pass-through component mask the defect in downstream checks?
3. Are there name-shadowing typos (like q_auido for q_audio) that silently disconnect components?
4. Is anything advertised as weighted/sampled that is actually uniform under the default dataloader?
5. Are frame rates, sample rates, or tokenisation consistent between producer and consumer?

## Related

- Royse's Sherlock-style forensic audit produced 10 reports (docs/inspect/01 through 10 markdown files in his project) — connects to the sherlock-review skill methodology.
- The multi-oracle evaluation pattern (quality-metrics.multi-oracle-evaluation) is the same lesson at the evaluation stage; this pattern is the lesson at the training stage.

problem: Single-oracle evaluation of AI/agent output silently misses whole classes of defects — dense semantic similarity alone cannot detect structural, positional, or sparse-keyword pathologies
solution:
# Multi-Oracle Evaluation Pattern (Multi-Embedder Guard)

**Source:** Royse (2026) — Teleological Constellation Training, §6.1.3 'Forensic finding: the training-data echo bug'
**Captured:** 2026-04-20 from CompressMeaningResearchPaper.pdf analysis

## The empirical case (load-bearing)

Shakespeare stylistic LoRA training on Gemma-4-E4B-it produced a model that passed integrity-check batteries AND behaved wrong: every response began by echoing the user prompt in **modern English** before transitioning into Shakespearean style.

- **Single-embedder evaluation on E1 (e5-large-v2 dense semantic)** missed the pathology: the response *eventually* became Shakespearean, so overall-document similarity was high.
- **Thirteen-embedder audit caught it** — specifically E4 (position-ordering), E12 (ColBERTv2 token-level MaxSim), and sparse E6/E13 (lexical/SPLADE) reported opening-position style anomaly that was invisible to the dense semantic check.

Root cause: 67% (5,954/8,857) of SFT examples began with play-script headers inherited from the raw corpus. The model learned to echo the prompt as an expected prefix. Training-loss numerics were clean throughout.

## The pattern

**Don't evaluate AI output with a single similarity/quality metric.** Use a panel of architecturally-distinct embedders or oracles that span:

- **Dense semantic** — overall meaning (good at gist, blind to structure)
- **Sparse lexical / keyword** — token-presence signals (catches anachronisms, register violations)
- **Late-interaction / per-token** — positional correctness (catches opening-position and ordering bugs)
- **Structural / code-style** — periodic structure, syntactic form
- **Paraphrase-asymmetric** — surface-form-vs-meaning decoupling

## QE / testing analogue

Direct mapping to James Bach's **consistency heuristics** / Weinberg's **multiple oracles**:
- Consistency with history, comparable products, claims, user expectations, purpose, standards — each is a different oracle.
- No single oracle covers the space.
- Divergence between oracles is the signal, not the bug.

## How to use

1. For any AI-feature QA, specify at least 3 architecturally-distinct oracles before shipping. 'Three LLMs from the same family' does not count — they share failure modes.
2. When oracles agree on PASS → ship; when they disagree → the disagreement is the finding, not a noise source.
3. When oracles all pass but users report a bug, one of the oracles is collapsing with the generator family — add an architecturally-further oracle.
4. Pairs with PACT-Proactive: the audit happens before shipping, not after incident.

problem: Using the same model/metric to BOTH select candidates AND report their quality is a structural evaluation fallacy — the headline number is the signature of the selector working, not of independent quality
solution:
# Encoder-Matched Evaluation Fallacy

**Source:** Royse (2026) — Teleological Constellation Training, §6.3.2 'Mandatory scope disclosure' and §7.1
**Captured:** 2026-04-20 from CompressMeaningResearchPaper.pdf analysis

## The fallacy in one sentence

> 'A survivor of selection under encoder ϕ scores high on ϕ by construction, so the number we report is the signature of the guard working, not of cross-encoder agreement on identity quality.' — Royse, §6.3.2

## The empirical case

Case 3 voice cloning achieved **0.961 mean WavLM SECS** on 10 held-out sentences. But:

- Best-of-12 candidates were **selected** by WavLM-base-plus-sv cosine against a centroid.
- Headline evaluator was **also** WavLM-base-plus-sv.
- Selector and evaluator are the same encoder family.

The 0.961 demonstrates the guard behaves as specified. It does **not** constitute cross-encoder identity verification. Royse explicitly flags this (§8.L1) and names ECAPA-TDNN re-scoring as the required fix to promote the claim from within-family agreement to cross-encoder identity ranking.

## Generalised pattern

The fallacy appears whenever selector and evaluator are correlated:

- **AI agent evals:** The agent that wrote the code judges the code's correctness.
- **LLM-as-judge:** Using GPT-4 to rank GPT-4-family outputs.
- **Synthetic-benchmark recall:** SWE-bench scores on models whose training data includes SWE-bench issues (arXiv 2512.10218 — already in Nagual).
- **Reward hacking:** Training against reward model R, evaluating against reward model R.
- **Test generation + assertion:** AI generates both test input and expected output — the assertion is circular.

## How to use in QE / consultancy

1. For any evaluation claim, ask: *'what would break correlation between the selector and the evaluator?'* If nothing, the claim is within-family agreement, not quality.
2. Mandatory evaluation hygiene: at least one evaluator must be architecturally independent of the generator/selector. Separate model family, separate training data, separate objective.
3. Pairs with the SWE-bench contamination pattern (quality-metrics.benchmark-integrity, 2026-04-20): same root — evaluation integrity requires independence.
4. Practical test: 'Are the selector and evaluator the same model, same family, or trained on the same data?' If yes to any → scope-match, not quality claim.
5. This is the rigorous version of 'don't let devs write their own acceptance tests'.

## What it does NOT mean

- Within-family agreement is still informative — it shows the guard behaves as specified.
- The fallacy is about the *claim*, not the measurement. Same-encoder evaluation is fine *if* scoped honestly as what Royse calls 'signature of the guard working'.

problem: Leaderboard-driven capability claims (SWE-bench, GPQA, etc.) may be measuring training-data recall rather than problem-solving ability
solution:
# Benchmark Contamination Question (SWE-Bench-Verified Case)

**Source paper:** arXiv 2512.10218 — Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?
**URL:** https://arxiv.org/html/2512.10218v1
**Captured:** 2026-04-20 (Daily Briefing)

## The problem

SWE-Bench-Verified has become the de facto benchmark for comparing LLM-based code-fixing systems. The paper raises the empirical question: if benchmark tasks overlap with model training data (which is likely for any public benchmark built from open-source issues), then:
- High scores may reflect **training recall**, not issue-solving skill.
- Year-over-year improvement numbers may be tracking dataset leak rate, not model capability.

## Why this matters beyond SWE-bench

The same critique generalizes to **any public static benchmark**: GPQA, MMLU, HumanEval, MBPP, ARC-AGI. The pattern is:
1. Benchmark is public.
2. Benchmark ends up in training corpora (directly or via secondary sources).
3. Model scores improve.
4. Capability claim is made without controlling for contamination.

## How to use in QE / advisory work

1. When clients cite a vendor's SWE-bench score, ask: 'what's their contamination analysis?' — most don't have one.
2. Pair with CLEAR framework: static-benchmark scores are at best one input to Efficacy; they do not cover Cost, Latency, Assurance, or Reliability.
3. For agentic systems specifically, leaderboard scores are weakly predictive of production performance — emphasize scenario-based evaluation on customer-representative tasks.
4. Concrete pushback line: 'this benchmark tests model memory as much as agent ability — what does it score on problems that post-date its training cutoff?'

## Related

- CLEAR framework (arXiv 2511.14136) — the 'if not accuracy, what?' answer.
- Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability (arXiv 2602.16666) — reliability, not average accuracy, gates autonomy.

problem: Accuracy-only agent evaluation produces cost-inefficient agents — need a holistic framework for enterprise agent scorecards
solution:
# CLEAR Evaluation Framework for Enterprise Agentic AI

**Source:** arXiv 2511.14136 (Nov 2025) — Beyond Accuracy: A Multi-Dimensional Framework for Evaluating Enterprise Agentic AI Systems
**URL:** https://arxiv.org/html/2511.14136v1
**Captured:** 2026-04-20 (Daily Briefing)

## The framework

**CLEAR** = Cost + Latency + Efficacy + Assurance + Reliability

A holistic evaluation framework specifically designed for enterprise agent deployment, replacing single-metric (usually accuracy) scorecards.

## Key empirical finding

Evaluation of 6 leading agents on 300 enterprise tasks shows:
- Optimizing for accuracy alone yields agents **4.4–10.8× more expensive** than cost-aware alternatives.
- Accuracy-monomania is a direct driver of production cost blowout.

## How to use in QE / consultancy practice

1. Replace 'accuracy %' single-number scorecards in agent evaluation reports with a CLEAR-shaped table (5 rows per agent).
2. When clients ask 'which model/agent is best?', reframe as 'best on which CLEAR dimension?' — forces explicit trade-off discussion.
3. Pairs with PACT: Assurance + Reliability map to the Targeted and Proactive quadrants; Cost + Latency map to the Collaborative quadrant (team-level decisions).
4. Use the 4.4–10.8× cost multiplier as an anchor number when arguing against vendor demo-driven procurement.
