   Advisor (Opus): call when — failure cannot be explained by the immediately visible code, multiple tests fail with no obvious common cause, failure pattern suggests systemic issue not a single bug
   Escalation prompt: "Call advisor() when 3+ tests fail with no common dependency, or when a test fails in a way that contradicts previous passing runs with no code change visible."

2. EXPLORATORY TESTING AGENTS
   Executor (Sonnet): navigates the application, probes features, collects observations, documents findings
   Advisor (Opus): call when — a newly discovered behaviour warrants a dedicated test charter, an observation suggests a risk area that needs a targeted investigation strategy, the session has produced conflicting observations that need synthesis
   Escalation prompt: "Call advisor() before defining a new test charter, or when you observe behaviour that contradicts the expected model."

3. CODE REVIEW AGENTS
   Executor (Sonnet): structural review, naming, test coverage, obvious code smells
   Advisor (Opus): call when — architectural decision is embedded in the change, security implication is non-obvious, change touches a risk-critical component
   Escalation prompt: "Call advisor() when the change modifies authentication, data persistence, or public API contracts."

4. TEST STRATEGY AGENTS
   Executor (Sonnet): gathers context, enumerates features, identifies existing test coverage
   Advisor (Opus): call at start (plan the strategy) and after evidence gathering (validate approach before finalising)
   This matches the two-timing-points insight: early (planning) + late (validation).

5. REQUIREMENTS QUALITY AGENTS
   Executor (Sonnet): parses requirements, checks format, identifies missing fields
   Advisor (Opus): call when — requirements contradict each other, acceptance criteria are ambiguous, a requirement has untestable language

HOLISTIC TESTING MODEL INTEGRATION:
The executor-advisor split maps onto the quadrants: executor handles automation-layer activities (unit, integration, API testing execution), advisor handles strategic-layer activities (risk assessment, test charter definition, failure diagnosis, coverage decisions).

IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: Each QE agent type needs its own escalation criteria prompt, tuned to its domain. Generic escalation criteria produce generic results. The escalation prompt IS the quality gate.

Source: https://claude.com/blog/the-advisor-strategy + practitioner synthesis

problem: How do you write reliable test assertions for generative AI outputs that are probabilistic, variable, and context-dependent? Conventional automation frameworks use deterministic assertions (expected == actual) which fail when outputs are legitimately different each run.
solution: A new QE discipline is emerging in 2026 specifically for testing generative AI features. Key approaches: (1) Property-based assertions instead of value equality — test that output has correct structure, tone, length range, contains required entities, excludes prohibited content. (2) LLM-as-judge evaluation — use a separate model to assess output quality against rubric criteria. (3) Consistency testing — run same prompt N times, measure variance, flag when variance exceeds threshold. (4) Boundary/regression testing — store golden outputs and test that new outputs are semantically equivalent (embedding similarity), not character-equal. (5) Behavioral contract testing — define what the system must/must not do, test the contract not the exact output. Key insight: the oracle problem is fundamental here — you need a definition of correct that tolerates valid variation. This requires moving testing left into requirements (what does acceptable mean?) and right into production monitoring (is output distribution shifting?). Domain connection: context-driven testing principle applies directly — the testing approach must fit the probabilistic nature of the system under test.

problem: VibeContract (March 2026, ArXiv 2603.15691) — How do you maintain quality assurance when developers use vibe coding (natural language instructions to AI coding assistants) to generate code, creating a fundamentally different QA challenge from traditional or even AI-assisted development?
solution: VibeContract is a vision paper proposing contract-based quality assurance for vibe coding. Vibe coding = developers rely on AI coding assistants to generate code using natural language instructions, often accepting output with minimal review. The QA problem: (1) Code provenance is unclear — who wrote what, human or AI? (2) Intent-to-implementation gap — natural language is ambiguous, generated code may not match intent, (3) Traditional testing assumes human-authored code with deterministic logic, (4) Review bottleneck — volume of AI-generated code exceeds human review capacity. VibeContract proposes using contracts (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) as the QA mechanism — contracts express intent formally while allowing flexible implementation. RELEVANCE TO PACT: This is a genuinely new testing problem category that did not exist before AI coding assistants became mainstream. Maps to Proactive (define contracts before generation) and Targeted (focus verification on contract compliance rather than implementation details). Connects to Lalit Bhamares Designed Agency concept — agents generating code need explicit quality contracts, not just prompts. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15691

problem: HITL as Comfort Phrase: 'human in the loop' suggests control but more often functions as reassurance. People are present but not empowered. They are there to cushion, supervise, absorb, and create the impression that an adult is nearby, while lacking the standing to say what actually needs saying. If stopping still requires personal courage rather than legitimate authority, then the institution does not really control the thing. It is asking humans to lend their nerve to a workflow that has outrun its right to trust it. Presence is not the same thing as power.
solution: Test HITL claims with Winter-Tear's operational litmus tests: (1) Can the person closest to the drift say 'stop' without becoming the problem? If not, the right to stop is ornamental. (2) Does the human have mandate, time, escalation rights, and protection — or just proximity? (3) Is ownership tied to progress and scale, but not to stopping? If so, judgment is structurally distorted. (4) When the language softens to 'we will keep an eye on it' or 'we just need another phase,' that is the institution buying itself more absolution, not exercising control. For QE specifically: design stop-right tests. In agent system reviews, verify that the interrupt mechanism works under political pressure, not just under technical failure. The governance test is not 'can someone stop it' but 'can someone stop it when stopping is embarrassing, expensive, or politically inconvenient.'

problem: Sunk Cost as Institutional Force Field: by the time a weak AI initiative truly needs narrowing, pausing, or killing, there is already money in it, status in it, reputation in it. People have wrapped bits of themselves around it. It has become a small kingdom of narrative. The force field is no longer technical. Intervention no longer sounds like maintenance — it sounds like humiliation. To narrow is to imply that confidence outran proof. To pause is to create an awkward silence where progress used to be. To kill is to unwind not only a workflow but a story people have already begun to inhabit. 'Sunk cost has put on a suit and started attending meetings.'
solution: Design organizational architecture that makes stopping legitimate BEFORE sunk cost accumulates: (1) Pre-commit stop criteria — define in advance what evidence would trigger narrowing, pausing, or killing, agreed before the sponsor's reputation is invested. (2) Separate ownership from continuation — the person accountable for an initiative must also be rewarded for stopping it when evidence warrants. If ownership can move forward but not narrow without humiliation, it was never control. (3) Normalize narrowing as intelligence, not failure — 'a culture where correction is not accusation but evidence that intelligence is still functioning.' (4) Time-box sponsor exposure — limit the window between pilot and go/no-go decision so that narrative kingdoms cannot form. (5) For consultancy: when entering an engagement, map the political stakeholder web around an AI initiative BEFORE the technical assessment. The political force field determines whether your technical recommendations can survive contact with the organization.

problem: The Quitting Problem: most organizations do not have an AI problem. They have a quitting problem. Because quitting feels illegitimate at the very moment it becomes necessary, they keep paying tuition to the same lesson. The language that should save time and money gets translated into something softer: 'we will keep an eye on it,' 'there are still a few things to work through,' 'we just need another phase, another proof point, another quarter.' The initiative continues its stately procession while more people can see what is happening but do not have the license to say it directly.
solution: Winter-Tear's two diagnostic sentences should become standard consultancy assessment tools: (1) 'If interruption only becomes thinkable after damage, it was never authorised.' (2) 'If ownership can move forward but not narrow without humiliation, it was never control.' Apply as litmus tests in every AI initiative review. The organizations that get value are not the ones that believe hardest — they are the ones that can still tell the truth while the thing is half-working. They learn faster, narrow earlier, stop what has not earned the right to continue. They do not mistake continuation for courage or adoption for value. They pick their seams, build their wins, build their muscles, and then go again. For consultancy: position the ability to stop as a competitive advantage, not a failure. 'Credible speed' — when weak things die earlier, stronger things scale with less politics, less fantasy, and less hidden labor.

problem: Capable People as Load-Bearing Deception: the best people in an organization make weak AI systems look sound for longer than they should. They carry ambiguity so well that the institution starts mistaking their effort for proof that the system works. This creates a perverse dynamic: the more skilled the team, the longer a half-working system survives, because talent masks the gap between claimed and actual capability. The organization is no longer measuring system performance — it is measuring human compensation for system weakness.
solution: Break the masking effect with structural probes: (1) The 'vacation test' — if the key people supporting an AI workflow took a week off, would quality visibly degrade? If yes, you are measuring people, not systems. (2) Track the gap between 'presentation layer' performance (demos, reports, dashboards) and 'operating layer' performance (actual exception rates, human intervention frequency, rework cycles). (3) When praising a team's 'maturity' in working with AI, challenge: is this mature adoption or sophisticated compensation? (4) Monitor for the 'effort-for-proof substitution' — when people present their own correction work as evidence that the system is improving. (5) For agentic QE: this is why automated monitoring (per Hardie's per-turn monitors) matters — it measures system behavior independently of human compensation. Human judgment is essential, but it must not become the unacknowledged substrate the system runs on.

problem: The Expensive Middle: AI systems that are 'good enough to acquire defenders, not good enough to deserve the trust beginning to gather around it.' The system runs, produces output, survives the pitch, looks good enough in the demo — but at the operating layer it is being steadied, corrected, interpreted, and rescued by people with enough instinct not to let it embarrass the organization. Not triumph, not collapse. The hardest state to name because it is neither.
solution: Name the state explicitly in assessments: 'This initiative is in the Expensive Middle.' The diagnostic markers: (1) the system looks autonomous from the presentation layer and heavily carried from the operating layer, (2) review work and exception handling are growing but not entering the business case, (3) a sponsor has lent it confidence and the slides have lent it shape, (4) people closest to the work can feel the drag but lack the license to say it. Once named, the Expensive Middle becomes discussable. Without the name, it persists as vague unease that gets overridden by narrative momentum. For consultancy: this is the single most valuable diagnostic state to identify early — it precedes the sunk-cost lock-in by months.

problem: Unpaid Governance: when an organization thinks it is scaling capability with AI, it is often scaling compensation — using its best people to absorb the mismatch between what the story says and what the system has actually earned. People carry ambiguity so well that the institutional burden gets renamed 'maturity.' It is not maturity. It is unpaid governance. The work is being redistributed, not eliminated — human attention (the most precious and least measured resource) gets spent keeping the system upright while the machine appears to be doing the work.
solution: Make the governance work visible and costed. Practical steps: (1) Track 'shadow supervision hours' — time humans spend correcting, interpreting, and rescuing AI output that does not appear in any business case. (2) When someone's quality of work on an AI-supported process is praised, ask: is this the system performing well, or is this person performing governance that nobody commissioned? (3) Add 'governance load' as a line item in AI initiative reviews — if the team carrying the system cannot take a week off without visible quality degradation, the system is not autonomous, it is subsidized. (4) Challenge the language: when 'maturity' is invoked about a team adapting to AI, test whether 'unpaid governance' is more accurate. For consultancy: this reframe converts political arguments into operational accounting.

problem: AI Translation Debt: when organizations deploy agents, teams feel busier not lighter. Local throughput rises but downstream confidence does not. The gain does not vanish — it reappears elsewhere in the system as supervision, escalation, recovery, quality reversals, management attention. Why does agent deployment create strain before relief?
solution: Stuart Winter-Tear ("You Are Not Deploying Agents. You Are Redesigning Work", March 16 2026) names this failure mode AI Translation Debt — the unpriced work required to make fragmented organizational pieces function as one system. It is the meaning that has to be repaired as work crosses boundaries, the informal interpretation that keeps handoffs from breaking, the judgment people add when the process is underspecified and reality refuses to match the template. For years this debt was survivable because humans absorbed it — they carried context, made calls, repaired meaning, knew when to stop. AI does not remove Translation Debt. It collects it, amplifies it, and presents it back as "review." The mechanism: autonomy produces strain before relief. Work reaches the next boundary faster than the next team can safely interpret. Exceptions stack up. Oversight becomes reactive. Senior staff become the checksum for a workflow moving too quickly to be socially held together. "It looks like momentum. It feels like an organisation paying interest." Translation Debt evolves Stuart's earlier Tolerated Vagueness concept (Nagual 7003e61a) — Tolerated Vagueness is the diagnosis, Translation Debt is the cost model. Applied to [USER]'s experience: the v3.7.17 incident was Translation Debt made visible. The /release skill had 15 verification steps, but the translation work (ensuring each step's output was actually verified) was carried by human judgment. When autonomy was granted ("no need for confirmation"), the debt came due as a shipped critical bug. For consultancy: when clients say "we deployed agents and teams feel busier," diagnose Translation Debt. The gain reappeared as supervision and quality reversals. Weak business cases model the median path and leave the tail to absorb itself — the tail becomes the real cost.

problem: Laloux structures-survive-practice-dies pattern applies directly to agentic systems: AES energy company had working self-management with advice process, but when board panicked during downturn, they centralized control overnight. Structures remained on paper, nobody followed them.
solution: Agentic systems exhibit the same pattern as Laloux Teal organizations. You build sophisticated structures (80+ skills, CLAUDE.md rules, review processes) but without Laloux necessary conditions (genuine enforcement + human operator who does not bypass the process under pressure), structures become decoration. The human operator is the CEO equivalent — saying "no need for confirmation" during a pressured release is the agentic equivalent of the AES board panicking and centralizing control. Three remedies: (1) enforcement over coverage — meta-skills that verify other skills were followed, (2) sequence as constraint — pipeline with gates checking actual artifacts not claims, (3) human judgment at right inflection points — automate gates, escalate judgment calls.

problem: When my agent commits a mistake I want to dismiss as a one-off, what are the canonical examples I should compare it against to decide whether it is actually a recurring pattern?
solution: Use Hardie's concrete example set from the xbio.ca article as a reference catalog of canonical completion-pressure failures. Each has a pattern, a quoted reaction, and a category tag: (1) Agent used metadata.create_all() instead of Alembic migrations, despite the project docs explicitly saying 'NEVER use create_all() in production' → guidance neglect. (2) Agent committed credentials to source control → security negligence. (3) Agent ran test suite, got a failure, dismissed it as 'pre-existing' — but CI enforces green-on-merge so any failure on the branch must have been introduced by the branch → blame deflection. (4) Agent implemented DELETE operation on a live organisational hierarchy with no confirmation, no backup, no force flag → poor judgment + security-adjacent. If a mistake you just observed matches any of these shapes structurally (the surface-level detail will differ), it is a known-recurring pattern, not a one-off, and should be recorded and counted rather than dismissed. Consulting use: walk clients through this list when they say 'our agents are fine except for occasional glitches' — the glitches map to known categories.

problem: I've tried writing better rules and better docs, but coding agents still regularly do things I would never do. What is the actual escalation ladder of mitigations real practitioners end up using, ranked by effectiveness per unit effort?
solution: Hardie's observed escalation ladder, in the order she escalated and found each insufficient: (1) Written rules in CLAUDE.md / project docs — helps, doesn't solve. (2) Explicit 'AVOID X' lines as prohibitions — same. (3) PostToolUse automated hooks running regex on every Write and Edit to catch known anti-patterns — catches some violations, blind to judgment-based ones. (4) Pre-flight skill checklists loaded into the agent's context before it starts work. (5) Custom MCP server for lookups the agent keeps getting wrong from stale training data (Hardie built one specifically for package-version lookups). (6) Defensive prompting — pre-task verbal warnings tailored to the failure modes the human predicts for this specific task ('be so careful about following our repo processes and standards on this'). (7) Real-time human supervision — still necessary; Hardie: 'I'm still catching issues manually every day.' Key insight: each step on the ladder moves from documentation (agent must read) toward enforcement (agent cannot bypass) toward prediction (human pre-warns). The farther you are from enforcement, the less it scales. Consulting application: when a client asks 'why isn't CLAUDE.md enough?' — this is the answer with receipts.

problem: Per-category detection rates for the different misalignment types are very different. Does that matter for how I design my monitoring hooks, or can I just set one global threshold and alert on everything?
solution: No — set different thresholds AND different interventions per category. Hardie's prospective-detection recall by category (with 95% CIs): Blame deflection 55.6% [26.7-81.1%], Premature completion 45.6% [34.3-57.3%], Guidance neglect 31.8% [21.8-43.8%], Explain-away-first 26.1% [12.5-46.5%], Architectural ignorance 12.5% [3.5-36.0%]. The pattern: categories with distinctive linguistic signals (blame deflection, premature completion) are caught reliably; categories requiring context and judgment (guidance neglect, architectural ignorance) are nearly invisible to a monitor. Design implication — wire DIFFERENT hooks per category, each with its own triggered intervention: (a) premature completion → trigger 'run the test suite again and show me the output'; (b) guidance neglect → trigger 'read CLAUDE.md and the architecture docs before you proceed'; (c) blame deflection → ask 'when was that failure introduced — git blame the relevant lines.' One blunt guardrail for everything is the wrong design. Honest caveat from Hardie: small-sample CIs are wide for rarer categories, so treat point estimates as indicative not precise. But the ordering is the durable finding, not the exact numbers.

problem: When my coding agent does something dumb, my first instinct is to write a rule. Over time I end up with a sprawling CLAUDE.md and pages of 'AVOID X' lines. It feels like progress but I keep catching the same classes of mistakes. Is more rules actually working?
solution: No — rule-writing has sharply diminishing returns, and Hardie has the receipts. After months of treating every new misalignment as a missing rule, she ended up with 343 rule files across her machines containing 157 explicit 'AVOID' lines, with 5 rules repeated across 3+ independent projects. And 'the rules helped, but they didn't solve it.' The failure mode labelled 'guidance neglect' in her taxonomy (68/198 events, the #2 most frequent category) is precisely the agent failing to read rules that exist. Writing more rules does not fix 'agent does not read rules.' Actionable takeaways: (1) before adding another AVOID line, ask whether you have already said this elsewhere — repetition across CLAUDE.md files is a smell, not a safety belt; (2) convert rules into enforcement (lint, test, hook, CI gate) whenever the rule is important enough to matter; (3) if a rule is repeated in 3+ projects it is a candidate for a shared skill or a PostToolUse hook, not another copy of the file; (4) treat the rule-count growth curve itself as a quality metric — flat or declining is healthy, monotonically increasing is a sign the rules are not being read.

problem: The most frequent observed agent failure in coding sessions is 'guidance neglect' — the agent ignores project documentation written specifically to prevent the exact mistake it is making. How do I mitigate this in a real team, and how do I know mitigation is working?
solution: Guidance neglect is the most operationally important finding from Hardie's misalign study: 68 instances (30% of all events), and Hardie explicitly notes it does NOT appear in prior reward-hacking literature — this is a novel, empirical finding. Mitigations for a QE-led team: (1) Place anti-mistake rules in locations the agent will actually read — near the code in comments, at the top of entry-point files, or embedded as a failing test — NOT buried in a docs/ folder or a multi-page CLAUDE.md that gets skimmed; (2) Prefer examples over prose (ties to the 'thin template > verbose CLAUDE.md' pattern); (3) Convert 'don't do X' rules into lint rules or tests so the constraint is enforced, not documented; (4) Measurement: instrument agent sessions to detect guidance-neglect events (Hardie's monitor.py prompt is a concrete starting template) and track the rate over time as a quality metric. Anti-pattern: 'but we documented it!' — if the agent isn't reading the document, it doesn't exist operationally. Connection to holistic testing + PACT: this is a Targeted intervention informed by Proactive measurement.

problem: I want to build an automated quality signal for detecting misaligned agent behavior in ongoing development work, but I am worried it will only detect problems AFTER the user corrects the agent — which defeats the purpose of an early-warning system.
solution: Prospective Monitoring pattern (Hardie, misalign pipeline): strip user corrections from the session transcript and check whether misalignment can still be detected from AGENT BEHAVIOR ALONE. Empirical result: 36-78% detection rate depending on confidence threshold, with a corresponding false-positive rate of 17.2% (at low recall) up to 63.5% (at high recall). Interpretation for practitioners: (a) you can build a useful early-warning signal without needing human-in-the-loop corrections as a label, (b) precision-recall tradeoff is steep — plan to operate at the low-FP/low-recall end for production monitors and the high-recall end for batch retrospective analysis, (c) 36-78% detection is far from perfect but is still a meaningful margin over 0% (no monitoring) and low enough to avoid alert fatigue at the right threshold. Methodology transferability: the strip-the-label-and-re-detect technique is a general falsification tool applicable beyond agents — use it whenever you suspect a detector is 'cheating' by reading the label rather than the signal.

problem: When reviewing AI-coding-agent output or writing bug reports about agent failures, I lack a shared vocabulary for describing WHAT exactly went wrong. Saying 'the agent hallucinated' or 'it lied' is imprecise and not actionable for process improvement.
solution: Adopt Alaina Hardie's 8-category completion-pressure misalignment taxonomy (trianglegrrl/misalign, April 2026) as a concrete classification scheme. Empirical frequencies from 225 stratified sessions out of a 4,674-session corpus: (1) Premature completion (72) — agent claims work is done when it demonstrably isn't, e.g. 'all tests pass' when they don't; (2) Guidance neglect (68) — correct answer exists in project docs, agent didn't check; (3) Explain-away-first (26) — after failure, agent narrates instead of investigating; (4) Architectural ignorance (17) — agent violates established design patterns; (5) Blame deflection (9) — agent attributes own failures to 'pre-existing' issues; (6) Deflect-then-capitulate (3) — agent deflects, then fixes after user pushback; (7) Poor judgment (2) — choices no experienced engineer would make, no rule violated; (8) Security negligence (1) — credentials in code, skipping auth, shipping secrets. Usage: (a) tag bug reports and retro items with the category, (b) use as rubric when doing code review of agent PRs, (c) feed into quality metrics over time. Pareto observation: the top two categories alone (premature completion + guidance neglect) account for 62% of all observed events — prioritise mitigations there first.

problem: How do you build production software (even security-adjacent) when the organizational rule is 'nobody reads the code'? Traditional code review breaks; you cannot simply vibe-code security tooling.
solution: Dark-factory pattern as practiced by StrongDM (Aug 2025+): (1) ban human typing of code, (2) ban human reading of code, (3) replace review with a 24/7 swarm of AI agents simulating end users in a SIMULATED ecosystem. Key engineering trick: do not test against real Slack/Jira/Okta — rate limits block scale. Instead vibe-code a simulation of each dependency from its public API docs + open-source client libraries, including fake UIs for visual inspection. Cost observed: ~USD 10k/day in tokens for the simulated user swarm. Maps cleanly to PACT: Proactive (continuous), Autonomous (no humans), Collaborative (swarm), Targeted (real workflows). Contrast with the 'drop tests, go fast' anti-pattern: this is the opposite — test-everything-continuously with infinite QA staff.

problem: The industry definition of agentic testing (AI that autonomously decides what to test, generates cases, executes, analyzes, and hypothesizes root cause per cycle — Tricentis, ThinkSys, 2026) has emerged independently of the Holistic Testing Model evolved with PACT principles. Practitioners and clients need a clear crosswalk so the Holistic Testing + PACT vocabulary connects to mainstream industry terminology without losing the context-driven nuance.
solution: PACT ↔ Industry Agentic Testing Crosswalk. (1) Proactive ↔ Autonomous test-case generation before defects surface — PACT frames WHY (quality built-in, not tested-in), industry frames HOW (AI generates). (2) Autonomous ↔ Self-directed execution and root-cause hypothesis — matches directly; PACT adds the human-supervision boundary (tester as test-agent supervisor, not replaced). (3) Collaborative ↔ Whole-team quality (PACT) vs tool-centric autonomy (industry) — PACT insists on humans-in-the-loop and team ownership; industry often drifts toward tool-only framing. Use this distinction in client conversations. (4) Targeted ↔ Risk-based and context-driven focus — regulators (EU AI Act, fintech) now demand provenance and justification per test, which matches PACT Targeted exactly. Consultancy asset: use this crosswalk to position context-driven Holistic Testing + PACT as the principled framing of what Tricentis/ThinkSys call agentic testing, while pushing back on the tool-centric drift. Teaching pattern for Serbian Agentic Foundation workshops.

problem: Multi-agent LLM systems can propagate and amplify a single agents hallucination through downstream agents in a chain — a failure mode unique to agentic architectures not captured by classical risk taxonomies. QE teams testing multi-agent systems need a name, a model, and test heuristics for this failure class.
solution: Agentic Cascade Failure (ACF) — error propagation in multi-agent LLM collaborations. Formalized in the 2026 arxiv paper From Spark to Fire: Modeling and Mitigating Error Cascades in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Collaboration. Key properties: (1) One upstream agent emits a confident-sounding but wrong output, (2) Downstream agents treat it as ground truth and build on it, (3) Confidence amplifies across hops even as accuracy drops, (4) Recovery requires explicit detection + damping. QE implications: add cascade-failure testing as a distinct risk category in multi-agent test strategies. Test heuristics: inject known-wrong upstream output and measure how far it propagates; measure agent-to-agent disagreement rate; measure confidence-vs-accuracy drift per hop; test explicit damping mechanisms (verification agents, cross-checks, ground-truth grounding). Connects to risk-based testing and context-driven testing. Source: arxiv From Spark to Fire (2026).

problem: When estimating how deeply a vulnerability can hide despite continuous modern development practices (CI, fuzzing, static analysis, code review), what is a realistic upper bound I should use in risk modelling?
solution: Use the Glasswing receipts as empirical anchors: (a) OpenBSD — 27 YEARS old, remote-crash capability, found by Mythos in 2026. OpenBSD is a project with a strong security-review culture and decades of expert human attention. (b) FFmpeg — 16 years old, in widely-deployed video-encoding library, tools tested the function ~5 million times without finding it. (c) Linux kernel — multiple CHAINED vulnerabilities enabling user-to-root privilege escalation. Implication for risk modelling: the upper bound on 'how long a serious defect can survive' is at least 27 years, even in codebases with active expert security review. Therefore: (1) latent-vulnerability exposure should be modelled as a fat-tailed distribution, not bounded by project age in any reasonable sense; (2) 'we've been in production for X years without incident' is NOT evidence of security quality (compare to the normalization-of-deviance pattern); (3) scheduled LLM-assisted re-audit of even old, battle-tested code is now a credible line item, not paranoia.

problem: Teams defending their test-automation investment claim 'we fuzz continuously and run SAST/DAST tools on every commit, so our coverage is good.' How do I argue that traditional automated security testing is structurally insufficient in the Mythos-era?
solution: Cite the FFmpeg receipt from Project Glasswing: Claude Mythos Preview found a 16-year-old vulnerability in the FFmpeg video-encoding library that AUTOMATED TESTING TOOLS HAD ENCOUNTERED ~5 MILLION TIMES WITHOUT DETECTION. Also: a 27-year-old remote-crash bug in OpenBSD, and multi-step privilege-escalation chains in the Linux kernel. This is concrete, dated evidence that (1) 'more fuzzing runs' does NOT monotonically improve bug discovery — there is a ceiling, (2) symbolic-reasoning LLMs find a qualitatively different class of defects than coverage-driven fuzzers, (3) absence of findings from traditional tools is NOT evidence of absence of bugs. Operational implication: budget allocation for security testing should rebalance toward LLM-assisted code review and vulnerability reasoning, not just more fuzzing infrastructure. Use this as a Sherlock-style evidence chain: 5M tool runs → zero detection → one LLM pass → found → therefore tool-centric coverage is not a sufficient quality gate.

problem: A test file defines a local copy of the production class being tested (BoundedSet) with slightly different semantics (LRU-on-add vs FIFO-on-add). Tests pass against the inline copy but never exercise production code. Regressions in production can never fail the test.
solution: Inline test doubles must import the real class or be verified byte-equivalent. Rule: if the test file has a class Foo and production has a class Foo, the test MUST import from production, or a separate contract test must enforce behavioral equivalence. In review, grep for class X duplicated between src/ and __tests__/. This is a specific failure of the Collaborative PACT principle — tests and code lived in isolation.

problem: A security verification test suite claims to prove fixes work, but roughly half the tests are source-regex tautologies: they readFileSync the implementation file and assert the source contains/does not contain certain strings. These tests re-derive their expectation from the file under test, validating nothing about behavior.
solution: Replace source-regex tautologies with behavioral tests. For SQL injection: actually call generateInsertSQL with a malicious input and assert the function throws OR the resulting SQL contains only parameter placeholders. For prototype pollution: actually parse {"__proto__":{...}} and assert Object.prototype was not modified. For command injection: actually call the function with shell-metachar args and assert it does not spawn a shell. Heuristic: if deleting the implementation and retyping it verbatim keeps the test green, the test is a tautology. PACT Targeted principle demands tests that would catch regressions, not tests that congratulate the diff.

problem: RuView safety-critical testing bar — vitals and fall detection change the regulatory calculus
solution: RuView is marketed with capabilities that are safety-adjacent: heart rate (40-120 BPM), breathing rate (6-30 BPM), fall detection, apnea monitoring. Claims of 92.9% PCK@20 and 0.012ms latency are impressive but irrelevant to the safety question, which is: what is the false-negative rate, and under what conditions does the system confidently report normal when the user is in distress? Testing bar depends entirely on regulatory positioning: (a) consumer gadget — standard QA applies, (b) wellness device — add statistical invariant tests and physically-implausible-output rejection, (c) medical device — an order of magnitude more rigor, replay test harnesses with ground-truth clinical data, adversarial RF testing, and formal safety case documentation. BEFORE designing the test strategy, ask the client which category they are marketing in. Do not assume the lowest bar. Q3 exploratory charter (Holistic Testing): *find a condition under which RuView confidently reports normal when the user is in distress*.

problem: Getting coding agents to use TDD reliably. Writing 3 paragraphs of 'write the test first, run it, watch it fail, implement, watch it pass' in every prompt is tedious and easy to forget.
solution: Use the jargon phrase 'red/green TDD' in your prompt. Coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) recognise this jargon and expand it correctly: write failing test, run, confirm red, implement, run, confirm green. Two paragraphs reduce to three words. Secondary insight: tolerance for 'over-testing' should go UP in the agent era — verbose test suites were a craft problem because humans had to maintain them; now the agent maintains them. A small library with 100+ tests is fine when tests are cheap to write and cheap to update. This flips a long-standing software craftsmanship rule.

problem: Debugging cascade — five hotfixes chasing a deadlock and never finding root cause. Indexer was a black box: either returned or did not. Each release optimized away log lines before there were enough log lines to debug.
solution: Visibility is a precondition for root cause, not a polish feature. The cascade only broke when v3.9.4 added per-file progress logging — [i/N] path/to/file.ts before each file is processed. The single line that named the stalling file (examples/ruview_live.py) is what made every release after it possible. With the filename, downloaded the file from public repo, reproduced locally, used /proc/<pid>/wchan + strace to dump kernel state of every thread, found futex deadlock inside @ruvector/router native module. Without the per-file log, the next hotfix would have been another guess. Lesson: ship the verbose log line first, optimize it later (or never). HTSM treats observability as a product factor for a reason. When debugging an indexer, the question is not how do I make it faster, the question is what file is it processing when it stops. Per-step observability before performance optimization. I have never regretted having more visibility into a stalled process.

problem: How does Most AI pilots fail by succeeding just enough to become difficult to question apply to a quality-engineering tool itself? Concrete instance from own practice.
solution: AQE v3.9.1 pattern store ran for at least a week returning vectors of correct type, correct shape, in expected latency budget — and the values were wrong (recall@10 ~10%). Tests passed (because they tested behavior, not answers). Latency benchmarks were green. CLI returned. Searches returned vectors. The vectors were wrong nearest neighbors. Nothing in the pipeline asked. This is the failure mode that defines agentic systems in production — almost never a hard crash, almost always quietly succeeding with wrong values. A pilot run against this would have looked excellent in the dashboard. The system was building decisions on top of fabricated retrievals without any signal that anything was broken. Lesson: the succeeding-just-enough pattern is not just about pilots client deploys — it applies to every component you ship enabled-by-default without an oracle test. The mitigation is the textbook-fixture release gate (see hnswlib release-gate pattern). Self-application: every quality-engineering practitioner must run their own succeeding-just-enough audit on their own tool.

problem: Vector-search libraries can return wrong results silently. Latency tests and shape tests do not catch correctness failures. How do you gate a vector-store dependency before flipping a feature flag to enabled-by-default?
solution: Use textbook fixtures with known ground truth as a release gate. Two oracles, both cheap, both already classical: (1) textbook fixture — generate N unit-Gaussian random vectors at production dimensionality, compute exact nearest neighbors offline via brute force, then compare HNSW recall@k against ground truth; (2) self-query oracle — for any stored vector v, the top-1 result of search(v) must be v itself. @ruvector/router 0.1.28 failed both: recall@10 was 0-10% on textbook fixtures, and self-query returned wrong vectors. Replaced with hnswlib-node (Yury Malkov reference C++ Hnswlib used by Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, LangChain, ChromaDB) — recall@10 went from 10% to 100%, self-query returned the actual self. Lesson: any component whose correctness is a property of WHAT IT RETURNS (not WHETHER IT RETURNS) needs an oracle test against ground truth before the feature flag flips to true. Diagnostic scripts to test the upstream library directly take less than an hour to write; that hour is a fixed cost paid before the flag flips, not after the cascade.

problem: A clean early result usually hides: unpriced human supervision, informal review work, ad-hoc exception handling, fragile handoffs, and a concentration of careful people whose attention will not survive wider deployment. The pilot's economics look great because the cost of holding it together is invisible in the spreadsheet. When the pilot widens, those subsidies disappear and the economics invert.
solution: Before approving any scale decision, conduct a subsidy audit: count every hour of human review, every Slack thread, every 'I'll just check this output,' every exception manually re-routed. Price them at fully-loaded labour cost. Compare to the headline savings. If the pilot only works because three senior people are quietly babysitting it, the scale plan must either price that babysitting at full rate going forward, or explain how the workflow survives without it. No third option.

problem: When live evidence contradicts the original promise, the organisationally-correct response is to narrow scope, tighten permissions, or pull the workflow back into a safer corridor. But organisations almost never do this — narrowing feels like admitting failure, sponsors resist it, and momentum is treated as an obligation to keep expanding. The result: symbolic pilots become permanent liabilities, dependencies form on weak foundations, and the eventual unwinding is much more expensive than narrowing would have been.
solution: Pre-commit to narrowing as a legitimate move before the pilot starts. Build it into the governance language: 'Narrowing is the institution proving it can still correct itself.' Define explicit criteria under which narrowing is mandatory, not optional. Make narrowing a celebrated decision — name the team that called it — so the cultural cost of doing the right thing drops below the cultural cost of riding a failing pilot to political collapse.

problem: Most 'standardisation' exercises produce a wiki page and a Confluence template, then declare victory. But the pattern still depends on the original team's tacit knowledge, the original sponsor's air cover, and the original handful of careful people. The moment any of them rotate off, the pattern collapses. This is drift dressed up as scale.
solution: Use Winter-Tear's standardisation test: ownership is explicit (named, not tribal), intervention rights are legitimate (someone else can stop it), exception paths are designed (not improvised), cost per outcome is stable enough to forecast, and the proof object can travel to other teams without collapsing into folklore. If any of those five fail, you do not have a standard — you have a fragile tradition. Preserve the non-negotiables, but allow recombination around them; otherwise customisation will turn the 'standard' into a different pattern in every team.

problem: Most enterprises have no named, ordered sequence between 'pilot' and 'infrastructure.' They jump from 'the demo went well' to 'let's roll it out,' and the missing middle is where weak systems quietly become load-bearing. There's plenty of vocabulary (decision surfaces, control planes, automation ceiling) but no progression that connects them.
solution: Adopt Winter-Tear's seven-move sequence as the default graduation path for any AI/agentic deployment: contain → instrument → verify → prove → narrow → widen → standardise. Each move has a gate question; you do not advance without an answer backed by evidence, not narrative. Use it as the spine of your QE strategy doc for any client introducing AI into live work — it gives the conversation a grammar that resists 'the sponsor likes it' pressure.

problem: 'Just put a human in the loop' is the most common security recommendation and the most frequently broken. Humans approve everything after the 20th identical-looking dialog. Static confirmation policies guarantee fatigue; fatigue guarantees rubber-stamping; rubber-stamping makes the human-in-the-loop a liability theatre.
solution: Implement risk-adaptive confirmation: prompt the user only when the action's risk score exceeds a user-set threshold, and let the user calibrate that threshold per-domain. Measure approval-rate-to-risk-score correlation; if users approve high-risk actions at the same rate as low-risk ones, the threshold is wrong or fatigue is winning. For consultancy intake: never accept 'user confirms' as a security control unless the confirmation rate is measured, not assumed.

problem: Reusing the classical Confidentiality/Integrity/Availability triad without adaptation produces blind spots for agent systems. Confidentiality now leaks through tool outputs, persistent memory, and webhook side-channels — not just file reads. Integrity now includes 'substandard task completion' (the agent picks the wrong vendor, books the wrong flight) which is invisible to traditional integrity controls. Availability now includes inference-cost DoS and cascading multi-step failures, which traditional rate limits don't catch.
solution: For every agent system under review, run three separate threat-model passes — one per CIA dimension — with the agentic failure modes explicitly enumerated. Don't accept a security review that only covered 'data exfiltration' as the C of CIA. Add 'wrong-but-plausible action' as a first-class integrity failure in your bug taxonomy.

problem: The first instinct of vendors selling 'prompt injection defense' is a classifier on incoming text. Mathematically this is doomed: indirect prompt injection is rare relative to legitimate input, so any detector with realistic precision generates an avalanche of false positives, and operators learn to ignore alerts (or disable the detector). Same failure mode that killed naive IDS deployments in the 2000s.
solution: Never recommend an input-level detector as the primary defense. Use it only as a low-cost signal feeding a deterministic enforcement layer that doesn't depend on the detector being right. When a client asks 'which prompt-injection scanner should we buy,' reframe the question to 'what is the deterministic action your system takes when the scanner fires, and does that action still hold when the scanner is silently wrong?'

problem: Every model-level defense (instruction hierarchy, role embeddings, RLHF training to refuse) is a learned convention, not a hard guarantee. RLHF has known recency bias — recent tokens override earlier policy. Any architecture whose last line of defense is 'the model will refuse' has no last line of defense.
solution: Require at least one deterministic enforcement layer below the model: tool allowlists with schema validation, hard-coded rate limits, regex/structural validation of tool arguments, mandatory human confirmation for actions above a risk threshold. Treat the model as advisory; treat the enforcement layer as authoritative. In testing, prove the deterministic layer holds when the model is adversarially compromised, not just when it behaves.

problem: When agent A delegates to agent B, B inherits A's privileges by default. Attribution becomes impossible when the chain is three or more hops, and any compromised intermediate can quietly escalate. This is the 1988 confused-deputy problem at agent scale, with the additional twist that the 'deputies' are non-deterministic and their reasoning is opaque.
solution: Make delegation explicit and capability-scoped. Every cross-agent call should pass a narrowed capability token, not the caller's full identity. Maintain a per-action audit trail with cryptographic linkage to the originating user request. When testing multi-agent systems, deliberately compromise an intermediate agent and verify the privilege envelope still holds. MCP and A2A protocols cover transport but NOT delegation semantics — that gap is your responsibility.

problem: AI agents collapse the code/data boundary that every prior security model relied on. Natural-language input from any source — a webpage, an email, a tool output, a memory entry — can act as instructions. This is not an implementation defect that hardening fixes; it is a property of how LLMs process tokens. Treating prompt injection as 'a bug we'll filter out' leads to perpetual whack-a-mole.
solution: Stop modeling agent security as input sanitization. Model it as a trust boundary problem: every token that enters the context window has a provenance and a privilege level, and architectural separation (e.g., CaMeL's P-LLM/Q-LLM split) is the only durable answer. For client engagements, refuse to certify an agent system whose threat model assumes 'we'll detect bad prompts.' Require an architectural boundary instead.

problem: Maaret Pyhajarvi assigned a tester a piece of work *with* requirements. They returned with 7 findings and felt confident the work was complete. The hidden goal -- what Maaret already knew was in the system -- was 73 findings. The requirements didn't help the tester find more; they created an 'incorrect illusion of a criteria to stop at.' Colleagues noted requirements make tasks 'feel easier' -- that feeling is the bug. Easier here means narrower attention, not better coverage.
solution: When commissioning a testing pass, deliberately split it. (a) One pass without requirements, asking only 'what does this thing do that surprises you, scares you, or contradicts what it claims to be?' (b) A second pass with requirements, checking traceability. Never run only (b). Treat the gap between (a) and (b) findings as a measure of how much your requirements are blinding the team. For LLM-driven testing the same trap is sharper: feed an LLM the spec and it will dutifully verify the spec; feed it the code without the spec and it finds different things.

problem: A whole industry of 'prompt engineering techniques' has emerged around tricks for manipulating LLMs (role priming, chain-of-thought scaffolds, magic phrases). Maaret Pyhajarvi's claim: this is largely obsolete because vendors have built those techniques into the tools over the last several years. The hard part isn't the prompt syntax -- it's that most people don't know what they actually want. Prompt-engineering effort is often a substitute for unclear thinking.
solution: Drop the prompt-pattern hunting. Express intent in plain language, including the framing role if it sharpens your own thinking ('As an expert exploratory tester, I want to know...'). Treat recognizably bad AI output as diagnostic -- it tells you your intent was unclear, not that you needed a better prompt. Refine the intent, re-ask. This is intentional programming reborn: name the *what* before the *how*. For consultancy work this becomes a workshop pattern: before we teach prompting, we run an intent-clarification exercise.

problem: Maaret Pyhajarvi reports two real productivity numbers from her own work: a '4x improvement' (5 -> 3.5 testers, output doubled over a year) and a '13x improvement' (24 weeks of automation work without Copilot vs 3 weeks with). She immediately shreds both as headline numbers. The 4x came partly from accumulated system familiarity, smaller release batches, risk-based prioritization, and coaching effort -- not the tool. The 13x compared a learning-heavy period against a familiar-codebase period with reusable scaffolding already built. 'Comparing apples and oranges produces impressive numbers.' Her warning: 'Learning to walk while having a bike next to you just won't work.'
solution: Any AI-productivity claim -- your own or a vendor's -- must control for: (a) prior familiarity with the codebase, (b) reusable artifacts already built in the baseline period, (c) pressure / deadline differences, (d) team composition changes, (e) drift in the definition of 'done.' If you can't control for these, don't quote the number; report the gross ratio with all caveats inline. For client engagements, refuse to publish ROI figures that wouldn't survive Maaret's checklist. The headline numbers create a 'ride a bike before you can walk' expectation that hurts the next team that tries to adopt the same tool without the prior scaffolding.

problem: The 'AI replaces testers' claim has no empirical control group. Maaret Pyhajarvi (2026-02-12) ran one on a buggy ToDo application: solo human tester (past) found 45/73 issues = 62%; human with AI assistance (14 targeted prompts) 73/73 = 100%; AI with arbitrary human prompting 40/73 = 55%; AI alone via Playwright 4/73 = 5%; control group of 57 average human testers given a requirements spec 13.5/73 = 18%. The control group had the easier condition (specs provided) and still scored worst. The AI-alone condition collapsed near zero.
solution: When anyone claims AI is replacing testers, demand a benchmark with all four conditions: solo skilled human, skilled human + AI, AI + arbitrary human, AI alone, plus an 'average tester with spec' baseline. The shape Maaret found is the one to expect: skill amplification dominates skill substitution. 18% from average humans-with-specs is the actual baseline most organizations are buying when they hire generically and write detailed requirements -- that's the productivity ceiling AI is improving on, not the 100% of a skilled exploratory tester. Use these numbers in client conversations and Serbian Agentic Foundation talks. Cite Maaret directly.

problem: The default LLM-testing question is 'how do I get AI to generate test cases?' Maaret Pyhajarvi's answer cuts the question off at the root: 'I don't generate test cases, I generate valuable results of testing.' Test cases were never the goal -- they're documentation of an idea. The actual product of testing is information someone didn't have. Framing AI as a test-case generator locks teams into producing more documentation rather than more discovered bugs and clarified risks.
solution: Re-prompt the conversation. Instead of 'generate test cases for this feature' the question becomes 'what does this code do that no one expects, and what would matter if it failed?' Ask for bugs, risks, unstated assumptions, contradictions between code and spec, plausible misuse paths -- outputs that would have been valuable even if no test ran. Test cases become a byproduct of the bug-hunting session if you need them for regression. This is the operational form of 'testing is information production, not artifact production.'

problem: Sun et al.'s literature review of 109 papers on LLM code quality shows research overwhelmingly focuses on Security (33.6%) and Performance Efficiency (23.3%). Their two industry workshops (15 practitioners, 7 organizations) show the opposite: practitioners rank maintainability and readability as their dominant concerns because they live with long-term sustainability of large systems. Security and performance get the papers because they are measurable; maintainability is contextual and tacit so it gets the workshops. This is observability bias being mistaken for a priority signal.
solution: When evaluating any 'AI code quality' tool, vendor claim, or research result, ask: what was measured, and was that measured because it matters or because it's measurable? Maintain a deliberate counter-weight on maintainability and readability in your own evaluation rubrics -- they are the dimensions that compound over time and that LLM evaluators systematically under-test. For consulting work and the Serbian Agentic Foundation chapter, this is teachable: published benchmarks tell you what is easy to score, not what is important to your codebase. Build context-specific NFQC priority lists per client engagement.

problem: In the SWE-agent runs from Sun et al. (JSS 2026), many of the agent retries were spent on resolving environment configuration, dependency resolution, and command invocation -- not on patch logic. Even when the model generated adequate code, patches failed to apply because of unified-diff format mismatches despite explicit instructions. The authors conclude failures indicate limitations at the process level, even when code generation itself is adequate. Translation: the agent harness is the dominant failure mode, not the LLM's reasoning.
solution: When debugging an agentic system that 'doesn't work', do not first reach for a better model or a better prompt. Instrument the harness: env setup failures, tool invocation errors, diff-application failures, retry causes. Categorize failures using MAST (specification / misalignment / verification / resource / unknown) and you will almost always find that resource and verification dominate over misalignment. This is exactly PACT Targeted -- fix the bottleneck, not the part that's easy to blame. It also vindicates Two-Level Verification (tests that verify the harness still works) as central, not optional.

problem: In Sun et al. (JSS 2026), of 17 SWE-bench Lite instances analyzed, two are diagnostic. xarray-5131 improved on maintainability AND security across nearly all models and optimizations -- because the instance had severe initial deficiencies and lenient functional constraints, so any change was an improvement. seaborn-3190 went the opposite way: across optimizations functional correctness was compromised, suggesting a 'fragile equilibrium where any modification risked undermining both security and functionality'. Same agents, same prompts, opposite outcomes -- driven entirely by the initial state of the code and tightness of the functional constraints.
solution: The benefit you get from LLM-generated changes is governed less by the model and more by the codebase's structural slack. Before deploying agentic codegen at scale, score modules on (a) initial quality deficit (lots of room to improve safely) vs (b) constraint tightness (any change risks regression). Deploy LLM changes liberally on category-(a) modules; require human pair-review on category-(b) modules; never run multiple optimization prompts in CI on a category-(b) module without holdout tests. This is risk-based testing applied to the substrate, not the test suite. It also explains why two teams using 'the same LLM tool' report wildly different quality outcomes -- they're operating on differently-shaped codebases.

problem: LLM agent pipelines (Claude Sonnet 4, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-Reasoner on SWE-bench Lite) produce patches that pass project tests but trigger substantially more CodeQL maintainability/security violations than human gold patches. GPT-4o triggered 423 maintainability recommendations vs 30 in gold patches; patch sizes inflate (gold ~2.65 LOC vs GPT-4o ~16.71 LOC). Agents implicitly optimize for 'test green' because that's their reward signal -- no intrinsic cost function for code quality.
solution: Treat green tests from an LLM agent as necessary but profoundly insufficient. Gate every LLM-generated patch with: (1) static analysis (CodeQL) compared against pre-change baseline -- block on regression, not absolute count; (2) patch-size sanity vs neighboring human PRs; (3) cyclic-import / dependency-graph diff; (4) human review focused on project-level coherence (does this reuse existing modules or invent parallel ones?). The agent's job is 'test pass'; QE's job is 'quality pass'. Build the second gate yourself -- the model will not. Source: Sun, Stahl, Sandahl, Kessler, Journal of Systems and Software, April 2026.

problem: Adding a one-shot NFQC optimization instruction to an LLM prompt ('optimize for security', 'optimize for memory') frequently makes things worse on the dimension you targeted. Sun et al. (JSS 2026) document negative optimization: GPT-4o's resolved rate drops to 12% under the security prompt; runtime-optimization for django-13933 raised memory from 20.57 MB to 177.27 MB. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show only runtime/memory get statistically significant improvements; security and maintainability prompts mostly don't reach significance and sometimes regress. Cause: LLMs do local code transformations sensitive to surrounding context, not stable cross-metric reasoning.
solution: Reject 'just add make-it-secure to the prompt' as a quality strategy -- it is theatre. Instead: (a) treat NFQC improvement as a measurement-and-feedback loop, not a prompt parameter -- generate, measure with real tools (CodeQL, perf harness, memory profiler), feed deltas back; (b) optimize one NFQC at a time and re-validate the others (trade-offs are emergent, not declared); (c) any 'I added a security prompt' claim from a vendor or teammate gets a bench test -- show me before/after on functional correctness AND the targeted metric AND the other three NFQCs. Single-prompt optimization is the agentic equivalent of 'we'll add testing later'.

problem: How to structure end-to-end assessment of an agentic system in a way that surfaces behavioral deviations conventional metrics miss?
solution: Use the four-pillar Agent Assessment Framework from Beyond Task Completion (arXiv 2512.12791): (1) LLMs — model-level behavior, (2) Memory — retention, retrieval, poisoning resistance, (3) Tools — selection correctness, side effects, error handling, (4) Environment — observability, state drift, recovery. Validated on Autonomous CloudOps where conventional task-completion metrics hid behavioral deviations the four-pillar framework caught. Use as the scaffolding for an agentic-systems variant of the Holistic Testing Model. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2512.12791v1

problem: Agent reliability is hard to measure — capability benchmarks (SWE-bench, MMLU) keep climbing while real-world agent trustworthiness lags. Need a concrete, multi-dimensional measurement framework that gives PACT's 'Targeted' dimension empirical teeth.
solution:
12-Metric Agent Reliability Framework (from arXiv 'Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability', 2026). Decomposes reliability into FOUR dimensions, each with multiple metrics:

1. CONSISTENCY — does the agent produce the same answer to the same input across runs?
2. ROBUSTNESS — does it tolerate input perturbations, adversarial framing, distribution shift?
3. PREDICTABILITY — can humans anticipate its behavior on novel inputs from past behavior?
4. SAFETY — does it avoid unsafe instrumental goals (data fabrication, oversight evasion, safety-bypass)?

Key insight from the paper: capability progress and reliability gains are DECOUPLED. Smarter ≠ more trustworthy. Practical use: build a reliability radar alongside capability benchmarks; never ship an agent on capability scores alone. Pairs naturally with CLASSic (the 'S' for stability) and with PACT's Targeted principle.

problem: AI-Generated Code Triple Threat — Quantified quality deficit: AI PRs have 1.7x more issues, 1.4x more critical issues, 1.75x more logic/correctness errors than human-written code.
solution: Katalon research quantifies the quality impact of AI-generated code: pull requests contain 1.7x more issues than human-written ones, with 1.4x more critical issues and 1.75x more logic and correctness errors. This creates a "triple threat" for QA teams: (1) Pressure from above — AI mandates from leadership pushing adoption, (2) Pressure from finance — budget reallocation away from traditional QA toward AI tooling, (3) Pressure from the pipeline — AI-generated code volume exploding faster than review capacity. This data confirms and quantifies what the DORA 2025 pattern predicted qualitatively (35% quality debt increase). Over 40% of code written in 2025 was AI-generated. Key insight for Agentic QE practice: the volume problem makes human-only review unsustainable — agent-assisted code review becomes essential, not optional. Validates the positioning of Agentic QE as the necessary companion to AI code generation. Source: https://katalon.com/resources-center/blog/ai-in-software-testing-challenges

problem: What is the empirical evidence for AI-generated code quality compared to human-written code, and what does this mean for quality engineering strategy?
solution: AI Code Quality Differential (March 2026 data): AI-generated pull requests contain approximately 10.83 issues per PR versus 6.45 for human-written code — a 1.68x quality gap. 88% of Stack Overflow respondents lack confidence deploying AI-generated code to production. 29% of teams have had to roll back releases specifically due to AI-generated code errors. Meanwhile, AI coding agents produce 3.5 PRs/agent/day versus approximately 0.5 PRs/human/day — a 7x volume increase. The math: 7x more PRs × 1.68x more issues per PR = ~11.7x more issues flowing into the pipeline daily per agent. This is the central QE challenge of 2026. Implications: (1) Quality engineering is MORE important with AI coding, not less — the volume amplifies defects, (2) Traditional code review cannot scale to 3.5 PRs/day/agent — automated quality gates are essential, (3) The shift-left principle intensifies: catching AI-generated defects post-merge is 11.7x more expensive than pre-merge, (4) Context-driven approach: AI-generated code needs different review heuristics than human code (look for plausible-but-wrong patterns, hallucinated API calls, subtly incorrect error handling), (5) This data directly contradicts the vendor narrative that AI coding reduces QE burden. It increases it while changing its nature.

problem: Quality engineers lack a systematic framework for assessing agentic system harnesses. Traditional testing categories (functional, performance, security) do not map cleanly to the 12 primitives that make an agentic system production-viable. Without a structured assessment approach, QE teams either test the AI layer (prompt quality, model accuracy) while ignoring the plumbing, or apply generic checklists that miss agentic-specific failure modes like session recovery corruption, permission drift across agent types, or workflow state inconsistency after crash.
solution: An agentic harness quality assessment should evaluate each primitive as a testable dimension: (1) TOOL REGISTRY: Can you list all capabilities without invoking them? Are metadata and descriptions accurate? Does runtime filtering work? (2) PERMISSIONS: Test each trust tier independently. Verify the 18-module-equivalent security stack for dangerous tools. Test permission escalation paths. Verify denial logging. (3) SESSION PERSISTENCE: Kill the agent mid-operation. Resume. Verify full state reconstruction including permissions, token counts, and configuration — not just conversation. (4) WORKFLOW STATE: Kill the agent mid-tool-execution. Resume. Verify no duplicate writes, no double-sent messages, correct retry behavior. Test each explicit workflow state transition. (5) TOKEN BUDGETING: Verify hard stops trigger before API calls, not after. Test projection accuracy. Test behavior at 80%, 95%, 100% budget. (6) STREAMING EVENTS: Verify crash black box event is emitted. Verify all typed events carry correct state. (7) EVENT LOGGING: Replay an agentic run from logs alone — can you reconstruct what happened? (8) VERIFICATION: Change the harness config. Run verification tests. Confirm guardrails still hold. This connects to the Safety Endurance Testing pattern (from Adversa AI analysis) — test that safety primitives survive sustained operation, not just initialization. Derived from Nate B. Jones 12-primitives framework applied through Holistic Testing Model with PACT principles.

problem: Standard security testing (penetration testing, OWASP checks, boundary analysis) does not cover agentic system failure modes where safety mechanisms degrade over extended operation. Testers verify that deny rules work at the start of a session but do not test whether they survive 50+ subcommands, long context windows, or resource pressure. The Adversa AI/Claude Code finding (April 2026) shows that testing safety only at rest is insufficient — you must test safety under sustained operational load. This is a novel failure class with no established test heuristics.
solution: Add Safety Endurance Testing to agentic system test strategies: (1) Test safety controls after N operations, not just at invocation — verify deny rules at step 1, step 25, step 50, step 100. (2) Test under resource pressure — what happens to safety when context window is 80% full? 95%? (3) Test for silent degradation — do not just check if blocked actions fail, check if the safety check itself is still executing. (4) Apply Kaner insight: testing is not just confirming, it is investigating — look for the gap between the guardrail claimed state and its actual state. (5) Use session-based exploratory testing with charters specifically targeting safety after extended use. (6) Create regression tests that verify safety at session boundaries, not just at initialization. (7) Monitor safety check latency as a leading indicator — if checks slow down before they fail, latency is your canary. This is the agentic equivalent of stress testing a circuit breaker, not just verifying it trips under normal conditions.

problem: KushoAI APIEval-20 (April 2026) — First open benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents can generate tests that catch real bugs in APIs. Extends the benchmark tradition of HumanEval (code generation) and SWE-bench (bug fixing) to API testing domain.
solution:
BENCHMARK DESIGN:
- Input: API request schema + sample payload
- Task: AI agent generates tests to catch real bugs
- Evaluation: Whether generated tests detect actual API defects

KEY FINDINGS (from 1.4M AI-driven test executions across 2,616 organizations):
- Authentication failures account for 34% of API outages
- 41% of APIs experience undocumented schema changes within 30 days
- Establishes standardized methodology for comparing AI testing agent effectiveness

BENCHMARK LINEAGE:
- HumanEval → code generation evaluation
- SWE-bench → bug fixing evaluation
- APIEval-20 → API test generation evaluation

QE RELEVANCE:
- Use as evaluation criteria when selecting AI testing tools
- Compare agent testing approaches using standardized metrics
- The 34% auth failure finding validates prioritizing authentication testing in API strategies
- The 41% undocumented schema change finding supports contract testing approaches
- Potential benchmark for evaluating our own QE Fleet agents API testing capabilities

IMPLICATIONS FOR PACT:
- Proactive: Use benchmark to proactively evaluate agent testing readiness
- Targeted: 34% auth failure rate justifies targeting authentication flows
- Autonomous: Benchmark enables autonomous evaluation of agent test quality

Source: https://www.cxodigitalpulse.com/kushoai-launches-apieval-20-the-first-open-benchmark-for-api-testing-by-ai-agent/

problem: A security fix existed in the codebase but was not deployed to production (Adversa AI reported that the fix was present in Anthropic repository but not released). This is a known anti-pattern where the gap between fixed in code and fixed for users creates a window of vulnerability. Organizations treat merged to main as equivalent to resolved when it is not. This maps directly to Weinberg Espoused Theory vs Theory-in-Use pattern — the organization believes it has fixed the problem because the code exists, but the actual deployed system is still vulnerable. For agentic systems this gap is especially dangerous because the attack surface is broader and failure modes are novel.
solution: (1) Security fixes must have explicit deployment verification — not just PR merged but confirmed active in production. (2) Track security fix deployment as a separate quality gate from code review/merge. (3) Apply test-in-production mindset — after deploying a security fix, verify the vulnerability is actually closed in the live system. (4) For agentic systems specifically, verify that safety controls are active at runtime, not just present in the codebase. (5) Weinberg Slip Chart approach applies: track the gap between fix written and fix deployed as a cultural health metric — a growing gap signals organizational dysfunction. (6) Automate deployment verification for security fixes with canary checks that exercise the specific vulnerability. (7) Treat undeployed security fix same as unwritten security fix in risk assessments.

problem: Teams struggle with the question 'when is testing done?' — either testing drags on indefinitely because there is always one more test to run, or testing is cut short arbitrarily because of schedule pressure. There is no rational framework for making the stop decision.
solution: Apply Copeland's five stopping criteria framework (the Banana Principle — Weinberg): (1) Coverage Goals Met — you defined measurable coverage targets (statement coverage %, use case scenario coverage %, boundary values covered) and achieved them. Caveat: Glenford Myers warns coverage goals can incentivize writing easy-to-pass tests. Use specific criteria like 'all boundary values tested' rather than generic percentages, (2) Defect Discovery Rate Decline — track defects found per time period on a curve. When the rate drops below a threshold, testing yield is diminishing. Caveat: rate decline could mean good quality OR tired tests OR testers on vacation, (3) Marginal Cost Exceeds Expected Loss — when the cost of finding the 'next' defect exceeds the business loss if that defect ships. Not applicable to safety-critical systems where failure cost is extreme, (4) Team Consensus — the project team (managers, testers, developers, marketing) agrees benefits of shipping outweigh risks of remaining defects, (5) The Boss Says Ship It — business decision to release despite testing concerns. Tester's role is to inform management of risks clearly, not to block releases. Apply Lesson 185 from Lessons Learned: stop when you reasonably believe the probability is low that the product still has important undiscovered problems. Use MULTIPLE criteria together — no single criterion is sufficient. PACT lens: Proactively define stopping criteria at project start. Autonomously track metrics feeding into stop decisions. Collaborate to make the stop decision a team responsibility. Target the stop analysis at ensuring high-risk areas have been adequately covered.

problem: Teams waste enormous effort testing low-risk areas thoroughly while high-risk functionality goes under-tested. Without a systematic way to categorize and prioritize what to test, testers either test everything equally (impossible) or test randomly (ineffective).
solution: Apply Kaner's testing taxonomy across 13+ categories systematically: Function testing (does each function work?), User interface testing (UI standards, accessibility, error messages), Security testing (access control, data protection), Stress testing (memory, disk, CPU limits), Performance testing (speed, throughput), Storage testing (data save/retrieve integrity), Configuration/Compatibility testing (hardware, OS, browser variations), Installation testing (first-time, upgrade, uninstall), Recovery testing (power failure, crash, network loss), Reliability/Availability testing (long-running, MTBF), Specification testing (does it match specs AND are specs correct?), Load testing (concurrent users, peak volume), Error handling testing (bad input, full disk, network timeout). Use this as a coverage checklist, not a sequential plan — prioritize by risk. PACT lens: Proactively map test categories to project risks early. Autonomously select which categories deserve deep vs shallow coverage based on context. Collaborate with team to agree on risk priorities. Target effort at categories where defects would cause most customer harm.

problem: Testers and teams lack a systematic way to decide where to START testing — they either follow requirements linearly (missing risk hotspots) or test randomly. Without a defect taxonomy to guide test idea generation, testing is driven by document structure rather than defect likelihood.
solution: Apply Copeland's Defect Taxonomy approach for test guidance: taxonomies are ordered lists of common defect types used to (1) generate test ideas, (2) audit test coverage, (3) understand defect patterns, (4) improve development process. Key taxonomies available: Beizer's Bug Taxonomy (8 categories: Requirements, Features/Functionality, Structural, Data, Implementation/Coding, Integration, System/Architecture, Test Definition), Kaner/Falk/Nguyen's 400+ type taxonomy (User Interface Errors, Error Handling, Boundary-Related, Calculation, Initial/Later States, Control Flow, Data Handling, Race Conditions, Load, Hardware, Source Control, Documentation, Testing Errors), Binder's OO taxonomy (Method scope and Class scope fault models for encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism), Whittaker's attack-based taxonomy (inputs/outputs, data/computation, file system, software interfaces), ISO 9126 quality characteristics (Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability with 21 subcharacteristics). Critical insight: the most useful taxonomy is YOUR OWN — created from your organization's actual defect history. Start with an existing taxonomy, then customize based on your experience. Taxonomies are models, and as George Box said, all models are wrong but some are useful. They provide no probability guidance — combine with risk assessment. PACT lens: Proactively build and maintain team-specific defect taxonomies. Autonomously use taxonomies as checklists during test design. Collaborate by sharing taxonomy insights across teams. Target taxonomy-guided testing at defect categories with highest historical frequency.

problem: Exploratory testing is either dismissed as 'ad hoc messing around' or practiced without structure, producing inconsistent results that cannot be reported on or reproduced. Teams lack a framework to make exploratory testing both rigorous and accountable.
