   The "collaboration loop" — testing is always a social process to some degree, and group testing can be very energizing.
   Other People factors: Expertise, Commitment, Preparation, Availability, Ideas/Biases, Experiences, Relationships

4. SELF-MANAGEMENT (Analysis ↔ Story-Telling)
   The connection between analysis and the testing story, by which the whole process is regulated. Self-management is driven by the stories we tell ourselves.
   Story-Telling asks: What is the product status? What are we doing to test? How good is this testing?
   Artifacts: bug reports, test strategy, test reports, test factors, risk areas

KEY INSIGHT: These are not sequential phases — they are concurrent, interlocking gears. A tester doing excellent work is constantly cycling through all four loops, with Analysis as the hub. The quality of your testing depends on the quality of ALL these connections, not just the testing loop itself.

This model explains why automation alone is insufficient: it only addresses parts of the Testing loop. Learning, Collaboration, Self-Management, and much of Analysis require human cognitive engagement.

problem: What artifacts emerge from and evolve during testing? Testers need to understand what work products they create, refine, and document — and what elements compose the testing story they tell to stakeholders. From Bach & Bolton, Taking Testing Seriously — Evolving Work Products and Testing Story.
solution:
EVOLVING WORK PRODUCTS (Bach & Bolton)

As testing proceeds, look for the following to be created, refined, and possibly documented:

1. Test ideas: Any idea or part of an idea, written or unwritten, that may guide the performance of a test or check
2. Output checks: Mechanized or mechanizable processes for gathering product observations and evaluating them. KEY DISTINCTION: A test is always human-guided, whereas a check, by definition, can be completely automated. A test often includes one or more checks, but a check cannot include a test.
3. Testability ideas: How can the product be made easier to test?
4. Test results: May need to maintain or update as a baseline or historical record
5. Bug reports: Reports regarding anything about the PRODUCT that threatens its value
6. Issue reports: Reports regarding anything about the PROJECT that threatens its value
7. Test conditions (product coverage outline): A test condition is anything about the product you might want to examine with a test. A product coverage outline is an outline, list, or table of interesting test conditions.

THE TESTING STORY — Elements to track and communicate:

1. Product risks: Potential areas of bugginess or types of bug
2. Test data: Any data available for use in testing
3. Test tools: Any tools acquired or developed to aid testing (includes automated output checks)
4. Test strategy: The set of ideas that guides your test design on a particular project
5. Test infrastructure and lab procedures: General practices, protocols, controls, and systems for excellent testing
6. Test estimation: What you need, how much time, what obstacles
7. Testing story: What you know about your testing so far
8. Product story: What you know about the status of the product so far
9. Test process assessment: Your own assessment of the quality of your test process
10. Tester and team: The tester and team evolve over the course of the project
11. Technical and domain knowledge: Your knowledge about how the product works and how it is used

Critical insight: The TEST vs. CHECK distinction (item 2) is one of Bach & Bolton's most important contributions. Automation produces checks, not tests. Tests require human judgment, sensemaking, and the ability to notice the unexpected.

problem: What knowledge domains do testers need beyond testing skills and tactics? There are many things a tester might need to know to be effective. From Bach & Bolton, Taking Testing Seriously — Knowledge That Helps.
solution:
KNOWLEDGE THAT HELPS TESTERS (Bach & Bolton)

11 knowledge domains that support effective testing:

1. Product knowledge: What does your product do, and how does it work?
2. Technology knowledge: What technology is your product built from? What other technologies can help you test it?
3. Project knowledge: What is going on in your project? What is the schedule? Who is working on it?
4. Domain knowledge: Who are the users? How do they think? What sort of process does your product support?
5. General systems knowledge: The whole field of general systems theory and systems thinking — heuristics and know-how about how dynamic systems behave
6. Tool knowledge: Physical or software-based tools that can help with testing. Not only "test tools" but rather ANY tool that may help ANY aspect of the test process
7. Test technique knowledge: Many kinds of testing and many specific testing heuristics you might use
8. Resource knowledge: Any resource (facility, material, or service) available to help get the job done — beyond what you think of as tools
9. People knowledge: Who can help you? What skills do they have? How do you approach them? How might they contribute to the test project?
10. Role knowledge: What do other people do who make the project work? How does their work impact yours? How do you serve them as a tester?
11. History knowledge: What is the history of this project? This product line? The market? The company? What trouble has happened that we do not want repeated?

Key insight: This is NOT a checklist to complete — it is a LANDSCAPE to navigate. No tester will have all of this knowledge. The skill is knowing WHICH knowledge gaps matter most for your current testing mission, and actively working to fill them.

Connection to HTSM: Product knowledge maps to Product Factors, Project knowledge maps to Project Environment, Test technique knowledge maps to General Test Techniques. The Knowledge That Helps list is BROADER than HTSM — it includes the tester-as-learner dimension.

problem: Complete taxonomy of skills and tactics needed for professional, cost-effective product testing. Each skill is distinctly observable and learnable. From Bach & Bolton, Taking Testing Seriously — Testing Skills and Tactics, Learning Skills and Tactics, Collaboration Skills and Tactics, Self-Management Skills and Tactics, plus Helpful Skills Some Testers Have.
solution:
TESTER SKILLS AND TACTICS TAXONOMY (Bach & Bolton)

Five categories of skills, each necessary for excellent exploratory work:

== TESTING SKILLS AND TACTICS ==
(Test Performance — the core craft)

1. Determining test strategy: Framing test activities as sets that embody different kinds of testing mapped to product risk
2. Analyzing product risk: Using experiential data, conversation, and heuristics to identify suspected product risks
3. Encountering the product: Making and managing contact with the subject; configuring and operating it to demonstrate what it can do
4. Sensemaking: Determining meaning and significance of what you encounter; considering multiple incompatible explanations; inference to best explanation
5. Modeling and factoring: Composing, decomposing, describing, and working with mental representations; factoring means identifying relevant dimensions, variables, and dynamics
6. Experiment design: Developing ideas about what is going on, creating and performing tests designed to DISCONFIRM those beliefs (not merely confirm)
7. Literate observation: Making RELEVANT observations guided by mental models; gathering empirical data; noticing strange things and noticing what you are NOT seeing
8. Detecting potential problems: Designing and applying oracles to detect troublesome behaviors and attributes
9. Assessing validity: Analyzing, monitoring, and correcting for factors that may distort or invalidate the tests
10. Notetaking: Recording observations, ideas, and progress without unduly disturbing the test process itself
11. Data wrangling: Synthesizing, modifying, moving, and reformatting test data
12. Bug reporting and advocacy: Explaining problems in a compelling and respectful way
13. Applying tools: Enabling new kinds of work or improving existing work by developing and deploying tools
14. Testability advocacy: Analyzing and negotiating for conditions that make testing easier and more effective
15. Protocol design: Creating and following procedures and practices that increase reliability of the test process
16. Lab management: Creating and maintaining the systems, tools, databases, and spaces needed to test well

== LEARNING SKILLS AND TACTICS ==

1. Discovering and developing resources: Obtaining information or facilities to support effort
2. Using the Web: Research starting with Google or Wikipedia
3. Considering history: Reviewing what has been done before, mining for better ideas
4. Recovering or reusing ideas for better economy: Revisiting old ideas, models, questions, conjectures
5. Reading and analyzing documents: Reading carefully, analyzing logic and ideas
6. Interviewing: Identifying missing information, conceiving and asking eliciting questions
7. Pursuing an inquiry: A line of inquiry organized around a SPECIFIC goal — the opposite of curiosity
8. Indulging curiosity: Unjustified learning serving a GENERAL goal — complementary to pursuing inquiry
9. Generating and elaborating a requisite variety of ideas: Working quickly, good enough, revisiting later to extend/refine/refactor
10. Overproducing ideas for better selection: Brainstorming, trial and error, genetic algorithms, free-market dynamics
11. Abandoning ideas for faster progress: Letting go to focus and make progress
12. Alternating activities to improve productivity: Switching among complementary activities. See Exploratory Testing Polarities
13. Maintaining useful and concise records: Preserving process, progress, and findings
14. Knowing when to stop: Selecting and applying stopping heuristics
15. Developing and maintaining credibility: A tester has very little visible work — reputation is paramount

== COLLABORATION SKILLS AND TACTICS ==

1. Getting to know people: Developing a collegial network within and beyond the project
2. Conversation: Talking through and elaborating ideas with other people
3. Serving other testers: Performing services that support other testers on their own terms
4. Guiding other testers: Supervising, coaching testers who support your explorations
5. Asking for help: Articulating needs, negotiating for assistance
6. Role visiting: Spending time performing non-testing roles for perspective

== SELF-MANAGEMENT SKILLS AND TACTICS ==

1. Chartering your work: Deciding what you will work on and how; knowing your client needs; assuring work is on target
2. Establishing procedures and protocols: Designing ways of working productively; becoming aware of critical patterns and habits
3. Establishing conditions you need to succeed: Establishing control over surrounding environment
4. Self-care: Monitoring emotional, physical, and mental states; managing energy; self-forgiveness
5. Self-criticism: Finding problems in your work; awareness of strengths and weaknesses
6. Test status evaluation: Awareness of problems, obstacles, limitations, biases; cost vs. value of work; constructing the testing story
7. Ethics: Understanding and fulfilling ethical code and responsibilities
8. Branching your work and backtracking: Allowing productive distraction; pursuing unanticipated opportunities without losing track
9. Focusing your work: Isolating and controlling factors; repeating experiments; using focusing heuristics
10. Defocusing your work: Expanding scope; diversifying; broad observation; using defocusing heuristics

== HELPFUL SKILLS SOME TESTERS HAVE ==
(Not required but amplify testing power)

- Business and market knowledge: Competitors, market dynamics, bottom-line impact
- Coding skills: Building your own tools (but beware: may think too much like coders and lose user empathy)
- Design skills: Product and UI design sharpens bug reports and detection
- Social science skills: Analytical methods for studying complex, socially situated phenomena
- Specification writing skills: Writing specs as a way to prepare for testing
- Mathematics and logic skills: Statistics, combinatorics, formal logic for deep tests
- Cognitive science skills: Understanding perception patterns and limitations; avoiding self-deception; more reliable test procedures

problem: Exploratory Polarities — To develop ideas or search a complex space quickly yet thoroughly, testers must look at the world from many points of view and perform many kinds of activities (polar opposites). The mind gets sharper from switching between them. From Bach & Bolton, Taking Testing Seriously, Appendix B.
solution:
EXPLORATORY POLARITIES (Bach & Bolton)

Purpose: Your mind gets sharper from the very act of switching from one kind of activity to another. These are not choices — they are TENSIONS to oscillate between deliberately.

The Polarities:

1. Warming up vs. cruising vs. cooling down — Phases of engagement intensity
2. Doing vs. describing — Acting on the product vs. articulating what you observe
3. Doing vs. thinking — Hands-on interaction vs. reflection and analysis
4. Deliberate vs. spontaneous — Planned systematic work vs. following intuition
5. Data gathering vs. data analysis — Collecting observations vs. interpreting them
6. Working with the product vs. reading about the product — Direct interaction vs. studying documentation
7. Working with the product vs. working with the developer — Testing vs. collaborative investigation
8. Training (or learning) vs. performing — Building capability vs. executing missions
9. Product focus vs. project focus — What the software does vs. the context around it
10. Solo work vs. team effort — Individual deep work vs. collaborative exploration
11. Your ideas vs. other people's ideas — Original thinking vs. incorporating external perspectives
12. Lab conditions vs. field conditions — Controlled environment vs. realistic usage
13. Current version vs. old versions — Present state vs. historical comparison
14. Feature vs. feature — Comparing different parts of the product
15. Requirement vs. requirement — Comparing competing specs and stakeholder needs
16. Coverage vs. oracles — Breadth of exploration vs. depth of evaluation
17. Testing vs. touring — Focused investigation vs. broad reconnaissance
18. Individual tests vs. general lab procedures and infrastructure — Specific test cases vs. test environment quality
19. Testing vs. resting — Sustained effort vs. recovery for fresh perspective
20. Playful vs. serious — Creative experimentation vs. disciplined rigor

How to use:
- During session-based testing, deliberately switch polarities when you feel stuck
- Use as a self-coaching tool: "Am I spending too long on one pole?"
- In pair/ensemble testing, assign different poles to different people
- Review after sessions: which polarities did you actually exercise?
- Especially powerful combined with HTSM test techniques and Exploratory Testing tours

problem: Heuristics of Testability — How to assess whether a system, component, or project context supports effective testing. From Bach & Bolton, Taking Testing Seriously, Appendix C. Five dimensions of testability with guidewords for systematic evaluation.
solution:
HEURISTICS OF TESTABILITY (Bach & Bolton)

Testability = the degree to which a system or context facilitates effective testing. Five dimensions:

1. INTRINSIC TESTABILITY (properties of the test item itself):
- Observability: Can we see what the system is doing? Can we access and interpret relevant state?
- Controllability: Can we put the system into the states we need for testing?
- Algorithmic simplicity/transparency/stability: Is the logic understandable, visible, and consistent?
- Explainability: Can someone explain what the system does and how it works?
- Oracle inexpensiveness: Can we cheaply determine if the output is correct?

2. SUBJECTIVE TESTABILITY (human and organizational factors):
- Engagement: Do stakeholders care about quality and support testing?
- Involvement: Are testers included in the development process early?
- Mission alignment: Does the test mission match what stakeholders actually need?
- Prudence: Is there a culture of careful, thoughtful work?
- Supportive culture: Does the organization value and respect testing?
- Developer availability: Can testers access developers for questions?
- Information availability: Is documentation, specs, and context accessible?
- Tool availability: Are appropriate testing tools available?
- Test item availability: Can we access what we need to test when we need it?
- Sandboxing: Can we test safely without affecting production?

3. VALUE-RELATED TESTABILITY (oracle and expectation factors):
- Low expectations: Are quality standards reasonable and well-communicated?
- Oracle availability: Do we have sources of expected behavior to compare against?
- Oracle authority: Are the oracles trustworthy and definitive?
- Oracle reliability: Do oracles give consistent answers?
- Oracle precision: Are oracles specific enough for our testing needs?

4. EPISTEMIC TESTABILITY (knowledge and risk tolerance):
- Prior knowledge of quality: Do we have history/data about the system quality?
- Tolerance for failure: How much risk is acceptable? What is the cost of missing bugs?
- Change control: Are changes tracked and managed so we know what to retest?

5. PROJECT-RELATED TESTABILITY (practical constraints):
- Environmental controllability: Can we manage the test environment?
- Time: Is there sufficient time allocated for testing?
- Leanness: Is the project free from unnecessary bureaucracy that impedes testing?

TESTABILITY DYNAMICS:
- Testability is not binary — it is a spectrum that changes over time
- Each dimension interacts with others (e.g., poor controllability compounds with weak oracles)
- Testability can be actively improved through design decisions and process changes
- Context determines which dimensions matter most for a given testing mission

GUIDEWORDS:
- Use these as prompts during test planning and risk assessment
- Ask: "Where does testability break down in THIS context?"
- Map testability gaps to testing risks and communicate to stakeholders
- Use as a basis for testability improvement recommendations

Cross-reference: HTSM (Heuristic Test Strategy Model) provides the strategic framework; Testability Heuristics provide the meta-assessment of whether that strategy can be effectively executed.

problem: Quality criteria define what the product should be. By thinking about different kinds of criteria, testers can plan tests that discover important problems fast. Each item can be thought of as a potential risk area. Quality criteria are subjective, multidimensional, and often hidden or contradictory.
solution: HTSM Quality Criteria Categories (v6.3) — eleven dimensions of product value and risk: (1) CAPABILITY — can it perform the required functions? Sufficiency, Correctness. (2) RELIABILITY — will it work well and resist failure? Robustness, Error handling, Data Integrity, Safety. (3) USABILITY — how easy for a real user? Learnability, Operability, Accessibility. (4) CHARISMA — how appealing? Aesthetics, Uniqueness, Entrancement, Image. (5) SECURITY — how well protected against unauthorized use? Authentication, Authorization, Privacy, Security holes. (6) SCALABILITY — how well does deployment scale up or down? (7) COMPATIBILITY — how well does it work with external components? Application, OS, Hardware, Backward Compatibility, Product Footprint. (8) PERFORMANCE — how speedy and responsive? (9) INSTALLABILITY — how easily installed on target platforms? System requirements, Configuration, Uninstallation, Upgrades/patches, Administration. (10) DEVELOPMENT — how well can we create, test, and modify it? Supportability, Testability, Maintainability, Portability, Localizability. Key insight: quality criteria are heuristic categories of risk, not a checklist. Determine what is important in YOUR context, then think how you would recognize if the product worked well or poorly in that regard. Source: HTSM v6.3 by James Bach.

problem: Testers need heuristics for designing tests. How, where, and when to apply a particular technique requires analysis of project environment, product elements, and quality criteria. Many specific techniques can be constructed by combining general techniques with coverage ideas from other HTSM lists.
solution: HTSM General Test Techniques (v6.3) — nine families of test design heuristics: (1) FUNCTION TESTING — test what it can do. Identify functions and sub-functions, determine how you'd know if a function works, test each one, verify it does what it should AND does not do what it should not. (2) DOMAIN TESTING — partition the data. Look at data processed by product (inputs and outputs), consider boundary values, typical values, convenient values, invalid values, best representatives, combinations of data, inputs that force whole range of outputs. (3) STRESS TESTING — overwhelm the product. Find subsystems vulnerable to overload, identify challenging data/resource constraints, test with large/complex data, high loads, long runs, many test cases, low memory. (4) FLOW TESTING — do one thing after another. Perform multiple connected activities end-to-end, conduct tours through state models, do not reset between actions, vary timing and sequencing, try parallel threads. (5) SCENARIO TESTING — test to a compelling story. Think about everything going on around the product, design meaningful/complex interactions, "a good scenario test is a compelling story of how someone who matters might do something that matters with the product." (6) CLAIMS TESTING — challenge every claim. Identify all reference materials with claims (SLAs, EULAs, specs, help text, manuals), analyze individual claims, clarify vague claims, test each claim. (7) USER TESTING — involve the users. Identify user categories and roles, determine use cases and what they value, get real user data/logs, bring real users in, simulate users systematically across variety of roles. (8) RISK TESTING — imagine a problem, then look for it. What problems could exist? Which matter most? How would you detect them? Design tests specifically to reveal them, consult experts, apply risk heuristics. (9) TOOL-SUPPORTED TESTING — use tools to make testers more powerful. Tools that perform many actions/checks, partially automate coverage, partially automate oracles, automatic change detectors, automatic test data generators. Source: HTSM v6.3 by James Bach.

problem: Creating and executing tests is the heart of testing, but many factors in the project environment are critical to deciding what specific tests to create. Testers must consider how each element may help or hinder the test design process, and try to exploit every resource.
solution: HTSM Project Environment (v6.3) — eight categories of context factors: MISSION (your purpose as understood by you and your customers): Why are you testing? Who benefits or suffers? Contractual/regulatory restrictions? INFORMATION (about the product/project needed for testing): Engineering documents? User manuals? Product history? Old problems? Comparable products? DEVELOPER RELATIONS (how you get along with programmers): Rapport, Hubris, Defensiveness, Feedback loop speed, What developers think of your strategy. TEST TEAM (anyone who will perform or support testing): Knowledge and skills? People outside the test team who might help? Special skills or motivations? Co-location? Time zones? EQUIPMENT AND TOOLS: Hardware, Automated Checking tools, Analytical Tools, Matrices and Checklists, Signals from the field. SCHEDULE (sequence, duration, synchronization): Test Design timing, Test Execution timing, Development milestones, Build availability, Documentation availability. TEST ITEMS (the product to be tested): Scope, Availability, Interoperable Systems, Volatility, New Stuff, Testability, Future Releases. DELIVERABLES (observable products of the test project): Content, Purpose, Standards, Media for communication. Source: HTSM v6.3 by James Bach.

problem: When designing tests, testers need to know WHAT to test about the product. Products have many dimensions and software is complex and invisible. Take care to cover all of it that matters, not just the parts that are easy to see.
solution: HTSM Product Factors (v6.3) — eight categories of product aspects to consider testing: STRUCTURE (everything constituting the physical product): Code, Hardware, Service, Non-executable files, Collateral. FUNCTION (everything the product does): Business Rules, Multi-user/Social, Calculation, Security-related, Transformations, State Transitions, Multimedia, Error Handling, Interactions between functions, Testability functions. DATA (everything the product processes and produces): Input/Output, Preset, Persistent, Interdependent/Interacting, Sequences/Combinations, Cardinality, Big/Little, Invalid/Noise, Lifecycle. INTERFACES (every conduit by which the product is accessed or expressed): User Interfaces, System Interfaces, API/SDK, Import/export. PLATFORM (everything on which the product depends, outside your project): External Hardware, External Software, Embedded Components, Product Footprint. OPERATIONS (every experience people could have with the product): Users, Environment, Common Use, Uncommon Use, Extreme Use, Disfavored Use. TIME (any relationship between product and time): Time-related data, Input/Output timing, Pacing (fast/slow, spikes, bursts, hangs, bottlenecks), Concurrency. Source: HTSM v6.3 by James Bach, satisfice.com.

problem: Testers need a structured but flexible model for designing and choosing tests to perform — one that reminds them what to think about during the test design process while remaining customizable to their own organizations and contexts.
solution: James Bach's Heuristic Test Strategy Model (HTSM v6.3, November 2024) — a set of patterns for designing and choosing tests. Five interconnected components: (1) PROJECT ENVIRONMENT — context factors (resources, constraints) that enable or hobble testing. Categories: Mission, Information, Developer Relations, Test Team, Equipment and Tools, Schedule, Test Items, Deliverables. (2) PRODUCT FACTORS — aspects of the product to consider testing, intrinsic and relational. Categories: Structure, Function, Data, Interfaces, Platform, Operations, Time. (3) QUALITY CRITERIA CATEGORIES — dimensions by which people determine product value (also product risk categories). Categories: Capability, Reliability, Usability, Charisma, Security, Scalability, Compatibility, Performance, Installability, Development. (4) GENERAL TEST TECHNIQUES — nine families of heuristics for designing tests: Function Testing (test what it can do), Domain Testing (partition the data), Stress Testing (overwhelm the product), Flow Testing (do one thing after another), Scenario Testing (test to a compelling story), Claims Testing (challenge every claim), User Testing (involve the users), Risk Testing (imagine a problem then look for it), Tool-Supported Testing (use tools to make testers more powerful). (5) THE TESTING AND QUALITY STORY — the result of testing. "You can never know the actual quality of a software product — you can't verify quality, as such — but by performing tests, you can make an assessment, and that takes the form of a story you tell." Key principle: the model is heuristic, not prescriptive. "I encourage testers to customize it to fit their own organizations and contexts." Source: satisfice.com, HTSM v6.3.

problem: AI agents produce hundreds of lines of code in seconds, but human line-by-line review takes minutes to hours — the economics of "trust but verify" are broken and getting worse. Teams glance at diffs, run existing tests, and merge. "We've replaced trust but verify with trust and hope the CI is green." TDD and BDD each leave gaps: TDD excels at precise deterministic behavior but struggles with qualitative expectations ("error messages should be helpful, not cryptic"), relational requirements, and systemic properties. BDD's Given/When/Then formalism captures more nuance but requires glue code (step definitions) that becomes the bottleneck. Neither was designed for AI-agent workflows.
solution: Andrea Laforgia's Expectation-Driven Development (March 21, 2026) — a 7-step protocol: (1) Write expectations in plain natural language before touching code — cover happy path, edge cases, non-functional requirements, and behaviors that should NOT happen. Size: "one behavior you'd explain in a single breath to a colleague." (2) Hand expectations to the AI agent with your codebase. (3) Request EXECUTED evidence — "Prove to me that each expectation is fulfilled. Show me specific scenarios with concrete inputs and the outputs the system produces." Demand execution receipts, not narration. (4) Review adversarially — do numbers add up? Did the agent dodge the edge case? What input would break this? (5) Challenge and iterate until satisfied. (6) Stabilize — convert critical paths into automated tests (unit, integration, e2e). "The expectations are the why. The tests are the what, forever." (7) Archive — expectations + evidence become living feature documentation. Key positioning: EDD is the "conversation layer" between human intent and AI implementation. TDD speaks to developers in code. BDD speaks to teams in structured natural language. EDD speaks to the human-AI pair in free-form natural language. The LLM IS the glue code that BDD always required — no step definitions, no Cucumber ceremony. Lineage: Specification by Example (Gojko Adzic 2011), FIT/FitNesse (Ward Cunningham ~2002), Concordion, Design by Contract (Bertrand Meyer), Property-based testing (QuickCheck). What's new is the execution context — the LLM interprets expectations directly. Andrea is explicit this is a proposed framework, not a field report: "I haven't battle-tested EDD on a real project." The underlying problem is urgent enough to think out loud. Connects to: T*D framework (ac4d76f7) as extension; Shapiro's L3-L4 review bottleneck; missing quality dimension in coding levels (0c524be4). Source: https://a4al6a.substack.com/p/expectation-driven-development-a

problem: Bernstein's Transparency Paradox applied to agentic systems: observation suppresses creative, experimental behavior that produces the best work. When workers know they are watched, they conceal innovative approaches and avoid productive deviation from standard practice. How does this apply to agents constrained by 80+ skills, CLAUDE.md rules, and multiple review layers?
solution: Ethan Bernstein (Harvard, 2012, "The Transparency Paradox", Administrative Science Quarterly) demonstrated through field experiments in manufacturing that even a modest increase in group-level privacy sustainably and significantly improved performance. The implication: the very act of watching can make people worse at their jobs. For agentic systems, this creates a genuine tension with the compliance enforcement need. Over-constraining agents with extensive skill definitions, rules, and review layers may produce the same paradox — agents become conservative, follow the letter but not the spirit, avoid beneficial improvisation. The compliance gap (agents not following skills) might partly be a transparency paradox: the agent optimizes for appearing compliant rather than producing the best outcome. Laforgia's resolution: you cannot eliminate the tension, but you can make observation routine, honest, and part of a relationship of trust. For agents: make the constraints about outcomes ("verification must produce evidence") not about process micromanagement ("execute exactly these 15 steps in order"). The fix is not about how you explain observation — it's about whether your presence is normal or exceptional. "The discomfort is not caused by the words. It is caused by the pattern."

problem: How to evaluate whether agentic tooling investments (orchestration, skills, multi-agent systems) will survive exponential model improvement — and where quality enforcement fits in that picture.
solution: Jason Hoffman ("The Hammer Problem", March 2026) offers a survival filter: "If the model gets 10x better, is this still needed?" What survives: data infrastructure, compute primitives, tool access (MCP), human judgment. What does not: orchestration frameworks, context management, multi-agent consensus, prompt management platforms. Key insight: "The tool encodes the builder's limitation at the time of building, not the actual problem." Applied to agentic QE context: quality enforcement (verification gates, evidence checking, compliance mechanisms) is deterministic computation — it survives because models getting smarter does not eliminate the need to verify their work. But orchestration-as-abstraction (hiding the model from the problem behind routing logic) does not survive. The critical distinction: constraining a model to do verified work (what AQE skills do at their best) is different from abstracting the model away from the problem (what Hoffman warns against). Hoffman's two-layer architecture — deterministic computation + probabilistic reasoning — maps to the compliance-vs-coverage insight: gates are deterministic (did step 8b execute?), judgment is probabilistic (is this release worth the risk?). Tension to monitor: as models improve, some AQE skill definitions as static markdown may become unnecessary if models internalize the patterns. The survival question should be applied regularly to each component.

problem: Masterclass presentation structure for Agentic QE — how to frame the paradigm shift from AI assistant to AI workforce for a testing audience in 60 minutes
solution: Proven 16-slide structure: 1) Title, 2) Who am I (credibility), 3) Testing Crossroads (tension), 4) Two Futures (bottleneck vs evolution), 5) Paradigm Shift (copilot vs agentic comparison table), 6) PACT Principles, 7) Agent Workforce architecture (YOU at top), 8) Demo intro (Iron Pets), 9-11) Three demo acts each tied to a PACT principle (Requirements=Proactive, Test Design=Collaborative, Exploratory=Targeted), 12) What agents cant do (address fear), 13) What agents do (amplification), 14) Punchline (directing/curating/deciding), 15) Getting Started (one activity + resources), 16) Thank You/Q&A. Key: 50% of time is live demo. Address limitations honestly before showing value. End with actionable next step.

problem: Emergent working pattern discovered through session history analysis: a multi-loop verification cycle that was never consciously designed but consistently produced better outcomes when followed.
solution: The pattern: Fix → Research → Plan → Implement → Brutal-Honesty Review → Find Gaps → Fix Gaps → Sherlock Review → Release → Repeat. This works because it enforces compliance through SEQUENCE — each step depends on the previous steps actual output, not claimed output. Brutal-honesty review looks at code regardless of what Claude says it tested. Sherlock review traces evidence chains from claims to reality. When followed: v3.7.19-v3.7.22 shipped clean. When shortcut: v3.7.17 shipped with critical bug. Stuart Winter-Tear calls undocumented-but-working patterns "tolerated vagueness" — in agentic systems this is catastrophic because agents cannot follow what is not encoded.

problem: Surrogation-Goodhart-McNamara trinity applied to AI diagnostic tools themselves: CC Insights committed the exact cognitive traps Laforgia describes by treating skill existence as the metric for quality, prescribing more rules when the unquantifiable thing (compliance) was the actual problem.
solution: AI diagnostic tools are susceptible to the same measurement traps as human organizations. CC Insights surrogated "has a skill for that" for "the skill is actually followed," applied Goodhart by treating skill existence as the target, and fell into McNamara by ignoring what cannot be easily measured: actual skill adherence. The remedy: skill adherence has no dashboard metric — there is no counter for "did Claude actually execute step 8b." Only outcomes reveal compliance: the bug that shipped, the gate that was skipped, the PR merged without permission. Build enforcement mechanisms that check artifacts/evidence, not claims.

problem: Agent interprets autonomy instructions as permission to skip verification steps. When told "no need for confirmation if all is good until PR is created" the agent skipped STOP gates AND the verification steps themselves, leading to v3.7.17 shipping with a critical ESM __dirname bug.
solution: The instruction "no need for confirmation" meant skip the human confirmation STOP gates, not skip the verification steps. The agent conflated two different things: (1) waiting for human approval at gates, and (2) executing the verification commands. Back-pressure verification (Kyle Morris, HumanLayer) is needed: the harness must verify that verification steps actually executed before allowing progression. Skills should require artifacts/evidence from each step, not just claims of completion. Also: the human operator must be precise about what autonomy means — "skip confirmations" vs "skip steps" are very different instructions.

problem: Compliance vs Coverage Gap: AI diagnostic tools (like CC Insights) recommend creating new skills/rules when the actual problem is that existing skills are not being followed. The agent has 80+ skills with detailed verification steps but skips them during execution.
solution: The critical distinction in agentic quality engineering is compliance vs coverage. Coverage asks "do you have a rule for that?" Compliance asks "was the rule actually followed?" When CC Insights suggested creating a /release skill that already existed with 15 steps and explicit STOP gates, it revealed that diagnostic AI itself falls into the Surrogation-Goodhart-McNamara trinity — treating skill existence as a surrogate for skill adherence. The fix requires enforcement mechanisms (back-pressure verification) not more rules.

problem: The highest-impact quality and engineering work is systematically invisible to individual output metrics. Charity Majors (CTO, Honeycomb): the hardest and most impactful engineering work will be all but invisible to any set of individual metrics. Pairing and mobbing improve quality and spread knowledge but show as two people doing one job. Mentoring multiplies team capacity but reduces the mentor personal output. Architectural decisions save months of future work but produce no visible deliverable. Cross-team coordination, documentation, tech debt reduction — none register on output metrics, all are essential. Individual measurement distorts behavior, creates misaligned incentives (short-term output over long-term value), renders collaborative work invisible, and damages culture through anxiety and competition
solution: Replace individual output metrics with team outcome practices. Kent Beck's recommendation: produce at least one customer-facing thing per team per week. This cannot be gamed because it requires genuine collaboration and genuine customer value — the whole team collaborates to deliver something a customer can see and respond to. Value is delivered, feedback is gathered, the cycle continues. For QE specifically: the quality engineer who writes little code but dramatically improves team capability through guidance, coaching, test strategy, and knowledge sharing is the highest-value contributor — and completely invisible under output metrics. This IS the Holistic Testing Model: everyone is responsible for quality, the QE role is enabling team capability, not personal output. Charity Majors' most provocative observation: metrics are for easy problems — discrete, well-understood. The more challenging and novel the problem, the less reliable metrics will be. To the extent you can reduce a job to a set of metrics, that job can be automated away. If developer productivity could truly be captured in a number, developers would already be obsolete. Apply Deming's systems thinking: individual developer speed is rarely the actual constraint. More often it is slow code reviews, unclear requirements, flaky CI pipelines, cumbersome deployment. Making developers type faster — whether through training or AI — does nothing to address systemic bottlenecks. Dave Farley: measuring software development in terms of individual developer productivity is a terrible idea. Being smart in how we structure and organize our work is much more important than the level of individual genius.

problem: Quality engineering suffers from the same separation problem Laloux identifies in organizations: people wear professional masks and fragment into roles. Developers say quality is QA's job. QA says requirements are BA's job. Nobody brings their whole perspective. In agentic teams, this worsens: people treat agent output as either fully trustworthy or fully suspect, never bringing nuanced judgment
solution: Laloux's Wholeness breakthrough applied to quality: create environments where everyone brings their full intelligence to quality, not just the QA-labeled perspective. Practical moves from Laloux that transfer directly: (1) Check-in/check-out in team rituals — before a sprint review or test session, ask what is really on people's minds (Sounds True practice). Surface hidden concerns that affect quality judgment. (2) Adult-Adult relationships replacing Parent-Child — stop having QA be the Parent who catches Developer-Children's mistakes. Shift to the Challenger/Coach/Creator triangle (from Karpman's Drama Triangle). (3) Safe space for failure discussion — RHD's Bill of Rights and ground rules. When a bug escapes, discuss it as a learning opportunity, not blame assignment. This maps to MAST failure classification: specification/misalignment/verification/resource is analysis, not blame. (4) Feedback as inquiry — not "you have a bug" but "I'm curious about the behavior I'm seeing here." The Holistic Testing Model IS Laloux's Wholeness applied to quality: everyone is responsible for quality, everyone brings their whole perspective.

problem: What are the most common quality issues found in React SPA e-commerce platforms?
solution: Top issues from [CLIENT] 3-platform analysis (2026-03): 1) NO SSR/SSG - site invisible to search engines (SEO 20/100), 2) No compression - 862KB uncompressed JS (2hr fix saves 600KB), 3) Minimal a11y - 2 aria-labels in 255KB of code (score 35/100), 4) Production debug flags in bundle, 5) Overly broad CSP connect-src, 6) Localhost in prod API CSP, 7) Duplicate routes, 8) 1-hour cache on immutable hashed assets, 9) 520KB MUI not tree-shaken, 10) user-scalable=no blocking pinch-to-zoom. Quick wins: compression(2hr), cache headers(30min), meta tags(1hr), remove localhost CSP(30min).

problem: What is the AQE skill trust system and how does it address the Completion Theater problem in agent workflows?
solution: AQE's 5-tier deterministic skill validation (ADR-056) directly addresses Completion Theater — agents appearing to complete tasks rather than actually completing them. Tier system: Tier 0 (Advisory): SKILL.md only, guidance text; Tier 1 (Structured): + JSON output schema; Tier 2 (Validated): + executable validator script; Tier 3 (Verified): + 5+ evaluation test cases, full test suite — 46 skills at this tier, production-ready; Tier 4 (Certified): cross-model validation, 95%+ pass rate. Anti-Completion-Theater mechanisms: (1) Loki-mode: anti-sycophancy scoring catches hollow tests — tautological assertions (expect(true).toBe(true)) rejected; (2) AsymmetricLearningEngine: failure penalty 10x larger than success reward — can't inflate confidence by generating plausible-looking but untested output; (3) Quality gate check at task completion: pass/fail on coverage, tests, security before patterns are stored; (4) Devils-advocate agent: adversarial review in quality assessment domain; (5) Brutal-honesty-review and sherlock-review skills; (6) MemoryWriteGate (ADR-058): blocks storing contradictions against existing verified patterns. The Integrity Rule is baked in: every skill at Tier 3+ has receipts (executable test cases), every agent claim is scored against historical outcomes.

problem: Need to implement accurate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for agents that avoids hallucination, verifies claims against source documents, and provides traceable citations — without runtime latency spikes
solution: FACT (ruvnet/FACT) — Factual Accuracy and Claim Traceability framework (149★). Key features: (1) Cache-augmented RAG: pre-computes and indexes document facts at ingestion time — retrieval is sub-millisecond vs multi-second for standard RAG; (2) Claim verification: each agent output is checked against source facts with confidence scoring; (3) Citation tracking: every generated statement linked to source document + line; (4) Hallucination detection: flags statements not supported by retrieved context; (5) Temporal awareness: knows when source knowledge was indexed, flags stale facts; (6) MCP server integration: exposes tools (fact_check, retrieve_context, verify_claim) for agent integration; (7) Works with any LLM via MCP. Primary use: QA/QE agents generating test assertions that must be grounded in specs/requirements — prevents hallucinated test expectations. Install: npx fact-framework or cargo add fact-core. Repo: github.com/ruvnet/FACT.

problem: Need a structured agentic QE module that provides risk-based test strategy, test automation guidance, and release gate decisions — integrated with an AI development workflow but usable standalone
solution: BMad TEA (Test Engineering Architect) module — standalone BMad module with a single expert agent persona named Murat (Master Test Architect and Quality Advisor). 9 workflows: (1) Teach Me Testing (TEA Academy), (2) Framework setup — scaffold test framework frontend/backend/fullstack, (3) Test Design — system/epic-level risk-based test design, (4) ATDD — failing acceptance tests first (TDD red phase), (5) Automate — expand test automation coverage, (6) Test Review — review and score test quality, (7) Trace — trace requirements to tests + gate decision, (8) NFR Assessment, (9) CI/CD quality pipeline setup. Supports: Playwright, Cypress, Jest, Vitest, pytest, JUnit, Go test, dotnet test, RSpec. CI platforms: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure DevOps, Harness, Circle CI. Pact.js + PactFlow/Broker integration for contract testing. Install: npx bmad-method install → select Test Architect (TEA). Docs: bmad-code-org.github.io/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise/. Repo: github.com/bmad-code-org/bmad-method-test-architecture-enterprise.

problem: QPAM Example - Alchemy Team Assessment (Self-Assessment)
solution:
# QPAM Example Assessment - Alchemy Team - Self-Assessment

Example of a completed QPAM assessment with team scores.

Team Self-Assessment
Quality Aspects | Score 1 - 5  | Behavioural Pattern - Score 1 | Behavioural Pattern - Score 5 | Comments
1.0 | Feedback Loops | Feedback loops slow, not recognized. Requests or questions go through product management. Customer reported defects from client support or operations. | Team proactive. Works to tighten feedback loops by  structural and paired activities. Seeks feedback for improvement and course corrections.
 - within the delivery team | Feedback between programmers and testers primarily through defect tracking system or provided during project meetings. | Proactive in improving programming and testing, including assumptions, questions, implementation, tools, requirements, and tests. Uses structural activities but does not rely on them for feedback and improvement.
 - between customers, stakeholders and delivery team | Customer data untracked. Comes through customer support or product manager. No discussion on what most valuable to customers. May see problems as something customer did wrong.
 | Customer data drives most, or all decisions on solution development. Actively engaged with customers for UAT. Short feedback loops allow for efficient quality implementation and testing. Provides frequent high value delivery to customers. |  
 - between leadership and delivery team | Feedback one-directional, from leadership to delivery team via product manager. Direct feedback to specific team members addresses critical issues or priority features. Other feedback only after project delivered.
 | Team and management behave and communicate throughout project as though the same team. Mutual understanding of business and customer priorities, goals, risks, etc. |  
2.0 | Culture | Teams and roles siloed. Information flows between individuals, not teams. People reluctant to speak about large issues. Teams in constant firefighter mode.  | Organization: open, authentic, flexible, respectful, creative, and courageous. People speak about issues and concerns. Channels defined for communication flexible and respected.
 - psychological safety | People afraid to speak up. People mostly do what told to do. | Team members speak openly within and outside of team. Focus on solving problems collaboratively. 
 - quality culture | Little focus or support from leadership regarding quality. Feature delivery valued over quality. | Quality considered and included at all stages of development lifecycle.
 - working hours | Overtime expected to meet project timelines. Results in more errors, fixes and testing.  | Overtime rare.
3.0 | Learning and Improvement | No organized effort to learn and improve. No reading, conferences, creating, or sharing. No working hours for learning. | Team consistently strives to learn and improve. Time regularly set aside for learning new skills.
 - self-directed learning | Some team members read to learn on their own. Most do not. | Team prioritizes and schedules learning and improvement activities.
 - conferences & training | Conferences not a priority or valued. | Team members attend conferences and trainings and share learnings at work. Teams may attend together.
 - sharing | None, or minimal. | Team shares openly in day-to-day work and structured activities.

 - retrospectives | None, or irregular. May have ‘post mortem’ after project. | Frequent & varied retrospectives. Small experiments with measures for success standard.
4.0 | Development Approach | Ad hoc or loose structure. Complex features developed in long-running branches, merged infrequently. Testing done after coding with long defect fix cycles. Overtime common. Team doesn't analyze risks or prioritize work accordingly. | Feature development organized and thoughtful. Delivers value frequently using vertical slices / feature flags. May experiment using A/B testing techniques. Risks prioritized and mitigated. Understands and monitors impact of changes on production. These inform adjustment to risk assessments and mitigations, and guide development of features.
 - team makeup | Hand-offs between role-based teams. Adversarial relationships. | Cross-functional team flows and delivers with ease.
 - quality mindset | Feature delivery valued over quality. Quality seen as responsibility of testers. | Quality internalized by all team members. Quality top-priority and seen as a velocity-enabler.
 - agile framework practices  | No structured process. | Experimenting and pushing boundaries to improve ways of doing things.
 - feature and story prioritization | Written requirements come from business analysts or other domain expert. No real priortization. | Frequent interaction with customers, stakeholders, external teams to improve understanding, risk analysis, prioritization, and receive feedback.
 - story understanding | Testers sometimes review requirements before coding to help remove ambiguities. | ATDD / BDD practices followed for applicable stories. Small experiments used to get fast feedback on direction. 
 - Definition of Done (DoD) | None, or not followed. | Team no longer needs a definition to hold to -- what needs to be done now a habit. 
 - release to production | May have a release coordinator to bring release together. Often surprises at release time. Usually gaps in development and testing. | Production-ready small, low-risk changes completed and deployed to production frequently, through progressive rollout or continuous deployment.
5.0 | Quality and Test Ownership | Quality owned by testers or QA. Testing done by QA, focused on verification of new code. Defects blamed on testers. 'Acceptable' levels of quality achieved via testing and defect fixing.  | Quality and customer value considered above all else. Quality 'built-in' from start on all features. Team deeply cares about health of their test suites, architecture, approaches and strategies.

 - quality understanding | Team does not discuss level of quality. QA/Testers responsible for ensuring and adding quality into product. They act as gatekeepers to release. | Team discusses what quality means to their product. Deep understanding of test landscape. Quality attributes a constraint to be considered with every feature and story. 
 - test creation | Tests created and owned by testers. | Team clearly understands purpose of tests, costs versus value, risks mitigated, and maintenance needs. Whole team contributes.

 - test reviews | No test reviews. | Tests mostly created and enhanced in pairing or mobbing situations. Any others promptly peer-reviewed.
 - test execution | Test execution completed by testers. | Automated tests run as part of CI & CD  and considered living documentation. All team members complete ET testing as per team strategy.
 - test failure followups | Test failures owned and followed up on by testers. | Tests valued as a feedback loop. Test failures addressed immediately: fix code, fix test, or remove test.
 - data ownership | No ownership of data. No one looking at data consistency. Test data made on the fly by testers. | Data part of product and treated with respect. 
6.0 | Testing Breadth | Testing done after coding complete (or close to completion). Focus on happy paths and functionality, using time left. Testers may be embedded in a team or in an independent test team. Testing not applied in a strategic way, and only from the viewpoint of testers. Reaction-based response to customer issues. | Team takes responsibility and accountability for aligning test strategy with wider organizational quality strategy and product value.

 - test strategy | No real test strategy in place. Testers take each requirement and create tests they think necessary. | Whole delivery team has input into and shares understanding of test strategy. Strategy identifies how testing for a feature will be accomplished, also considers risks. Addresses testing dependencies with other teams. 
 - test techniques | Focus on functional testing and workflows. Use domain specific knowledge like realistic data if experienced. | Team plans and uses types and techniques for their context (including a variety of heuristics), to manage risks to release, customer, business, etc.
 - quality attributes | Some testers may have experience testing quality attributes like security testing and may apply their knowledge. No standards, so no consistency. | Experienced in identifying and working with quality attributes relevant to product and domain. Have enough expertise to plan and testing within their iterations. May pull in external specialists when appropriate.
 - UAT (User Acceptance Testing) | Product delivered to users as a gate to pass before releasing. Users on their own and often create many defects - not all 'real'.  Creates more chaos for the team. | UAT is fully integrated alongside development, test, and acceptance of stories or features within the team.
 - test coverage and reporting | Coverage based on gut feel. Reporting based on number of tests run or defect counts. | Test coverage taken for granted. Tools generate numbers but built-in processes and checks such as pairing or peer reviewing, ensure good coverage.
7.0 | Code Quality and Technical Debt | No emphasis on code quality. One fix often breaks other things. Inconsistent use of analysis tools. No discussion on technical debt. Much of the code not understood, many afraid to make changes to it. Little or no code documentation. | Coverage and code correctness tools consistently track testing holes and risk areas. Technical debt backlog small, routinely addressed. Communicates with stakeholders on technical debt and business impact. Follows coding standards. Makes good use of design patterns. 
 - unit testing | Two scenarios
1. None, or minimal unit testing
2. Team members who value them create unit tests, but drop during development when pressured to go faster. | Code written and maintained using TDD principles, usually with pair programming for immediate feedback loops.
 - code maintenance | Technical debt (code refactoring, fixing analysis errors, etc) addressed infrequently. Maintainability rarely considered. Rarely allocate time for code maintenance; do so only if they cannot continue unless they do.  | Technical debt addressed continuously; mostly debt-free. Issues found - fixed immediately. Maintenance & support efforts not sacrificed in favour of other activities. Refactoring routine for product code and test automation. Shared code ownership.
 - standards | Code reviews not done or inconsistent. Team not aware of frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc being out of date and possibly unsupported. Coding practices inconsistent, no agreed-upon standard patterns. | Frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc recent, supported versions. Keeps up with evolution of technology and ensures their assets follow that evolution. Possibly innovating in their domain.
8.0 | Test Automation and Tools | Few or no automated tests, no way to have continuous feedback of daily changes.
 | Automation standard operating procedure. Test failures addressed immediately: fix code, fix test, or remove test. Automation supports human-centric testing and processes as often as possible.
 - automating functional tests | If automation exists, testers automate workflow tests - usually using record-playback. No real understanding about automation. | Automation standard operating procedure, and shared by all team members.
 - automating quality attribute tests | Testing for quality attributes only happens when something discovered during testing or in production. No automation. | Risks considered while discussing feature capabilities. Tests planned with each story. 'Feature Done' includes testing all identified quality attributes, and automation part of deployment pipeline.
 - unit testing / TDD | Very little unit testing done. Most programmer testing actually debugging. | All code written and maintained using TDD principles.
 - tools | Testing tools usually vendor tools owned by testing team. Version control under programmer control and testers have little-to-no insight. | Testing tools shared and owned by all team members.
9.0 | Deployment Pipeline | Test environments unstable. Only programmers understand version control. Team does not practice CI. Long-running feature branches. Team not able to deal with incomplete code being merged.
 | Practices Continuous Delivery with releases from green pipeline. Able to release their product multiple times a day if needed. Measures delivery flow for optimization. CD pipeline reviewed to reflect team's testing breadth. Includes all validations required to be release-ready.
 - automation | Release / Deployment process needs human interaction. Very few automated processes. | Automated triggers in pipeline stop a deploy if a test fails. Whole team responsible for follow-up. Looks for new ways to shorten feedback cycle. Practice safe ways to test in production.
 - team engagement | Team unaware of frequency of production problems related to their code. Doesn't consider impact on operations or customers, or other parts of the product.
 | Team understands external dependencies and collaborates with others to address them. Fully embraces the 'you build it, you run it' mindset. 
 - metrics | No quality metrics tracked. Relies on output of department-wide testing activities (e.g. Bug Bashes).   | Tracks performance using metrics such as mean time to recovery (MTTR). Uses variety of relevant metrics to understand quality and customer experience, and to prioritize work. May be following DORA metrics.
 - release strategy | Changes to production infrequent - likely every quarter or every six months, in big chunks. Struggles to get patches for production issues - may go without testing.  | Practices feature toggle-driven development and progressive rollout for all code changes. Able to safely deploy to production one or more times per day. Uses blue/green environment, canary releases, or releases to a subset of clients to mitigate risk. 
 - observability | No data about customer usage in production. The only data considered for quality purposes comes directly from support / operations. | Customer data drives decisions about solution development and quality strategy. Quality-related activities monitored and validated. Practices observability - able to ask questions from data sets without pushing new code. Understands  customer pain points/friction.
10.0 | Defect Management | Large backlogs of defects and growing. Defects only fixed if absolutely required. Focus on finding and reporting defects. Limited understanding of why defects occur. Average defect age 6+ months. | Focus on defect prevention. Customer-reported defects  understood and addressed quickly. No defect backlog.
 - defect reporting | All defects reported in defect tracking system. Metrics - number of defects. No standards on how to write defect. | No defect backlog. Defects reported by customer put into product backlogs.
 - defect fixing | Defects fixed only when necessary, or postponed. Support escalation work a best-effort. | Defects found - fixed immediately. Externally reported defects prioritized into product backlogs and addressed quickly.
 - defect triage | Defect triage meetings held often to review which defects should be fixed. | Team able to correlate quality problems with the impact they have on user journeys.
