 - team engagement | Team unaware of frequency of production problems related to their code. Doesn't consider impact on operations or customers, or other parts of the product.
 | Fixing broken builds prioritized over feature development. Test failures fixed as fast as possible, trying never to finish day with failing tests - not always successful. | Team actively involved with deploying & releasing to production. Investigates production problems that could be related to changes they made. Team looks for impact from their changes to other parts of system. | Team understands external dependencies and collaborates with others to address them. Fully embraces the 'you build it, you run it' mindset. 
 - metrics | No quality metrics tracked. Relies on output of department-wide testing activities (e.g. Bug Bashes).   | Some data collected to understand quality, mostly from test activities. May be some from other parts of product lifecycle (e.g. maintenance & support). Data not always used. Instrumentation focused on monitoring for errors. | Quality metrics in place to help understand feature quality and customer experience. Crosses several parts of product lifecycle (maintenance, support, design, etc). Any gaps in interpreting data addressed quickly.  | Tracks performance using metrics such as mean time to recovery (MTTR). Uses variety of relevant metrics to understand quality and customer experience, and to prioritize work. May be following DORA metrics.
 - release strategy | Changes to production infrequent - likely every quarter or every six months, in big chunks. Struggles to get patches for production issues - may go without testing.  | Deploys changes to production regularly - every iteration, or up to 3 months. Feature toggles used mainly to hide uncompleted features. Some usage of progressive rollout. | Small production-ready chunks ready for deployment every iteration (or more often). Actively involved with deploying and releasing to production. Feature toggles consistently used. Progressive rollout for all high-impact code changes to minimize impact on customers. | Practices feature toggle-driven development and progressive rollout for all code changes. Able to safely deploy to production one or more times per day. Uses blue/green environment, canary releases, or releases to a subset of clients to mitigate risk. 
 - observability | No data about customer usage in production. The only data considered for quality purposes comes directly from support / operations. | Starting to instrument code to collect quality telemetry data from production, though often added after feature complete. | Analytics / instrumentation part of the ready / done definition, and almost always done as part of feature development. | Customer data drives decisions about solution development and quality strategy. Quality-related activities monitored and validated. Practices observability - able to ask questions from data sets without pushing new code. Understands  customer pain points/friction.
10.0 | Defect Management | Large backlogs of defects and growing. Defects only fixed if absolutely required. Focus on finding and reporting defects. Limited understanding of why defects occur. Average defect age 6+ months. | Moving towards defect prevention, but focus still on finding defects. Starting to think about cause of defects and to address them. Average defect age 3+ months. | Focus on defect prevention and understanding customer reported defects. Minimal defect backlog - integrated into product backlogs. | Focus on defect prevention. Customer-reported defects  understood and addressed quickly. No defect backlog.
 - defect reporting | All defects reported in defect tracking system. Metrics - number of defects. No standards on how to write defect. | Only defects not fixed right away or those reported by customer entered into the defect tracking system. Metrics: where defects found, how many escape an iteration or story. | Defects in development not fixed immediately put into the product backlog to be addressed next iteration. Only customer-reported defects entered into defect tracking system.  | No defect backlog. Defects reported by customer put into product backlogs.
 - defect fixing | Defects fixed only when necessary, or postponed. Support escalation work a best-effort. | Defects may be fixed if found early, but majority waiting to be triaged. Critical defects related to features released in last 6-9 months addressed. Team may budget time for maintenance and defect fixing. | Defects found - fixed immediately, or as priority in the next iteration. Team has clear view of which maintenance and support issues priority.
 | Defects found - fixed immediately. Externally reported defects prioritized into product backlogs and addressed quickly.
 - defect triage | Defect triage meetings held often to review which defects should be fixed. | One major defect triage meeting held before release to decide upon risks of releasing defects. Most held informally.  | No triage except for defects which may need design changes. | Team able to correlate quality problems with the impact they have on user journeys.

problem: Team Quality Practices Self-Assessment - Questions
solution:
# Team Quality Practices - Questions

QPAM Questions to Ask
Quality Practices | Questions to ask | What to look for | Comments
1.0 | Feedback Loops
 - within the delivery team | What mechanisms do team members use to communicate with each other?  | Think about how different roles in the team communicate (tester, programmer, BA, PO) and others like operations. Is it collaborative and face-to-face? Or is everything written down?  
How does a tester or team member know what is ready for testing?
How do team members share feedback on ideas, designs, practices, processes and other types of work (before coding and testing the code)?
Does the team document the decisions they make?
Does the team have daily standups? | What kind of information is shared?
How long do they run?
Do people find them effective?
How is it facilitated?
How does the team discover and share feedback about the quality of the code? | Do they use code reviews? Pair programming? Mobbing or ensembling?
What code analysis tools are used? When do they use them?
Do they have automated unit tests? Do they run regularly? How often? What do they do with the results?
Do they use test-first practices like TDD?
Are there other automated tests? If so, what are they? How often are they run?
What other types of testing do they complete? How often? Are the results used to adapt?
How is feedback from testing shared amongst team members? | Is testing feedback formal through defect tracking systems and/or written documents, or is it more informal during standups?
Does the team think of tests as a form of feedback?
 - between customers, stakeholders and delivery team | What kinds of interactions does the team have with stakeholders?  What about end users? | Does the team know who their stakeholders are? 
Have they ever talked with end users to understand who they are building for? 
Is everything channelled through the product owner or manager, or is there direct interaction with stakeholders and the team?
What do the team demos look like? Do stakeholders and end users attend? How does feedback get captured?
How does the team learn about customer needs?  | How are customer needs communicated? Directly from the product owner as features and user stories? Or another method?
Do team members learn about customer needs directly from customers? Or do they rely on support or operations for feedback?
Do team members participate in any way in fleshing out the customer's needs?
How do they learn whether they met the needs appropriately? | Does the team employ practices like observability to gather feedback about customer use and engagement?
Do they have customer surveys?
How does the team know the releases are successful? | How do they measure success? 
Do they include anything regarding the actual end users in their measurement of success?
 - between leadership and delivery team | How does the team communicate with line managers and the leadership team? | Is there an informal mechanism for feedback to managers and the leadership team, or is it more formal through the chain of command?
How is new information from leadership passed to the team?
 | Is there transparency? 
Does the delivery team understand how the features they work on support organizational goals?
How does leadership get the information it needs to make decisions? | Does it rely wholly on reports, or is there some verbal interaction
Does the leadership team or managers dictate what reports are needed? Or do they work with the team to determine the best way to get the information?
2.0 | Culture
 - psychological safety | How are problems and challenges discussed and dealt with? | Do people feel safe speaking up and pushing back on new additions, or do people mostly keep quiet and not rock the boat? 
Watch for an environment of psychological safety.
Do people suggest small experiments to solve problems?
Do people ask for help, or do they try to fix something on their own? Or do they leave it for someone else to pick up?
Do they feel safe to fail? Or do they worry about getting blamed for failures?
What does leadership care about most? | Is there good communication between leadership and the people doing the work? Is there transparency? 
Do people feel safe asking questions, sharing concerns, identifying problems, and saying no?
Does leadership want innovation, and if so, do they support experiments?
How does leadership respond to failures? Do they blame?
Does leadership say one thing – for example, putting up posters — but respond differently?
Does the team have a charter that identifies how the team should act and treat each other? | Does the charter reflect the values of the organization?
 - quality culture | How is quality talked about and encouraged in the organization? | Does leadership emphasize quality first - over quantity and speed? 
How is quality discussed? What are people saying? 
Does the environment allow teams to consistently integrate quality practices without compromise? 
Is quality focused upon throughout, or only talked about once and then forgotten?
Who is responsible for quality? | Is it the whole team, or the testers (or the QA staff)?
Do team members know how they contribute to quality?
 - working hours | Does anyone work overtime to complete stories before the beginning of the next iteration? | If so, are they testers or programmers? Or a combination of both?
Why are they working overtime? Is it because they are pressured to do so?
What is the office culture expectation and practice of working at a sustainable pace? | Are people focused on the necessary work? 
Do they work in silos, or are they collaborative?
Do they use practices that enable a sustainable pace, such as continuous integration, TDD, ATDD, refactoring, pairing, and test automation?
3.0 | Learning and improvement
 - self-directed learning | What books, articles, or blogs have team members read lately? What webinars or YouTube videos have they watched or attended?  | Were these on their own time, during work hours, or a mixture?
Is learning encouraged by the team or management? 
Did they learn anything helpful to bring back to their team or useful for their work?
Do team members choose their online learning and reading activities?
 | How often do they do so? 
How much time do they spend?
Does the team plan to learn together and discuss those learnings using the same sources (as a study and practice group)? | Is this a scheduled activity?
How often does the team do so? How much time is spent?
How do team members prefer to learn? | Do they mentor with someone?
Do they practice pair-learning or learn as a team?
 - conferences and training | How do team members learn new practices, ideas, skills? | Do they attend in-house training? External training? 
Do they attend as a team, or send only one person?
Do they attend conferences and workshops?
If team members attend a conference, how do they share new ideas? | Are they sharing with the team and applying them in their work? Is the team receptive?
Do they have to create presentations to show what they did? 
Note: often, this is only helpful for the managers, although there is value in teaching to others.
How is new information from books / workshops / conferences brought back to the team and shared?  | How do they share new ideas from external sources back at work, or do they keep that to themselves?
 - sharing | How do team members share new practices, ideas, and skills? | Do team members teach others?
Do they pair with others? 
Do they create blog posts, articles, guides, videos, audio, etc (for internal or external use)?
How do they bring back and share new information from books, workshops, and conferences? | How do they share new ideas from external sources back at work, or do they keep that to themselves?
 - retrospectives | Does the team have retrospectives? | What are the retrospectives like? How often are they? Who is involved? How is it structured? How frequently are they held?
Or is there a major retrospective at the end of a release? Or is there nothing? If so, how are action items determined?
Do all team members get a chance to participate by adding sticky notes (physical or virtual) or other hands-on activities? Do they feel heard?
How well does the team reflect and adapt?
What happens after a retrospective? | Does the team try a small experiment to address a problem or do some other action?
Do they follow up on retrospective actions, and if so, how? 
Do they feel ownership to make changes within their team?
How do they know when they have changed something for the better?
4.0 | Development Approach
 - team makeup | How do team members work together? | Are there specific roles? If so, how are they defined?
Do they stick to them or blur the roles?
Does the team have a product owner (PO)? | How do they contribute? 
Do they help the team understand features/stories?
Are they available to collaborate? 
If not, who helps get requirements and helps the team understand the desired behaviour?
Does the PO serve more than one feature team? 
Does the team have a facilitator (scrum master), agile coach, or neither? | If so, how do they contribute? Are they dedicated to that team?
Does the team have a facilitator for meetings, someone to help them stay on track and make sure everyone can contribute, or do they do it themselves?
Do working sessions and meetings accomplish what they are meant for?
Does the delivery team interact with other teams or third parties? | Are interactions with other teams visible?
How do they interact?
Are there frequent blockers due to dependencies? If so, how do they deal with them?
 - quality mindset | Is the whole team responsible for quality, and what does that mean to the team? | Is there a consistent message? Answers may vary by team member.
Are the answers about process quality, or are some about product quality? In this evaluation, we are only concerned about the processes, but it tells the team’s maturity if they also discuss product quality.
Can team members articulate how they contribute to quality?
Do programmers tend to give their code to the testers thinking that it is their job to test?
Is there a customer or technical support group? Is there an operations group? | Who answers client issues?
Is the delivery team involved in understanding the problem? 
Does the delivery team take ownership of issues in production?
 - agile framework practices | Describe your organization and team approach to agile. | What practices do they follow (Scrum, Kanban, hybrid, or something else)?
Is it formal or informal?
How are new people inducted into the team? Do they have to read documentation? Do they get a mentor? 
Do team members consistently understand agile and how it is applied in their team and organization?
What are the regular ‘meetings’ the team participates in? For example, daily stand-ups, iteration planning, story readiness workshops (backlog refinement), feature planning, story slicing, story mapping, retrospectives, and demos to the stakeholders. 
Does the whole team attend all of these? Or do testers come in later after early planning?
What other meetings do team members attend? Are these all necessary to do their work?
How is the prioritization of features done? | Is there an overall product management group that gets together to discuss the priorities of the organization?
Does each product owner have complete control over their product?
Do priorities compete against each other when scheduling dependencies?
Does the team have story readiness workshops (backlog refinement sessions)? | What is the format they use, and who attends?
What do testers do during these meetings and workshops? What about other roles?
How much pre-planning do they do (how often and how long)? 
Do they have a definition of Ready?
If the team is doing time-boxed iterations, how do they know how much to take into an iteration? | Who decides how much? Does the team decide, or is it pushed on them?
How do they decide how much work to take? 
Do they have heavy capacity planning sessions, or is there a lighter-weight mechanism? 
Do they use velocity as a planning tool? 
Do they estimate? If so, do they have small stories (for example, one day in duration) so they don’t have to task out the story? Or do they have larger stories they need to task, and if so, do they estimate those tasks?
Large stories that take more than two or three days may be a red flag for finishing.
How does the team plan for an iteration (Scrum) or a new story (Kanban)? If possible, sit in a meeting and observe. | How does the team work together?
How are the sessions run? As meetings or as workshops? 
How are people seated in relationship with one another (if in person)? 
What do communication and collaboration sound like?
What do testers do during these meetings and workshops?
Is there a specific outcome at the end of the session?
How does the iteration (or story) progress? | How much time does a story usually take?
Are testing activities completed on a regular cadence with every story? Or is testing left until the end of the iteration?
Are all stories brought into an iteration completed? (Irrelevant if doing Kanban)
How are retrospectives structured? | How does the team arrive at outcomes?
Does the team follow up on improvement suggestions?
Does the team define small experiments or just identify improvements?
Looking at previous retrospectives can help to see the team’s behaviours.
What training or documentation is needed for end users, customer support, and other stakeholders?   | Who is responsible for creating the necessary training and documentation?
Do all team members know what is required?
Do all team members participate in creating necessary documentation and training?
 - feature and story prioritization | Does the team understand the value of a feature?  | Do they know what problem they are trying to solve?
How does the team get introduced to a feature?  | How are features broken down into stories?        
Do they do any working sessions to do this, for example, mind mapping?
Does the team know what problem they are trying to solve?
What method is used to slice the feature into stories? Do they use story mapping, flow diagrams, or something else?
Who is involved? Is the whole delivery team involved?
How do stories come to the team?  How are they created? | How are they refined?
How well are the stories defined? Are they small, valuable, and testable?
Are the stories prioritized? Does the team know which ones to implement first?
What format is used for stories?
Does the team have a Definition of Ready? If so, what is it? | Do they have the ability to refuse to take a story if they are already overloaded?
Does the team talk about risks or dependencies to consider when prioritizing?
If possible, try to see examples of stories in the team’s backlog. | Do they have vertical slices or component-oriented stories?
What techniques do people in the team use to help build a shared understanding of features and stories? | Who participates in those conversations?
How do they know when a feature is completed?
 - story understanding | Does the delivery team practice ATDD or BDD? If so, what does it look like? | Can they describe their process? 
How is it implemented?
Do they start with Gherkin immediately, or do they have a conversation first?
Who creates acceptance tests (or criteria)? | Does the team assist in creating the acceptance tests, or does the product owner do it in isolation?
How are they created - independently, in triads, as a group, or in another way?
When are the acceptance tests (criteria) created?  | Are they written before a story is talked about, or during the conversation about the story?
Does the team use them to define the scope of the story? 
Do the acceptance tests give the scope of the story? | Can the acceptance tests be used to know when the story is complete?
Can team members know from the acceptance tests what needs to be done? 
 - Definition of Done (DoD) | Is there a common Definition of Done? | Does each team member share the same understanding?
Does the team adhere to the definition of done?
Is there a definition of done for stories, iteration, and release?
How do you prioritize?
 - release to production | How often does the team release to customers? (This is different than deploying to production) | What is their release cadence? Do they know how their process works?
Do all team members understand when they release to their customers?
Who is responsible for releasing to the customers?  | Is the release automated? Or does a person have to manage it?
Is there a release readiness checklist?
Is the release process consistent? Or a bit chaotic every time?
5.0 | Quality and Test Ownership
 - quality understanding | How does the team determine what quality means for their product? | Does the team have conversations around quality for the product? 
Do they have the vocabulary to express it?
How does the team determine the processes they use? | Does the team realize that there is a difference between good practices and good porduct quality?  
Can they name the techniques they use? (ex. ATDD, TDD, or reviews)
Who contributes to quality conversations? | Do testers own decisions on quality and quality practices, or does the team share it? 
How does the team talk about quality and test approaches (like quality attributes, the test automation pyramid, etc)?
Who makes final decisions about product quality? | Is it the business? Or does the team decide? Or a combination?
Who makes the decisions about the processes the team uses? | Does the team get to determine what processes are good for them?
Are they decided by managers, practice leads, others, or a combination?
Who decides if they need to adapt?
 - test creation | Do team members have specific areas they are responsible for?  | Are specific team members responsible for particular domains, tasks, code, and tests? For example, is it the testers who create the tests?
Does the team create tests together, or is it an individual effort?
Does the team look at customer behaviour (from observing) to define new tests or exploratory charters?
Do all team members know the different types of testing activities?  | Do all team members understand the types of testing?
What kind of heuristics do people use for testing? 
Do they create scenarios that may challenge the business rules?
Are team members fluid, and do they jointly feel responsible and able to take on other types of work in other areas - specifically creating tests?
Are different people responsible for automating at different levels?  | Does one person specify the tests to automate, and another write the automation code, or is there hared responsibility?
Do programmers create automated tests, and to what scale?
Do they bring in experts to do some of the testing – load, performance, and security? Or do they try to learn so they can do their own?
Are the tests created primarily intended for team members to execute?  | Are these scripted tests that should be automated?
Where are the tests stored?  | In the same repository as the production code?
In some other repository or location?
 - test review | Is there a process for reviewing tests once they have been written? If so, which testing types does it apply to? | Is there more than one pair of eyes on the tests?
Does the team practice reviews on a regular basis, or is the process ad-hoc?
Does the team practice pairing or use ensembles (mobbing) while creating the tests? If so, how does that impact other reviews?
Does the team think the reviews are effective?
 - test execution | Who executes the human-centric tests (exploratory charters or scripted tests)?  | Do the testers do all the testing or do others in the team help?
Is test execution done collaboratively or solo? 
 - test failures and follow-ups | What is the process if an automated test suite fails?  | Who identifies the test that failed, who does the debugging, who fixes, and who retests?
Does it differ depending on the type of test, for example, unit tests versus API or workflow tests?
Do they register failures as defects? 
Depending on the context, are there different options for following up on a failing test? | Who is involved, and what approach is used?
Look for differences between tests that break during a regular development cycle versus “hot fixes” going into production.
Who responds to defects found in production? | Who is involved, what approach is used? 
Is it the whole team, or specific people all the time
How is priority set, and how do defects get into the team’s hands?
Are new tests created as a result?
Who reports production defects? | Is it always the customer?
Are some defects found by proactively looking at logs or dashboards?
If so, is the method for addressing those defects different than if the customer finds them?
 - data ownership | Who creates the data for tests? Or how is it generated? | Do different people have different responsibilities? For example, are programmers responsible for unit test data and testers for functional test data?
Does the product owner contribute to obtaining test data?
Do automated tests set up and tear down the test data?
Is production data used? If so, is it used responsibly – scrubbed of any personal data?
How is the data stored and used?  | Is it hard coded into the tests, or can it be accessed separately? 
Is it easy to find?
Is it different for different test types?
Is there confidence that the data used is correct and representative of production data?
6.0 | Testing Breadth
 - test strategy | What is the team's testing approach? | Can they articulate what this even means?
Does the team use a visual model, such as the agile testing quadrants, to help discuss testing?  | Who is responsible for the model? 
Who uses it?  
Do they use the agile testing quadrants? | If so, which quadrants are their tests most prevalent in?
Do they have balance and breadth across the quadrants?
Note: if the team does not know them, share a quick explanation of the testing quadrants to see if it resonates with anyone.
Do they use other models to understand and plan their testing? For example, quadrant variations, V-model, or the test automation pyramid? | How do they visualize and share information?
How do they document their testing strategy?  | Do they use simple techniques such as pictures, or is there extensive documentation making it difficult for people to read and understand?
 - test techniques used | What kinds of testing are carried out by the team?         | Does the whole team know the types of tests that are done? Or just the tester?
Are they all using the same vocabulary? 
Do they know what tests are automated? 
How do they determine what to test? How do they plan? | What tools do they use? State diagrams, flow diagrams, heuristics, or others?
Can they articulate how they know what to test?
Has anyone had training of any kind in testing? 
What do the tests look like? | Are they all the same type, such as scripted, or do they have a variety? 
Are they scripted, automated, exploratory test charters, mind maps, or something else?
What do the acceptance tests or criteria look like? | Do they use Given/When/Then, tabular format, or bullet points? 
Does the team decide what the tests/criteria are all together? If not, who decides?
How do they determine what tests to perform and when? | Do they know what a heuristic is? Can they articulate it?
What are their favourite heuristics to use?
Does the team practice exploratory testing?  | If so, can they articulate how it is carried out?
Consider exploratory testing on a sliding scale from ad-hoc testing on one end to using test charters with well-reviewed documented notes on the other.
Do they use different techniques, such as personas, or do they use the same user journey approach all the time?
Do they pair when exploring? Do they explore as a group (ensemble or mob)?
Do they debrief and review the notes looking for missed possibilities?
Does the team practice risk-based testing?  | If so, in what circumstances?        
Do they practice it with every story, only doing the most critical tests?
Do they do it during regression testing?
 - quality attributes | What are the most important quality attributes that are tested? | How does the team determine what to test?
Are there any links between what they test and the risks they identify?
Is the team consistent in their testing of the quality attributes? Or do they do it only when they have time?
Does the whole team have the same opinion about what is important?
How does the team determine when to test the quality attributes?  | Do they discuss it as an afterthought right before release, or do they discuss it with every story?
Does the team talk about risks when a feature is introduced? If so, do they identify which quality attributes should be tested as part of risk mitigation?
Do they create stories for quality attributes, or is testing part of the Definition of Feature Done and considered with every story, or somewhere in between? 
Is the team well educated in knowing how to code for and test the quality attributes that are important?   | Do the programmers know how to code to prevent format exploits like SQL injection or other security issues? 
Do they know how to code and test for accessibility?
Do the testers know how to test quality attributes, or do they bring in specialists such as security testers after completing a feature (this is also part of test ownership)?
 - User acceptance testing (UAT) | Is UAT a thing the team does? If so, how do they do it?  | Do they give the tests to the users? Or do they collaborate? Or do they hand over the system and let the users figure it out?
What other help does the team give the users?
How often is UAT scheduled? | Do they complete UAT at regular intervals and for every feature? Or is it left to the end before release?
How is customer feedback on the stories and features acquired? | Do people from the team pair with the users? 
Do the users enter defects into the system? How do they determine what are considered defects?
 - Test coverage and reporting | What kinds of test results are kept? | How are the automated test results saved and reported?
How are the human-centric test results, such as exploratory testing notes, kept and reported? 
How are the results of the quality attribute testing saved and reported?
Does someone dictate what the test results should look like? Or can the team determine what the best way to report is?
Do they document too much? If so, is it because they feel they need to so that they have 'evidence' in case they are blamed for missing something? This might be an indication of culture.
Who cares about the testing results? | Does anyone ask about them?
What do they ask for? 
What do they care about?
How are the testing results shared?  | Spreadsheets, email, big visible charts, or something else?
Are results from various types of testing shared in different ways?
How do they know the tests cover enough? | Do they have standards, hope for the best, or have a review session to determine test coverage?
7.0 | Code Quality
 - unit testing | Do the programmers know what scenarios they need to support before they start? | Or do the programmers need to guess what they are building?
How much unit testing is done? | Do they have any idea of the coverage?
How is it made visible to other team members? 
How does the team know if the unit tests are ‘good’?
Do any programmers do TDD (test-driven development)?   | Is it a common practice, or only practiced by a couple of programmers?
Did they try it once and decide it was too hard?
If they are learning, how are they doing that? With a consultant, training, or pairing?
 - code maintenance | How does the team define technical debt? | Do they only include legacy code they don’t think they can update?
Do they realize they may be creating it as they take shortcuts?
Do they include defects?
Do they think differently about legacy code and current code?
How much technical debt is in the system?   | Do they have ideas on how to quantify technical debt?
When do the programmers refactor? | Do they feel they can refactor as they add new features, or do refactoring tasks need approval by the product owner, or is there a hybrid solution?
Does the team keep an impediment backlog? If so, how much time do they spend addressing the items on the list? | Do they talk about how they address technical debt?
Consider culture and code maintenance. Do they schedule a bit each iteration, or do they need a 'stabilization' sprint to fix things when it builds up?
Do they have a timeline for addressing technical debt issues?
How do programmers document their code? | Is it part of their regular process? 
Do they look at it during code reviews?
Are there automated tests that document system behaviour?
Is the team using third-party tools (such as libraries and test frameworks)? If so, who keeps track of them? | Can they name all of them?
Do they include their frameworks and libraries as part of the list?
Does the team know how they are tracked, or if they are? 
Is it part of their typical process?
How does the team ensure code uses the latest versions of tools? | How do testers know if the tools are up to date, so they know their testing is valid?
Who is responsible for updating tools?
 - coding standards | What are the coding standards?  | Focus on high-level, not the details.
Do they have any? If so, do they know what they are?
If not, why not?
What kinds of standards are they for automated tests? | Many teams have standards for production code but not automated tests.
If they have standards, who knows them - programmers? Or only testers?
Are there test patterns they follow for consistency?
How does the team ensure the coding standards are followed? | Is it self-discipline or mandated?
Do they have code reviews? For production code and automated test code?
What kinds of reviews are done? | Look for any kind of reviews, including code and test automation.
Who is involved?
What is the most common way to do code reviews?  | Are they formal, informal, peer reviews?
Does the team do any kind of pairing: programming, testing?  What about mobbing? | if they pair or mob, is it all the time, or sproadically? If so, how do they decide when?
How is testability defined within the team? | Do they know what that means?
Does the team practice continuous integration and understand their versioning and merging practices well? | Does the team have long-running branches?
Does every new check-in run all the unit tests?
How often are there merging issues, and code needs to be retested?
8.0 | Automation and Tools
- general | When does the team start automating? 
Does the team or organization have a test automation strategy?
Does the team have automation retrospectives or a review of the automation test suite? | Do they ever question their automation strategy if they have one? 
Do they try to improve or find better ways of working?
Is it only their team that tries to improve automation, or does it happen across the company (this is also part of continuous improvement)?
 - automating functional tests | What levels of testing are automated?  | Do they follow the test automation pyramid idea? Try sketching the pyramid and have them fill it in to see if they understand the concept.
Are the automated tests only at the workflow level and through the UI?
When do they complete their functional automation activities for a story? | Are the automation tests at the API carried into the next iteration, left to the very end before release, or are they finished within the iteration?
Are the workflow tests automated at the feature level and kept to a minimum number?
When do they complete their automated tests for feature workflows through the UI (end-to-end type of tests)?
How much time does the team spend maintaining the tests? | Do they even know how much time they spend? 
Have they spent time reviewing the tests, so they know what is covered and if the test does what it is supposed to?
Who writes and maintains the automated tests? | Are the automation tasks shared among the team, or do programmers only write unit tests and testers do everything else? 
Who diagnoses failed automated tests? Who watches for failures? Does it differ depending on the test suite?
How easy is it to diagnose the problem when a test fails?
What is the skill level of the automators? | Do they use patterns like mocks, or do they have dependencies on other products? 
Are they written like contract tests for API microservices, or are they chained or follow other anti-patterns?
How do the automated tests get the data? | Is the data self-contained, so it can easily be set up and torn down?
Is it easy to debug? Can they easily identify the problem?
Is the data imported into the database for each run, so it starts cleanly, or is the data reused or shared by others?
How are the automated test suites scheduled? | Do they run within the CI (continuous integration), are they scheduled separately, or run on an ad hoc basis?  Or is there a hybrid approach?

problem: QPAM v7 - Quality Aspects and Dimensions Model
solution:
# QPAM Model - Quality Practices Assessment Model for Agile Teams

## Behavioral Patterns / Dimensions

1. Beginning - The starting place for a team
2. Unifying - Starting to have a common shared understanding
3. Practicing - Consistent quality, consistently delivering value
4. Innovating - Reading their market, trying new things

Quality Aspects | Beginning - 1: The starting place for a team | Unifying - 2: Starting to have a common shared understanding of quality and testing needs | Practicing - 3: Consistent quality in many dimensions, consistently delivering value to market
 | Innovating - 4: Reading their market, getting stronger (high quality in all dimensions), trying new things, adding to the practice
1.0 | Feedback Loops | Feedback loops slow, not recognized. Requests or questions go through product management. Customer reported defects from client support or operations. | Structure such as Scrum or Kanban. Several feedback mechanisms in place to prioritize, understand, develop, and deliver features. | Feedback mechanisms as part of structural activities in organization allow for short feedback loops between all parties. Enable fast pivots when needed.
 | Team proactive. Works to tighten feedback loops by  structural and paired activities. Seeks feedback for improvement and course corrections.
 - within the delivery team | Feedback between programmers and testers primarily through defect tracking system or provided during project meetings. | Relies on structural activities for feedback between programmers and testers - story planning sessions, daily stand-ups, retrospectives. Some may try for more regular communication. Found defects put in defect tracking or added to team board. | Pivots easily for incorrect assumptions, misunderstandings, wrong implementations, or improvements using story / iteration planning, daily stand-ups, paired programming, testing and retrospectives. | Proactive in improving programming and testing, including assumptions, questions, implementation, tools, requirements, and tests. Uses structural activities but does not rely on them for feedback and improvement.
 - between customers, stakeholders and delivery team | Customer data untracked. Comes through customer support or product manager. No discussion on what most valuable to customers. May see problems as something customer did wrong.
 | Little or no direct customer interaction. Priortizes feedback from product owner, support, or IT. May help on-call people analyze production issues. Iteration demo used for direct feedback from stakeholders to the team. | Gathers customer data to understand and make decisions about solution development. Interacts with customers regularly to understand needs, and receive feedback on solution development. Sometimes works with customers for UAT. | Customer data drives most, or all decisions on solution development. Actively engaged with customers for UAT. Short feedback loops allow for efficient quality implementation and testing. Provides frequent high value delivery to customers.
- between leadership and delivery team | Feedback one-directional, from leadership to delivery team via product manager. Direct feedback to specific team members addresses critical issues or priority features. Other feedback only after project delivered.
 | Feedback primarily funnelled through product owner/manager. Leadership may attend iteration demos. | Feedback in both directions through product owner and iteration demos. Team speaks openly with leadership about concerns. Leadership does not distract team from their commitments. | Team and management behave and communicate throughout project as though the same team. Mutual understanding of business and customer priorities, goals, risks, etc.
2.0 | Culture | Teams and roles siloed. Information flows between individuals, not teams. People reluctant to speak about large issues. Teams in constant firefighter mode.  | Information flows through teams via product owner and scrum master. Roles less rigid. Teams starting to communicate directly to coordinate overlaps and risks. People speaking up in team sessions. Team disruptions becoming exception.
 | Flow mechanisms in place respected. Team aims to deliver value with high quality. Team disruptions rare. Teams communicate directly. People speak openly about big issues. | Organization: open, authentic, flexible, respectful, creative, and courageous. People speak about issues and concerns. Channels defined for communication flexible and respected.
 - psychological safety | People afraid to speak up. People mostly do what told to do. | Team members starting to speak openly in team sessions, but not with management. Team may say no to product owner about additional work. Small experiments happen.
 | Team members negotiate with product owner with ease. Team speaks relatively openly with leadership and feel heard and respected. Small experiments the norm. | Team members speak openly within and outside of team. Focus on solving problems collaboratively. 
 - quality culture | Little focus or support from leadership regarding quality. Feature delivery valued over quality. | Quality driven through extensive scorecards or other means. Quality decisions and strategy driven by leadership.
 | Leadership provides and reinforces a clear vision of quality. Team makes quality decisions. | Quality considered and included at all stages of development lifecycle.
 - working hours | Overtime expected to meet project timelines. Results in more errors, fixes and testing.  | Trying to limit how often overtime happens. Team aims for sustainable pace and reasonable understanding of stories. Sometimes take on more work than comfortable when pressured.
 | Minimal overtime. Team plans according to knowns and unknowns for sustainable pace. | Overtime rare.
3.0 | Learning and Improvement | No organized effort to learn and improve. No reading, conferences, creating, or sharing. No working hours for learning. | Some learning activities like root cause analysis of defects. Retrospectives held but improvement actions occur irregularly. No working hours for learning, except for some conferences. | Retrospectives and root cause analysis valued. Learning and improvement occur frequently, during work hours. | Team consistently strives to learn and improve. Time regularly set aside for learning new skills.
 - self-directed learning | Some team members read to learn on their own. Most do not. | Several team members actively read and try to disseminate learnings within team. Organized efforts to read and learn as team often co-opted by project work. | Team prioritizes learning as a team, including books, webinars, courses. | Team prioritizes and schedules learning and improvement activities.
 - conferences and training | Conferences not a priority or valued. | Budget exists to attend conferences - some team members attend at least one a year. Many team members not interested. Project work often prioritized over conference attendance. | Budget for conferences and training. Team members expected to attend at least one a year and most do. 
 | Team members attend conferences and trainings and share learnings at work. Teams may attend together.
 - sharing | None, or minimal. | Some team members organize ways to share ideas, learnings, and practice new ways of working. Attendance optional, many team members may not attend. | Team budgets time to share ideas and learnings. Most team members attend. | Team shares openly in day-to-day work and structured activities.

 - retrospectives | None, or irregular. May have ‘post mortem’ after project. | Regular retrospectives often formulaic. Team struggles to complete improvements.  | Regular retrospectives on different topics. Team schedules improvements into iterations. | Frequent & varied retrospectives. Small experiments with measures for success standard.
4.0 | Development Approach | Ad hoc or loose structure. Complex features developed in long-running branches, merged infrequently. Testing done after coding with long defect fix cycles. Overtime common. Team doesn't analyze risks or prioritize work accordingly. | Some structure. Development often done in large batches. Moving towards continuous integration. Basic risk analysis for major changes. New features sliced into smaller chunks. Testing sometimes occurs alongside coding. Team works together and sometimes has a sustainable pace. Some transparency within team and stakeholders. | Focuses on quality and flow. Identifies a thin end-to-end slice for major new changes. Work prioritized based on value to customers and risk analysis. Works cohesively at a sustainable pace. Small production-ready chunks regularly ready for deployment. | Feature development organized and thoughtful. Delivers value frequently using vertical slices / feature flags. May experiment using A/B testing techniques. Risks prioritized and mitigated. Understands and monitors impact of changes on production. These inform adjustment to risk assessments and mitigations, and guide development of features.
 - team makeup | Hand-offs between role-based teams. Adversarial relationships. | Cross-functional team. May still be some adversarial behaviour but more cooperation. | Cross-functional team focuses on flow and collaboration. Works with other teams to understand dependencies and work within constraints. | Cross-functional team flows and delivers with ease.
 - quality mindset | Feature delivery valued over quality. Quality seen as responsibility of testers. | Whole-team-approach to quality accepted. Sometimes still rely on a dedicated “expert” to mitigate risks.
 | Leadership provides guidance, but team makes quality decisions. Focuses on quality and value delivery to customer. | Quality internalized by all team members. Quality top-priority and seen as a velocity-enabler.
 - agile framework practices  | No structured process. | Use prescribed practices as set by methodology followed without really understanding why.  | Team chooses synergistic practices that make sense for them. Practices now habit but adapted as needed. | Experimenting and pushing boundaries to improve ways of doing things.
 - feature and story prioritization | Written requirements come from business analysts or other domain expert. No real priortization. | Working with user stories and prioritizing value. Team members siloed in dev/test/customer roles in discussions. | Works cohesively to understand, slice, and prioritize stories. Discussions of quality, risks, programming and testing needs involve all team member roles. Have added Definition of Ready. | Frequent interaction with customers, stakeholders, external teams to improve understanding, risk analysis, prioritization, and receive feedback.
 - story understanding | Testers sometimes review requirements before coding to help remove ambiguities. | Team members discuss stories to understand customer needs, risks, technical implementation, and testing needs. Loosely worded acceptance criteria for each story, if any. | Whole team guides development with examples. Many stories completed following ATDD/BDD practices. | ATDD / BDD practices followed for applicable stories. Small experiments used to get fast feedback on direction. 
 - Definition of Done (DoD) | None, or not followed. | Definition of done exists. Often has gaps, ignored, or misunderstood. | 'Done' definition followed. Analytics/instrumentation part of Ready/Done definitions. | Team no longer needs a definition to hold to -- what needs to be done now a habit. 
 - release to production | May have a release coordinator to bring release together. Often surprises at release time. Usually gaps in development and testing. | Releasing sometimes every iteration, most teams closer to quarterly. Larger organizations may have release coordinators. | Small production-ready chunks ready for deployment each week, or iteration. Team actively involved with deploy and release to production. | Production-ready small, low-risk changes completed and deployed to production frequently, through progressive rollout or continuous deployment.
5.0 | Quality and Test Ownership | Quality owned by testers or QA. Testing done by QA, focused on verification of new code. Defects blamed on testers. 'Acceptable' levels of quality achieved via testing and defect fixing.  | Programmers start to participate in functional testing, write test frameworks, and add automated regression tests. Testers focus on functional testing, do some other testing activities, pair with programmers, or develop and implement quality strategies. | All team members write tests and value quality. Programmers (or SDETS) automate functional tests, and contribute to testing quality attributes. Testers act as quality advocates and improve quality by influencing other team members. | Quality and customer value considered above all else. Quality 'built-in' from start on all features. Team deeply cares about health of their test suites, architecture, approaches and strategies.

 - quality understanding | Team does not discuss level of quality. QA/Testers responsible for ensuring and adding quality into product. They act as gatekeepers to release. | Team starts to understands quality comes from quality questions, discussions, and testing early, throughout development cycle. Most agree that quality owned by whole team. | Whole team owns quality and acts accordingly. Most members have a good understanding of test landscape, including quality attributes to test. | Team discusses what quality means to their product. Deep understanding of test landscape. Quality attributes a constraint to be considered with every feature and story. 
 - test creation | Tests created and owned by testers. | Functional tests created and maintained by testers and programmers. Testing quality attributes gaining focus, often driven by testers. | Tests owned and maintained by all roles on team, sometimes while pairing. Processes exist to review test code and look for gaps. Team effectively manages risks in test coverage gaps. | Team clearly understands purpose of tests, costs versus value, risks mitigated, and maintenance needs. Whole team contributes.

 - test reviews | No test reviews. | Some review of tests with other testers or product owner. | Tests reviewed by all roles on the team. | Tests mostly created and enhanced in pairing or mobbing situations. Any others promptly peer-reviewed.
 - test execution | Test execution completed by testers. | Some tests automated and monitored by programmers, some by testers. Execution of non-automated tests mostly by testers. | Automated tests run automatically as part of CI & CD processes, owned by all team members. Exploratory testing (ET) mostly done by testers. | Automated tests run as part of CI & CD  and considered living documentation. All team members complete ET testing as per team strategy.
 - test failure followups | Test failures owned and followed up on by testers. | Automated failing tests investigated, not necessarily fixed. Test failures usually followed up by testers.
 | Tests are feedback loops — defects found during testing (automated or human-centric) get fixed. | Tests valued as a feedback loop. Test failures addressed immediately: fix code, fix test, or remove test.
 - data ownership | No ownership of data. No one looking at data consistency. Test data made on the fly by testers. | Team considers quality of data, asks product owner for examples. Mostly owned by testers. | Quality of data put into system analyzed and tested. Test data realistic and available. | Data part of product and treated with respect. 
6.0 | Testing Breadth | Testing done after coding complete (or close to completion). Focus on happy paths and functionality, using time left. Testers may be embedded in a team or in an independent test team. Testing not applied in a strategic way, and only from the viewpoint of testers. Reaction-based response to customer issues. | Testers understand more to testing than functional testing. Starting to discuss test strategies. Testing quality attributes an afterthought. Programmers starting to help with unit tests and automating functional and integration tests. Most testing completed after coding finished, questions may be asked earlier. | Team understands nuances of agile testing quadrants and the types of tests they need to deliver successfully. Strategy in place, although may not be formalized. | Team takes responsibility and accountability for aligning test strategy with wider organizational quality strategy and product value.

 - test strategy | No real test strategy in place. Testers take each requirement and create tests they think necessary. | Test strategy created by testers for a release, may include ideas from others. Starting to use models such as automation test pyramid or testing quadrants to help identify types of tests, and who can help. Likely in document form but trying to make more lightweight. | Test strategy from a holistic point of view, covering quality attributes as well as functional testing. Adapted models to meet their needs keeping to original intent. Testers still own the strategy, but whole team contributes. | Whole delivery team has input into and shares understanding of test strategy. Strategy identifies how testing for a feature will be accomplished, also considers risks. Addresses testing dependencies with other teams. 
 - test techniques | Focus on functional testing and workflows. Use domain specific knowledge like realistic data if experienced. | Testers can use heuristics deliberately. Exploring new ways to test and asking questions earlier in the cycle. May start to think about data and how it will affect testing.  | Risk management a priority in deciding techniques. Team uses a variety of types and techniques applied to their context. | Team plans and uses types and techniques for their context (including a variety of heuristics), to manage risks to release, customer, business, etc.
 - quality attributes | Some testers may have experience testing quality attributes like security testing and may apply their knowledge. No standards, so no consistency. | Testing quality attributes starting to be discussed, planned for, and tested against. Likely focus is security, performance, usability, interoperability. Some may ask questions early. At most 2-3 quality attributes considered. | Not all skills needed to do all the testing for identified attributes available in team, but they take responsibility for completion by specialists. Trying to do quality attribute testing themselves. | Experienced in identifying and working with quality attributes relevant to product and domain. Have enough expertise to plan and testing within their iterations. May pull in external specialists when appropriate.
 - UAT (User Acceptance Testing) | Product delivered to users as a gate to pass before releasing. Users on their own and often create many defects - not all 'real'.  Creates more chaos for the team. | Work with product owner to accept stories. Actual UAT is after code is complete and often a gate to pass before release. | UAT is beginning to occur in parallel with story acceptance, or more likely, feature acceptance. | UAT is fully integrated alongside development, test, and acceptance of stories or features within the team.
 - test coverage and reporting | Coverage based on gut feel. Reporting based on number of tests run or defect counts. | May count test cases, use basic analysis tools for automated tests, or other easy to measure metrics. Coverage hard to articulate or quantify. Testers may know about version control / merge process and add extra testing. Often test in every environment 'just to make sure'. | Test coverage generated by tools augmented with human-centric tools such as mind-maps. Team can articulate how they measure test coverage. Version control and merging not an issue. Well understood so no unneeded testing. | Test coverage taken for granted. Tools generate numbers but built-in processes and checks such as pairing or peer reviewing, ensure good coverage.
7.0 | Code Quality and Technical Debt | No emphasis on code quality. One fix often breaks other things. Inconsistent use of analysis tools. No discussion on technical debt. Much of the code not understood, many afraid to make changes to it. Little or no code documentation. | Code quality starting to be emphasized. Code analysis and coverage starting to be used for test coverage. Check-in gates may use tools to monitor code quality. Documentation for complex areas of code considered.
 | Code coverage used to find test holes and to focus testing needs. Values coverage and analysis tools. Takes time to work on tasks/stories identified as technical debt. All code well understood by at least some team members and they aren't afraid to make changes.  | Coverage and code correctness tools consistently track testing holes and risk areas. Technical debt backlog small, routinely addressed. Communicates with stakeholders on technical debt and business impact. Follows coding standards. Makes good use of design patterns. 
 - unit testing | Two scenarios
1. None, or minimal unit testing
2. Team members who value them create unit tests, but drop during development when pressured to go faster. | Unit tests introduced and completed by some, if not all, programmers. Tests usually reviewed. TDD might be used. Some team members may use pair programming. | Unit testing expected by all programmers. Test-driven development used by most (if not all) programmers for production code and maybe automation code. Often use pair programming. | Code written and maintained using TDD principles, usually with pair programming for immediate feedback loops.
 - code maintenance | Technical debt (code refactoring, fixing analysis errors, etc) addressed infrequently. Maintainability rarely considered. Rarely allocate time for code maintenance; do so only if they cannot continue unless they do.  | Technical debt addressed, but may be an individual effort rather than something the whole team owns. Maintainability of code primarily a reactive effort. | Technical debt levels minimal and tracked with appropriate priority. Maintainability proactive effort. Shared code ownership  practiced and most team members can pick up any code and work on it. | Technical debt addressed continuously; mostly debt-free. Issues found - fixed immediately. Maintenance & support efforts not sacrificed in favour of other activities. Refactoring routine for product code and test automation. Shared code ownership.
 - standards | Code reviews not done or inconsistent. Team not aware of frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc being out of date and possibly unsupported. Coding practices inconsistent, no agreed-upon standard patterns. | Coding standards exist and followed in most cases. Team aware frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc. outdated  and upgrades will be time-consuming and difficult. Team agreed-upon coding patterns and standards, but reviews inconsistent. | Frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc all supported versions; may not be the latest ones. Coding standards and design patterns enforced with peer or code reviews and pair programming. Discuss how to make code testable and maintainable. | Frameworks, tools, third-party libraries, etc recent, supported versions. Keeps up with evolution of technology and ensures their assets follow that evolution. Possibly innovating in their domain.
8.0 | Test Automation and Tools | Few or no automated tests, no way to have continuous feedback of daily changes.
 | Starting automation for functional testing - part of feature development (unit, low-level integration, business rules, API, functional story-level, etc). Integrating with CI when possible. | Automation a priority for all functional and quality attribute tests as part of team test and automation strategies. Tests run as part of CI, and failures addressed immediately. | Automation standard operating procedure. Test failures addressed immediately: fix code, fix test, or remove test. Automation supports human-centric testing and processes as often as possible.
 - automating functional tests | If automation exists, testers automate workflow tests - usually using record-playback. No real understanding about automation. | Automation for functional testing part of feature development (unit, integration, business rules, API, functional story-level, etc). Programmers and testers automate tests traditionally responsible for. | Team members share responsibility for automation of functional and non-functional tests. Automation frequently a pairing activity, using TDD, ATDD, and BDD principles. | Automation standard operating procedure, and shared by all team members.
 - automating quality attribute tests | Testing for quality attributes only happens when something discovered during testing or in production. No automation. | Question prior to coding about risks, tries to test some quality attributes earlier. Separate teams may exist for testing specific quality attributes like security or performance. Automation  owned and run by them after feature complete. | Risks discussed early, and tests identified. Most quality attribute testing at feature level. Delivery team starting to take some ownership for automating and may include instrumentation of the code. | Risks considered while discussing feature capabilities. Tests planned with each story. 'Feature Done' includes testing all identified quality attributes, and automation part of deployment pipeline.
 - unit testing / TDD | Very little unit testing done. Most programmer testing actually debugging. | Unit tests expected and completed by most if not all, programmers. TDD might be used. | Test-driven development practices used for most production code, and maybe automation code. | All code written and maintained using TDD principles.
 - tools | Testing tools usually vendor tools owned by testing team. Version control under programmer control and testers have little-to-no insight. | Testing tools split between team-shared, programmer-focused, or tester-focused. | Testing tools shared and owned by all team members; programmers/testers/customer-facing roles can all use them. | Testing tools shared and owned by all team members.
9.0 | Deployment Pipeline | Test environments unstable. Only programmers understand version control. Team does not practice CI. Long-running feature branches. Team not able to deal with incomplete code being merged.
 | Test and development environments still cause issues and delays for team members. Testers starting to understand and work with version control. Working towards CI, but little integration with other teams.  | Clear strategy for all environments; well maintained - can rely on their operation. Version control used for production and test code. Full CI, integrates with other teams. Uses contract testing (or similiar) to optimize testing without having all dependencies deployed. | Practices Continuous Delivery with releases from green pipeline. Able to release their product multiple times a day if needed. Measures delivery flow for optimization. CD pipeline reviewed to reflect team's testing breadth. Includes all validations required to be release-ready.
 - automation | Release / Deployment process needs human interaction. Very few automated processes. | Some automated tests, including integration in deployment pipeline. Working to complete testing activities in timely manner, for more frequent deploys to production. Trying to use automation to validate it works with rest of product. | Actively manages automated tests suites, deleting old tests, tracking their feedback loop, practicing test escape. Automated tests run as part of CI. | Automated triggers in pipeline stop a deploy if a test fails. Whole team responsible for follow-up. Looks for new ways to shorten feedback cycle. Practice safe ways to test in production.
 - team engagement | Team unaware of frequency of production problems related to their code. Doesn't consider impact on operations or customers, or other parts of the product.
 | Fixing broken builds prioritized over feature development. Test failures fixed as fast as possible, trying never to finish day with failing tests - not always successful. | Team actively involved with deploying & releasing to production. Investigates production problems that could be related to changes they made. Team looks for impact from their changes to other parts of system. | Team understands external dependencies and collaborates with others to address them. Fully embraces the 'you build it, you run it' mindset. 
 - metrics | No quality metrics tracked. Relies on output of department-wide testing activities (e.g. Bug Bashes).   | Some data collected to understand quality, mostly from test activities. May be some from other parts of product lifecycle (e.g. maintenance & support). Data not always used. Instrumentation focused on monitoring for errors. | Quality metrics in place to help understand feature quality and customer experience. Crosses several parts of product lifecycle (maintenance, support, design, etc). Any gaps in interpreting data addressed quickly.  | Tracks performance using metrics such as mean time to recovery (MTTR). Uses variety of relevant metrics to understand quality and customer experience, and to prioritize work. May be following DORA metrics.
 - release strategy | Changes to production infrequent - likely every quarter or every six months, in big chunks. Struggles to get patches for production issues - may go without testing.  | Deploys changes to production regularly - every iteration, or up to 3 months. Feature toggles used mainly to hide uncompleted features. Some usage of progressive rollout. | Small production-ready chunks ready for deployment every iteration (or more often). Actively involved with deploying and releasing to production. Feature toggles consistently used. Progressive rollout for all high-impact code changes to minimize impact on customers. | Practices feature toggle-driven development and progressive rollout for all code changes. Able to safely deploy to production one or more times per day. Uses blue/green environment, canary releases, or releases to a subset of clients to mitigate risk. 
 - observability | No data about customer usage in production. The only data considered for quality purposes comes directly from support / operations. | Starting to instrument code to collect quality telemetry data from production, though often added after feature complete. | Analytics / instrumentation part of the ready / done definition, and almost always done as part of feature development. | Customer data drives decisions about solution development and quality strategy. Quality-related activities monitored and validated. Practices observability - able to ask questions from data sets without pushing new code. Understands  customer pain points/friction.
10.0 | Defect Management | Large backlogs of defects and growing. Defects only fixed if absolutely required. Focus on finding and reporting defects. Limited understanding of why defects occur. Average defect age 6+ months. | Moving towards defect prevention, but focus still on finding defects. Starting to think about cause of defects and to address them. Average defect age 3+ months. | Focus on defect prevention and understanding customer reported defects. Minimal defect backlog - integrated into product backlogs. | Focus on defect prevention. Customer-reported defects  understood and addressed quickly. No defect backlog.
 - defect reporting | All defects reported in defect tracking system. Metrics - number of defects. No standards on how to write defect. | Only defects not fixed right away or those reported by customer entered into the defect tracking system. Metrics: where defects found, how many escape an iteration or story. | Defects in development not fixed immediately put into the product backlog to be addressed next iteration. Only customer-reported defects entered into defect tracking system.  | No defect backlog. Defects reported by customer put into product backlogs.
 - defect fixing | Defects fixed only when necessary, or postponed. Support escalation work a best-effort. | Defects may be fixed if found early, but majority waiting to be triaged. Critical defects related to features released in last 6-9 months addressed. Team may budget time for maintenance and defect fixing. | Defects found - fixed immediately, or as priority in the next iteration. Team has clear view of which maintenance and support issues priority.
 | Defects found - fixed immediately. Externally reported defects prioritized into product backlogs and addressed quickly.
 - defect triage | Defect triage meetings held often to review which defects should be fixed. | One major defect triage meeting held before release to decide upon risks of releasing defects. Most held informally.  | No triage except for defects which may need design changes. | Team able to correlate quality problems with the impact they have on user journeys.

problem: QPAM v7 - Assessment Questions and Guidance
solution:
# QPAM Assessment Questions

Questions and 'What to Look For' guidance for each quality aspect.

QPAM Questions to Ask
Quality Practices | Questions to ask | What to look for | Comments
1.0 | Feedback Loops
 - within the delivery team | What mechanisms do team members use to communicate with each other?  | Think about how different roles in the team communicate (tester, programmer, BA, PO) and others like operations. Is it collaborative and face-to-face? Or is everything written down?  
How does a tester or team member know what is ready for testing?
How do team members share feedback on ideas, designs, practices, processes and other types of work (before coding and testing the code)?
Does the team document the decisions they make?
Does the team have daily standups? | What kind of information is shared?
How long do they run?
Do people find them effective?
How is it facilitated?
How does the team discover and share feedback about the quality of the code? | Do they use code reviews? Pair programming? Mobbing or ensembling?
What code analysis tools are used? When do they use them?
Do they have automated unit tests? Do they run regularly? How often? What do they do with the results?
Do they use test-first practices like TDD?
Are there other automated tests? If so, what are they? How often are they run?
What other types of testing do they complete? How often? Are the results used to adapt?
How is feedback from testing shared amongst team members? | Is testing feedback formal through defect tracking systems and/or written documents, or is it more informal during standups?
Does the team think of tests as a form of feedback?
 - between customers, stakeholders and delivery team | What kinds of interactions does the team have with stakeholders?  What about end users? | Does the team know who their stakeholders are? 
Have they ever talked with end users to understand who they are building for? 
Is everything channelled through the product owner or manager, or is there direct interaction with stakeholders and the team?
What do the team demos look like? Do stakeholders and end users attend? How does feedback get captured?
How does the team learn about customer needs?  | How are customer needs communicated? Directly from the product owner as features and user stories? Or another method?
Do team members learn about customer needs directly from customers? Or do they rely on support or operations for feedback?
Do team members participate in any way in fleshing out the customer's needs?
How do they learn whether they met the needs appropriately? | Does the team employ practices like observability to gather feedback about customer use and engagement?
Do they have customer surveys?
How does the team know the releases are successful? | How do they measure success? 
Do they include anything regarding the actual end users in their measurement of success?
 - between leadership and delivery team | How does the team communicate with line managers and the leadership team? | Is there an informal mechanism for feedback to managers and the leadership team, or is it more formal through the chain of command?
How is new information from leadership passed to the team?
 | Is there transparency? 
Does the delivery team understand how the features they work on support organizational goals?
How does leadership get the information it needs to make decisions? | Does it rely wholly on reports, or is there some verbal interaction

 - release strategy | How often do they deploy the product to production? | Are they practicing continuous delivery or continuous deployment?
How often do they release to their customers?
Do they have some method of testing in production safely, such as feature flags?
How is the build deployed to each development and test environment? | Are all deployments automated, or is there a mixture of automation and human intervention? 
In the case of human-based deployments, who is responsible? What does it take to deploy? Are there wait times?
How does the team know when testing is complete in each test environment or deployment pipeline stage? | Is it an automated process, or manual?
How are they alerted about test or pipeline stage failures?
How long does it take the team to respond to a pipeline stage failure?
Who supports the deployment pipeline? | Is there a platform team who builds and maintains, or does the development team(s) do it all themselves?
Who does the final release to production? What does that look like? | Is there a separate release team that decides when it's ready to go? Or is there a continuous delivery and deployment strategy?
Do they use an implementation checklist?
Do they feel confident to release on a Friday?
How does the team manage production issues? | Is there a different process for emergency fixes?
Can the team roll back easily or get the fix out very quickly?
Does a production issue cause a major disruption in work?
How quickly can they identify and diagnose a production issue?
Is there a customer support group that is involved in resolving issues? | How does the team handle that?
 - observability | Does the team instrument their code to capture all data needed to monitor system health, detect anomalies, provide alerts, and investigate unexpected issues?   | Who looks at the warnings and errors? Is it only operations, or does the delivery team have access? Or is it a shared responsibility?
Do the testers query log data and watch monitoring dashboards while testing for errors and warnings?
How does the team know what parts of the application the customers use? | What telemetry do they add for analytics?
Who looks at the data if they have any? Is it fed back to the team?
Can they tell the system’s health from the data they collect?
What does the data tell them about their product quality? 
What does the data tell them about the customer experience?  | For example, do some customers have to wait a long time to load images?
10.0 | Defect management
 - defect reporting | How are defects found within the iteration or in a story managed?  | Are they logging them all, fixing them all, or triaging for later? Is communication handled entirely through the defect tracking system?
Do developers and testers pair on defects? Either to show or to fix?
Is what they do consistent across teams, or does every team manage them differently?
Do they handle some defects one way and others another way?
Do individual testers handle them differently?
Does the team recognize that they are catching potential defects during discovery, discussions, prototyping or other early testing mechanisms?
How are defects found later in the cycle, perhaps in staging, handled? | Do they handle these differently?
How are defects found in production managed/tracked? | What is the process? How does it integrate with the team?
Do they do a root cause analysis to see if they could have done something different to avoid that type of bug in the future?
 - defect fixing | How does the team determine what defects to fix? (and when)? | Who makes the decision?
How long does it take to get into the flow to fix?
How does it get into the flow?
Do distinct types of defects get handled differently? For example, production defects versus defects found within a story. | Does the team revisit the initial story? Or try to make a workaround?
What happens when the defect highlights a bigger problem – perhaps in the design or understanding of the original story?

Are they used for blaming or for learning?
Does anyone beyond the reporter look at them?
How many open defects are there against your product?  | If more than ten, how does the team plan to address the backlog? 
How old are the defects? Are there any open for more than six months or a year?
Do they go into the defect database to die? 
Do they have a plan to reduce the number of open defects? 
Do they see the number of defects (if they have lots) as a problem?
Do they differentiate between priorities (critical versus minor)? 
Have they been gaming the system, for example, changing severity from critical to high because there is a workaround?
When was the last time the open defects were triaged? | What did they do about the triage?
How was it handled?
Was it productive?
